vce-psych12-approaches-to-understanding-: psych12a1-appr-1

Roger Sperry's split-brain research involved participants whose corpus callosum had been surgically cut. When an object was flashed to the left visual field only, these participants typically could not
point to the object with their left hand
verbally name the object
see anything in the left visual field
recognise the object by touch with the left hand

Information from the left visual field goes to the right hemisphere, and language production is usually lateralised to the left hemisphere. With the corpus callosum cut, the information cannot reach the left hemisphere, so the person cannot name it, though the left hand (right hemisphere) can still select it.
psych12a1-appr-2
Which neuroimaging technique detects changes in blood oxygen levels to show which brain regions are active during a task, and has relatively good spatial resolution?
Computed tomography (CT)
Lesion analysis
Electroencephalography (EEG)
Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)

fMRI measures the blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signal and gives good spatial resolution. EEG measures electrical activity at the scalp with excellent temporal but poor spatial resolution; CT shows structure only.
psych12a1-appr-3
A researcher records electrical activity at the scalp while participants listen to tones, looking at changes over milliseconds. The main strength of this technique is its
high spatial resolution of deep brain structures
ability to show the brain's anatomy in detail
high temporal resolution
use of a radioactive tracer
EEG has high temporal resolution (milliseconds) but poor spatial resolution. Detailed anatomy is the strength of CT or MRI, and radioactive tracers are used in PET.
psych12a1-appr-4
Phineas Gage survived an accident in which an iron rod passed through his frontal lobe. Reports of personality change after the accident are best described as
a longitudinal study using fMRI
an experiment with a control group
a case study that suggested a link between the frontal lobe and personality
a double-blind trial of a brain stimulation technique

Gage is a classic case study, which provides rich detail on one individual but limits generalisation. It suggested the frontal lobe is involved in personality and social behaviour; it was not an experiment.
psych12a1-appr-5
Which of the following is a limitation of using case studies of brain damage to understand brain function?
They can never be ethically conducted
Findings may not generalise because the damage is unique to each individual
They always use large random samples
They cannot provide detailed information
Each injury differs in location, extent and the person's prior history, so results from one case may not generalise. Case studies do provide detailed, in-depth information.
psych12a1-appr-6
Explain one similarity and one difference between fMRI and EEG as techniques used to study the brain. (3 marks)

Similarity: both are non-invasive (do not require surgery) and can be used with healthy participants to study brain activity during tasks (1); Difference: fMRI has high spatial resolution because it detects blood oxygen changes in specific regions, whereas EEG has poor spatial resolution (1); EEG has high temporal resolution (milliseconds) whereas fMRI has lower temporal resolution because blood flow changes are slower (1).
psych12a1-appr-7

In a study, a participant with a surgically severed corpus callosum is shown the word KEY in their right visual field and the word RING in their left visual field. (a) State what the participant would say they saw. (b) Explain why. (3 marks)

(a) The participant would say they saw 'key' (1); (b) The right visual field is processed by the left hemisphere, which controls speech, so the word 'key' can be named (1); the left visual field is processed by the right hemisphere, which lacks language production, and the corpus callosum cannot transfer the information so 'ring' cannot be verbalised (1).
psych12a1-appr-8

A researcher wants to find which brain areas are most active when a person solves a maths problem. Identify an appropriate technique, and justify your choice with reference to one strength and one limitation. (3 marks)

Technique: fMRI (or PET) (1); Strength: shows which specific regions have increased blood flow/oxygen use during the task, with good spatial resolution (1); Limitation: expensive, participant must lie still in a scanner, and poor temporal resolution so it cannot show rapid changes (1). Accept a justified alternative such as EEG if its strength and limitation are correct.
psych12a1-appr-9
Paul Broca's patient 'Tan' could understand speech well but could produce only the one word 'tan'. After the patient's death, post-mortem examination found damage to which region?
the left frontal lobe
the right temporal lobe
the left occipital lobe
the cerebellum

Tan's damage was in the left frontal region linked to speech production, while understanding was relatively preserved. Right temporal damage is not the typical cause of this pattern, and the occipital lobe and cerebellum are not associated with fluent speech.
psych12a1-appr-10
A limitation of lesion analysis in human patients with brain damage is that
the damage cannot be seen on any scan
the results always contradict those from animal studies
researchers cannot control the location or extent of the damage
participants cannot give informed consent

Damage from stroke or injury occurs naturally, so researchers cannot choose its location or size, and it may spread across several regions. Damage can usually be seen on CT or MRI, and the other options are not general features of lesion analysis.
psych12a1-appr-11
A patient arrives at an emergency department with a sudden severe headache and possible bleeding in the brain. Which technique is most appropriate for a quick check of the bleed?
electroencephalography (EEG)
functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)
positron emission tomography (PET)
computed tomography (CT)

CT is fast and readily shows bleeding and skull fractures, which makes it suited to emergencies. EEG and fMRI measure activity rather than giving a quick structural picture, and PET is slower and requires a radioactive tracer.
psych12a1-appr-12
Positron emission tomography (PET) produces images by detecting
changes in blood oxygen levels in the brain
the uptake of a radioactive tracer that indicates metabolic activity
electrical signals from the scalp
the absorption of X-rays passing through the head

PET tracks a radioactive tracer, such as a glucose analogue, to show where metabolic activity is high. Blood oxygen changes describe fMRI, scalp electrical signals describe EEG, and X-ray absorption describes CT.
psych12a1-appr-13
Compared with CT, structural MRI has the advantage that it
gives more detailed soft-tissue images without ionising radiation
is cheaper and faster to perform
measures electrical activity in neurons
uses a radioactive tracer to show blood flow

MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves, so it avoids ionising radiation and shows soft tissue in more detail than CT. MRI is generally slower and more costly than CT, while electrical activity and radioactive tracers belong to EEG and PET.
psych12a1-appr-14
In fMRI studies, researchers often subtract the brain activity recorded during a control task from that recorded during an experimental task. The purpose of this is to
remove the need for a control group
increase the temporal resolution of the scan
isolate activity linked to the cognitive process of interest
measure electrical activity that the BOLD signal cannot show

Both tasks share general visual and motor demands, so subtraction leaves activity specific to the process being studied. Subtraction does not change temporal resolution, which remains limited by the slow BOLD response.
psych12a1-appr-15
A split-brain participant holds a familiar object in their right hand, out of sight, and can usually say what it is. This is because
the corpus callosum carries touch information from the right hand to the right hemisphere
touch is processed equally by both hemispheres
the right hand is controlled by the right hemisphere, which can name objects
touch from the right hand is processed by the left hemisphere, which controls speech

Touch from each hand is sent to the opposite hemisphere, so input from the right hand reaches the left hemisphere, where language is usually produced. This input does not need to cross the corpus callosum, so it can be named.
psych12a1-appr-16
Lateralisation of brain function refers to the idea that
each hemisphere performs identical functions
some functions are mainly controlled by one hemisphere rather than the other
functions are spread evenly across the whole cortex
the lateral (outer) areas of the brain control all sensory input
Lateralisation describes specialised functions, such as language production in the left hemisphere for most people. The other options describe equal distribution of function or misread the term.
psych12a1-appr-17
A researcher lesions the hippocampus of some rats and leaves others intact, then compares maze performance between the two groups. This is best described as
a correlational study, because brain structure and behaviour are measured
a case study, because individual rats are studied in depth
an experiment, because the researcher manipulates the lesion (the independent variable)
a longitudinal study, because the rats are observed over time

The researcher controls which rats receive the lesion and compares them with a control group, which defines an experiment. Correlational designs measure existing variables without manipulating them, and this study compares groups rather than in-depth single cases.
psych12a1-appr-18
Before an MRI scan, people with metal implants (such as some surgical devices) are screened because the strong magnetic field can
absorb X-rays and hide the brain's structure
move or heat metal objects in the body
block the radio waves needed to make an image
expose the person to ionising radiation
The strong magnet can pull on ferromagnetic implants and heat some metals, creating a serious safety risk. MRI does not use X-rays or ionising radiation, and absorbing X-rays describes CT.
psych12a1-appr-19
The electrical signals recorded by EEG mainly reflect
the firing of single neurons in the brainstem
changes in blood flow to deep brain structures
the synchronised activity of large groups of cortical neurons
the decay of a radioactive tracer

EEG electrodes on the scalp detect summed activity from large populations of cortical neurons firing together. Single deep neurons are too far from the scalp to be recorded, and blood flow and tracer decay are measured by fMRI and PET.
psych12a1-appr-20
A key limitation of animal lesion studies is that
results may not generalise to humans because of species differences in brain structure and function
the lesions can never be precisely placed
they cannot provide any information about brain function
they are always conducted without ethical approval

Animal lesion studies allow controlled placement of damage, but the brains of rats or monkeys differ from the human brain, so findings must be applied to humans cautiously. Lesions in animals can often be placed precisely, and these studies do yield information about brain function.
psych12a1-appr-21
Which of the following is an example of a naturally occurring lesion used in case study research?
an electrode placed deliberately in the visual cortex of a rat
a surgeon's removal of the hippocampus to test memory
a deliberate electrical lesion made in a rat's cortex
a stroke that damages the left frontal lobe

Strokes, injuries and disease produce damage without researchers' intervention, which is what makes them natural lesions studied in case studies. Deliberate surgical or electrical lesions are made by researchers for experimental purposes.
psych12a1-appr-22
The BOLD signal measured in fMRI is best described as
a direct record of electrical firing from individual neurons
an indirect measure of neural activity, based on changes in oxygenated blood flow
a measure of the amount of radioactive glucose used by cells
an image of the brain's structure showing fibre pathways

Active neurons increase demand for oxygen, and the local blood flow response changes the ratio of oxygenated to deoxygenated haemoglobin, which fMRI detects. The other options describe EEG, PET and structural imaging respectively.
psych12a1-appr-23
Many fMRI studies use small samples. The main practical reason for this is that
the BOLD signal can only be detected in very small numbers of people
ethics committees set a standard limit of ten participants
scanning is expensive and time-consuming, which limits the number of participants
participants cannot be scanned more than once

fMRI equipment is costly and each session takes time, so sample sizes are often limited for practical reasons. There is no standard ethical limit of ten participants, and fMRI participants can often be scanned repeatedly, which is a strength over PET.
psych12a1-appr-24
In a healthy brain, the main role of the corpus callosum is to
transfer information between the two cerebral hemispheres
control the body's voluntary movements directly
store long-term memories in the frontal lobe
send visual information from the eyes to the occipital lobe

The corpus callosum is a large bundle of nerve fibres connecting the two hemispheres, so it lets them share information. The other options describe the motor cortex, memory systems and visual pathways rather than this structure.
psych12a1-appr-25
Describe the difference between a case study and an experiment as approaches to understanding the brain. (2 marks)

Case study: an in-depth investigation of one person or a small group with naturally occurring brain damage or a condition, in which the researcher does not manipulate variables [1]; Experiment: the researcher manipulates an independent variable under controlled conditions, usually with a control group, to establish cause and effect [1].
psych12a1-appr-26
Identify one ethical consideration when researching people with brain damage, and explain why it is important. (2 marks)

Informed consent: participants, or a legally recognised substitute if their capacity is impaired, must understand and agree to take part [1]; this is important because people with brain injuries may have reduced ability to make decisions, so their rights must be protected [1].
psych12a1-appr-27

A researcher wants to (a) find which brain areas are active while participants complete a memory task, and (b) check participants for structural abnormalities before the study. For each purpose, recommend a suitable technique and justify your choice. (4 marks)

(a) fMRI [1], as it detects changes in blood oxygenation that indicate which regions are active during the task, with good spatial resolution [1]; (b) MRI (or CT) [1], as it shows the brain's structure in detail so abnormalities can be identified, and MRI does not use ionising radiation [1].
psych12a1-appr-28
Name the neuroimaging technique that builds cross-sectional images of the brain from X-rays taken at many angles. (1 mark)
Computed tomography (CT) [1].
psych12a1-appr-29
Penfield used electrical stimulation of the cortex during surgery. Outline how this technique was used to identify brain function, and state one limitation of the approach. (2 marks)

Stimulating a specific area and recording the movement or sensation the patient reported links that area to a function [1]; limitation: it is only possible in the small number of patients undergoing surgery, so the sample is limited and may not be representative [1].
psych12a1-appr-30
A neuroimaging study finds that a region is more active when participants perform a task. Explain why this finding does not, on its own, show that the region is necessary for the task. (2 marks)

The finding is correlational: it shows an association between activity and the task, not cause and effect [1]; the activity could be incidental or a consequence of the task, so evidence such as lesions or stimulation is needed to show necessity [1].
psych12a1-appr-31
State one advantage of fMRI over PET for researching the same participant on several occasions. (1 mark)
fMRI does not use a radioactive tracer, so the participant is not exposed to radiation and can be scanned repeatedly [1].
psych12a1-appr-32

The case of patient H.M., who had his hippocampus removed, suggested a role for the hippocampus in memory. Describe what this case showed, and state one limitation of drawing this conclusion. (2 marks)

After removal of the hippocampus, H.M. could not form new long-term (declarative) memories, suggesting the hippocampus is needed for memory formation [1]; limitation: this is a single case, and the surgical damage extended beyond the hippocampus, so the conclusion may not generalise [1].
psych12a1-appr-33
Explain the difference between structural and functional brain imaging techniques, giving one example of each. (3 marks)

Structural techniques show the anatomy of the brain, such as CT or MRI [1]; functional techniques show activity or processes in the brain, such as fMRI or PET [1]; functional techniques are used to link regions to tasks, whereas structural techniques are used to identify damage or abnormalities [1].
psych12a1-appr-34
Evaluate the use of case studies of brain damage as an approach to understanding brain function. In your answer, refer to one strength and one limitation. (4 marks)

Strength: case studies provide detailed, in-depth information about the effects of specific injuries, which may be rare and cannot be deliberately produced in humans [1]; they can suggest hypotheses about the role of particular regions [1]; limitation: each injury differs in location, extent and the person's prior functioning, so findings may not generalise [1]; the researcher cannot control the damage, so cause and effect cannot be firmly established [1].
psych12a1-appr-35

A researcher chooses EEG rather than fMRI to study brain activity in children in a school classroom, because the equipment is portable and does not require a scanner. Which limitation of EEG must the researcher accept?
It cannot record any electrical activity from the cortex
It has poor spatial resolution, so the source of activity is hard to locate precisely
It requires the injection of a radioactive tracer
It needs the participant to lie inside a large magnet for each recording

EEG records electrical activity from the scalp, which gives excellent timing but makes it difficult to locate where the activity originates. EEG does record cortical activity and needs no tracer, as tracers are used in PET, and the magnet option describes MRI rather than EEG.
psych12a1-appr-36

A researcher proposes to create small lesions in the memory areas of healthy adult volunteers to see how their memory changes. Which is the most important reason an ethics committee would reject this proposal?
The sample of volunteers would be too small to generalise
Lesions cannot be seen on any scan
The lesions would cause permanent, unnecessary harm to people who gain no benefit from the study
Memory cannot be measured accurately in adults

Deliberately causing permanent brain damage in healthy people breaches the ethical principle of avoiding harm, because participants gain no therapeutic benefit. Lesions can be detected on scans and memory can be measured in adults, while sample size is a methodological concern rather than the deciding ethical issue.
psych12a1-appr-37
Researchers report that an fMRI finding about a memory task came from only 12 participants. Why would other researchers want the study repeated with a larger, independent sample?
To check whether the finding is reliable and can be reproduced, rather than a chance result from a small sample
To prove that the memory task caused the brain activity
To allow the use of a radioactive tracer in the next study
Because larger samples always show a larger brain

Replication with a larger, independent sample tests whether a result holds up and is not an artefact of chance or a small group. Replication does not by itself prove causation, tracer use is a feature of PET, and sample size does not change the size of the brain.
psych12a1-appr-38
Compare the spatial and temporal resolution of CT and EEG. (3 marks)

CT has good spatial resolution and shows the brain's structure in detail [1]; CT produces a static image and has poor temporal resolution, so it cannot track changes over time [1]; EEG has good temporal resolution, recording changes within milliseconds, but poor spatial resolution [1]
psych12a1-appr-39
Outline the purpose of a control group in a study that lesions the hippocampus of some rats. (2 marks)

The control group receives no lesion (or a sham operation) and shows normal performance, providing a baseline for comparison [1]; any difference between the groups can then be attributed to the lesion rather than to other factors [1]
vce-psych12-ab-c1
A researcher wants to see which brain areas become most active while participants solve a memory task. The best technique is:
CT, because it shows bone and tissue structure
Structural MRI, because it gives detailed images of brain anatomy
fMRI, because it detects changes in blood oxygen linked to neural activity
Phrenology, because it measures bumps on the skull
Functional techniques (fMRI, PET) show activity; structural techniques (CT, MRI) show anatomy. Phrenology has no scientific support.
vce-psych12-structure-and-function-of-th: After a stroke, a man can understand speech but his speech is slow, effortful and poorly formed. Damage is most likely to the
Broca's area, in the left frontal lobe, is involved in speech production. Damage to Wernicke's area typically results in fluent but meaningless speech and poor comprehension.
Which structure of the limbic system is mainly involved in forming new explicit memories?
The hippocampus is critical for forming new explicit (declarative) memories. The amygdala is associated with emotional responses such as fear and with emotional memories.
The primary somatosensory cortex is located in the
The primary somatosensory cortex receives touch, temperature and pain information and lies in the parietal lobe. The primary motor cortex is in the frontal lobe.
A cyclist has a head injury and afterwards has difficulty with balance and coordinating smooth movements, although her thinking and memory are normal. Which structure is most likely damaged?
The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement, balance and posture. Prefrontal cortex damage would be expected to affect planning and decision-making.
Which statement about the two cerebral hemispheres is correct?
Only the right hemisphere is involved in language in most people
The left hemisphere controls the left side of the body
The hemispheres cannot communicate with each other
The corpus callosum is a bundle of fibres that connects the hemispheres

The corpus callosum allows communication between the hemispheres. Each hemisphere mainly controls the contralateral (opposite) side of the body, and language is usually lateralised to the left hemisphere.

A person is injured in an accident and afterwards cannot recognise familiar faces although their vision is intact, and they feel less fear in dangerous situations. Identify two brain structures that may have been affected and the function of each. (4 marks)

Accept two well-justified structures, e.g. temporal lobe (involved in recognising faces/auditory and object recognition) (1+1); amygdala (processes fear and emotional responses, so reduced fear suggests damage) (1+1). Each structure named (1) and linked to its function (1).
Describe the role of the frontal lobe, and give one example of how damage to the prefrontal cortex could change a person's behaviour. (3 marks)

Frontal lobe: involved in voluntary movement (motor cortex), planning, decision-making, reasoning, judgement and personality (1-2); Example: damage to the prefrontal cortex may lead to impulsive behaviour, poor judgement or changes in personality/emotional regulation (1).
Distinguish between the hippocampus and the amygdala in terms of their functions. (2 marks)

Hippocampus: forms new explicit/declarative memories and is involved in spatial memory (1); Amygdala: processes emotions, especially fear and aggression, and adds emotional significance to memories (1).
The primary visual cortex, which receives information from the eyes, is located in the
The primary visual cortex sits in the occipital lobe at the back of the brain. The temporal lobe is mainly associated with hearing and object recognition, so it is a tempting but incorrect choice.
The primary auditory cortex, which processes sound information from the ears, is located in the
The primary auditory cortex lies in the temporal lobe, on the side of the brain above the ears. The occipital lobe is the visual area, so choosing it confuses hearing with vision.
Which brain structure, at the base of the brainstem, controls automatic functions such as heart rate and breathing?

The medulla oblongata regulates vital automatic functions such as heart rate and breathing. The cerebellum controls balance and coordination, so it is a common confusion because it is also found towards the back of the brain.
Sensory information from the eyes, ears, skin and body (other than smell) is relayed to the cerebral cortex by which structure?

The thalamus acts as a relay station, directing sensory signals to the appropriate areas of the cortex. The hypothalamus regulates hunger, thirst and body temperature, so it is a tempting but incorrect choice.
Which structure, located below the thalamus, regulates body temperature, hunger and thirst?

The hypothalamus sits below the thalamus and maintains homeostasis by regulating hunger, thirst and body temperature. The amygdala is involved in fear and emotion, so it is a tempting but incorrect choice.
A woman with damage to the right parietal lobe tends to ignore objects on her left side, even though her vision is normal. Which function is most affected?
Recognition of the meaning of spoken words
Awareness of space and of the positions of objects around the body
Control of heart rate and breathing

The parietal lobe integrates sensory information to represent space, and right parietal damage often leads to neglect of the left side. Understanding spoken words is linked to Wernicke's area rather than spatial awareness.
Why is the surface of the cerebral cortex folded into ridges and grooves?
It separates the brain into the four lobes
It increases the number of cerebral hemispheres
It increases the surface area available for neurons
Folding packs a large area of neural tissue into the limited space of the skull, so more neurons fit. Folding does not change the number of hemispheres, which is always two.
Which hemisphere is generally more involved in visual-spatial processing, such as judging the layout of a room?
Both hemispheres equally in all people
In most people the right hemisphere is more involved in visual-spatial processing. The left hemisphere is usually dominant for language, so choosing it confuses spatial and language functions.
Which of the following is NOT part of the limbic system?
The medulla is part of the brainstem, not the limbic system, which includes the amygdala, hippocampus and hypothalamus. Each of the other three options is a limbic structure.
Which structure, although only about a tenth of the brain's volume, contains the majority of the brain's neurons?
The cerebellum is small compared with the cerebrum but packs in the majority of the brain's neurons. The cerebral cortex is far larger in volume but contains fewer neurons.
Which structure controls the pituitary gland, which releases hormones into the bloodstream?
The hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland, which in turn regulates hormone release. The hippocampus and amygdala are limbic structures involved in memory and emotion rather than hormone control.
After a stroke, a woman loses vision in the right half of her visual field in both eyes. Which area is most likely damaged?
The left primary visual cortex processes information from the right visual field, so damage there causes loss of right-side vision. Right occipital damage would affect the left visual field instead.
How many lobes does each cerebral hemisphere contain?
Each cerebral hemisphere has four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital. Choosing three is a common mistake that overlooks one of these lobes.
Which group of structures forms the link between the spinal cord and the rest of the brain?

The brainstem, which includes the medulla, pons and midbrain, connects the spinal cord to higher brain structures. The limbic system is involved in emotion and memory, and the corpus callosum connects the two cerebral hemispheres.
The corpus callosum is made up mainly of which type of tissue?

The corpus callosum is a bundle of myelinated axons, which is white matter. Grey matter, made of cell bodies and dendrites, is found mainly in the cortex, so choosing it confuses the two tissue types.
In which lobe of the cerebrum is the hippocampus located?

The hippocampus sits deep within the temporal lobe, close to the amygdala. The frontal lobe, at the front of the brain, is mainly involved in movement, planning and decision-making, so it is a common confusion.
Electrical stimulation of the primary visual cortex during brain surgery would most likely produce which experience?
A sensation of touch on the hand
A ringing sound in one ear

Stimulating the primary visual cortex typically produces visual sensations such as flashes of light, because that is where visual signals are processed. Stimulating the somatosensory cortex would produce touch sensations rather than light.
Which groove separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe?

The central sulcus separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe, with the primary motor cortex lying just in front of it. The longitudinal fissure divides the two hemispheres rather than the lobes, so it is a common mix-up.
The primary motor cortex has a much larger area devoted to the fingers and lips than to the back and legs. What does this suggest about the function of the motor cortex? (1 mark)
Body parts requiring fine, precise movement have a larger representation in the motor cortex [1]
Name the lobe of the cerebral cortex in which Wernicke's area is located. (1 mark)
A stroke damages the right primary motor cortex. Explain why the weakness is seen on the left side of the body. (2 marks)

Motor pathways cross over in the lower brainstem, so each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body [1]; the right motor cortex therefore controls the left side of the body, so the left side is weakened [1]
Explain how the cerebellum contributes to learning a skill such as riding a bicycle. (2 marks)
The cerebellum fine-tunes movement, coordinating timing and balance as the skill is practised [1]; with repetition, movements become smoother and more automatic [1]
Explain how the hypothalamus contributes to regulating the sleep-wake cycle. (2 marks)

The hypothalamus contains a group of cells (the suprachiasmatic nucleus) that acts as the body's internal clock [1]; it uses light signals from the eyes to regulate daily rhythms of sleepiness and alertness [1]
A person has damage to their left temporal lobe. Explain why they can still hear sounds in both ears. (2 marks)
Auditory pathways are bilateral, so each ear sends signals to both auditory cortices [1]; the right temporal lobe, which is undamaged, still receives input from both ears [1]

A patient whose corpus callosum has been surgically cut is shown the word 'key' only in their left visual field. Describe what they can do with their left hand and what they are unable to say, and explain why. (3 marks)

The left visual field is processed by the right hemisphere [1]; the right hemisphere controls the left hand, so the patient can point to or pick up a key with the left hand [1]; the patient cannot say 'key' aloud because the information cannot cross the severed corpus callosum to the left hemisphere's language areas [1]

Research on London taxi drivers, who must memorise the city's streets, found that their hippocampus was larger than that of comparison participants. Explain what this suggests about the hippocampus. (3 marks)

The hippocampus is involved in spatial memory and navigation [1]; the larger hippocampus suggests that learning and storing detailed spatial maps is associated with changes in its structure [1]; the study is correlational, so it cannot prove that the training caused the enlargement [1]
Explain how myelin increases the speed of messages travelling through the white matter of the brain. (3 marks)

Myelin is a fatty insulating sheath that wraps around axons [1]; it allows the electrical impulse to jump between gaps in the sheath, which is faster than travelling along the whole axon [1]; so messages travel more quickly between brain regions [1]

A patient has damage to the medulla oblongata and to the cerebellum. Describe one function affected by each structure, and explain why damage to the medulla is more likely to be life-threatening. (4 marks)

Medulla oblongata: controls automatic functions such as breathing and heart rate [1]; Cerebellum: coordinates balance and smooth voluntary movement [1]; Damage to the medulla can disrupt breathing and heart rate, which are essential for survival [1]; Cerebellum damage affects coordination but does not directly control vital functions, so it is less immediately life-threatening [1]
Describe how the amygdala and the prefrontal cortex interact when a person perceives a threat, and explain how this interaction can help regulate fear. (4 marks)

The amygdala detects the threat and triggers a rapid fear response [1]; it sends signals that produce physiological arousal and an immediate reaction [1]; the prefrontal cortex evaluates the situation and sends regulatory signals that can dampen the amygdala's response [1]; this allows the person to respond to the threat in a controlled rather than impulsive way [1]
Name each of the four lobes of the cerebral cortex and give one function of each. (4 marks)

Frontal lobe: voluntary movement, planning and decision-making [1]; Parietal lobe: processing touch, pain and temperature [1]; Temporal lobe: auditory processing and object recognition [1]; Occipital lobe: visual processing [1]
Which brainstem structure acts as a bridge that relays signals between the cerebral cortex and the cerebellum?

The pons lies between the medulla and midbrain and carries signals between the cerebral cortex and the cerebellum. The medulla controls breathing and heart rate, the midbrain is involved in visual and auditory reflexes, and the amygdala is a limbic structure rather than part of the brainstem.
Damage to Wernicke's area (usually in the left temporal lobe) would most likely cause:
Slow, effortful speech with good understanding of what others say
Fluent speech that makes little sense, and poor understanding of language
Loss of vision in both eyes, although language remains unaffected
Loss of balance and coordination when walking or reaching
Wernicke's area is linked to language comprehension. Broca's area (frontal lobe) is linked to speech production; the cerebellum to coordination.
vce-psych12-neuroplasticity-and-adolesce: psych12a1-neur-1
Synaptic pruning during adolescence refers to
the elimination of weaker, rarely used synaptic connections
the production of myelin around all axons
the strengthening of connections through repeated use
the growth of new neurons in the hippocampus
Pruning removes less-used synapses to make neural networks more efficient. Strengthening through repeated use is long-term potentiation, and myelination is a separate process.
psych12a1-neur-2
Long-term potentiation (LTP) is best described as
the formation of the myelin sheath
a long-lasting strengthening of synaptic connections after repeated stimulation
the loss of neurons after injury
a weakening of synapses due to lack of stimulation
LTP is the long-lasting increase in synaptic strength that follows repeated activation, underlying learning and memory. The weakening of synapses with disuse is long-term depression (LTD).
psych12a1-neur-3
Compared with adults, the adolescent brain typically shows
a prefrontal cortex that is still developing, with the limbic system relatively more active
no neuroplasticity
no synaptic pruning
a fully developed prefrontal cortex

The prefrontal cortex (planning, impulse control) continues developing into the mid-20s, while the limbic system matures earlier. This helps explain greater risk-taking and emotional reactivity in adolescence.
psych12a1-neur-4
A woman loses function in her left arm after a stroke damages part of her motor cortex. Over months of rehabilitation, a nearby undamaged region begins to control the arm. This is an example of
adaptive plasticity involving rerouting
a reflex response
synaptic pruning
long-term depression

Adaptive plasticity after injury can involve rerouting, where neural connections are redirected around damaged areas, and sprouting of new connections. Pruning removes unused synapses and LTD weakens them.
psych12a1-neur-5
Which of the following best describes sprouting?
Neurons forming new dendrites and synaptic connections
Elimination of unused neural pathways
A decrease in the strength of a synapse
Loss of the myelin sheath
Sprouting is the growth of new nerve endings and synaptic connections. Elimination of unused connections is pruning; weakening of synapses is LTD.
psych12a1-neur-6
Explain how neuroplasticity contributes to a person learning to play a new musical instrument. (3 marks)

Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to change its structure and function in response to experience (1); repeated practice repeatedly activates the same neural pathways, strengthening synaptic connections through long-term potentiation (1); new synaptic connections may form (sprouting) while unused connections weaken or are pruned, making the neural network more efficient so skills improve (1).
psych12a1-neur-7
Describe two changes in the brain during adolescence and explain how one of them may be linked to risk-taking behaviour. (3 marks)

Changes (any two): synaptic pruning of unused connections; myelination increasing the speed of neural transmission; ongoing development of the prefrontal cortex; limbic system maturing earlier (1 for two changes identified); Link: the prefrontal cortex, responsible for judgement and impulse control, is still developing while the limbic system (reward and emotion) is highly active, so adolescents may be more prone to risk-taking (2).
psych12a1-neur-8
Distinguish between long-term potentiation and long-term depression. (2 marks)

LTP: long-lasting strengthening of synapses after frequent/repeated stimulation, making transmission more efficient (1); LTD: long-lasting weakening of synaptic connections after infrequent or low stimulation, which can lead to the connection being pruned (1).
psych12a1-neur-9
Neuroplasticity refers to the brain's ability to
change its structure and function in response to experience
remain the same size whatever a person experiences
replace damaged neurons within days of an injury
keep its neural connections fixed once childhood ends

Neuroplasticity is the capacity of the brain to reorganise its structure and function in response to learning, experience and injury. The idea that connections are fixed after childhood is outdated, and the brain does not rapidly replace large numbers of lost neurons.
psych12a1-neur-10
Myelination during adolescence mainly leads to
a reduction in the total number of synapses across the brain
faster transmission of nerve impulses along axons
the birth of new neurons in the cerebral cortex
a permanent weakening of rarely used synapses

Myelin is a fatty sheath around axons that speeds up the transmission of nerve impulses, and myelination continues into early adulthood. The reduction in synapses is caused by pruning, while most cortical neurons are generated before birth.
psych12a1-neur-11
In a study of licensed London taxi drivers, researchers found a larger posterior hippocampus than in matched non-drivers. The most appropriate conclusion is that
the hippocampus is fixed in size and cannot be changed by experience
the hippocampus controls the hand movements used when driving
long-term, intensive spatial navigation is associated with structural change in the hippocampus
drivers have fewer neurons than non-drivers in every brain region

The finding shows an association between extensive navigation experience and hippocampal structure, which supports experience-driven plasticity. It does not prove cause and effect on its own, and it does not show that the hippocampus controls movement.
psych12a1-neur-12
People who have been blind since early childhood sometimes show activity in the visual cortex when reading Braille by touch. This best illustrates
a fixed, innate function of the visual cortex that cannot change
a reflex response in which touch automatically triggers vision
the loss of myelin in the somatosensory cortex
cross-modal reorganisation in response to altered sensory experience

The visual cortex, normally used for sight, is recruited for touch when vision is absent, which shows plasticity in response to altered experience. A reflex is an automatic, rapid response that does not involve this kind of cortical reorganisation, and myelin loss would not explain the recruitment.
psych12a1-neur-13
The principle 'use it or lose it' in neuroplasticity means that
neural connections that are rarely activated are more likely to be weakened or eliminated
skills, once learned, can never be forgotten or changed
neurons that are not used daily die within a year
the brain stops responding to experience after adolescence

Frequently used connections are strengthened, while rarely used connections are weakened or pruned. Learned skills can decline with disuse, and neurons do not die within a year simply because they are not used every day.
psych12a1-neur-14

Rats raised in enriched environments, with more space, toys and social contact, show more dendritic branching and synapses in the cortex than rats kept in standard cages. This finding supports the idea that
brain structure is set by genes and cannot be altered by the environment
experience can change the physical structure of the brain
dendritic branching decreases when animals are more active
enriched environments remove myelin from axons

The brains of the enriched rats changed physically in response to their surroundings, which is evidence of experience-dependent plasticity. The other options contradict this finding: structure is not fixed by genes alone, branching increased rather than decreased, and the environment did not remove myelin.
psych12a1-neur-15
Between early adolescence and the mid-20s, grey matter volume in many cortical regions typically decreases, while white matter volume increases. Which processes best explain this pattern?
neurogenesis and long-term potentiation
dendritic growth and the removal of myelin
synaptic pruning and myelination
long-term potentiation and the formation of new neurons

Pruning removes unused synapses, which reduces grey matter, while myelination adds myelin, which is white matter, to axons. Neurogenesis is largely complete before birth in the cortex, so it cannot explain the adolescent pattern.
psych12a1-neur-16
What is a 'critical period' in brain development?
the time after which the brain can no longer form new synapses
the age at which the brain reaches its maximum weight
a stage when all neurons stop dividing and the brain is fully wired
a time of heightened sensitivity to particular experiences, such as exposure to language

During a critical period the brain is especially responsive to particular experiences, such as language exposure in early childhood. Plasticity does not end abruptly at the close of this period; the brain can still change afterwards, usually less readily.
psych12a1-neur-17
Children often recover more function than adults after a similar brain injury. The main reason is that children's brains
are more plastic and better able to reorganise neural networks
have no synaptic pruning, so damage is less severe
are fully myelinated, so signals are not disrupted
have more neurons in the prefrontal cortex than adults do

Younger brains show greater plasticity, so other regions and networks can take over functions after damage. Children do undergo synaptic pruning, and their brains are not fully myelinated, so those options are incorrect.
psych12a1-neur-18

After an arm amputation, some people feel pain in the missing limb. Brain-imaging studies have shown that the cortical area that once represented the hand may become responsive to touch on the face. This is an example of
adaptive plasticity that restores the lost limb's function
maladaptive plasticity, in which reorganisation is linked to persistent pain
long-term potentiation of a spinal reflex arc
neurogenesis in the primary motor cortex

Cortical reorganisation that does not restore function and is linked to pain is maladaptive plasticity. The reorganisation cannot restore the missing limb, and long-term potentiation and neurogenesis do not describe this change.
psych12a1-neur-19
Hebb's principle, often summarised as 'neurons that fire together wire together', best describes which process?
the permanent removal of neurons that are inactive for long periods
all neurons in a network firing at the same time during learning
the strengthening of connections between neurons that are repeatedly active together
the removal of myelin from axons that are used most often

Connections between neurons that are repeatedly active at the same time are strengthened, which is one basis for learning and memory. Permanent removal of inactive neurons does not reflect the principle, and myelin is added to, not removed from, frequently used pathways.
psych12a1-neur-20
Synapse density in the prefrontal cortex is highest in early childhood and declines during adolescence. This pattern is most consistent with
neurogenesis increasing in the prefrontal cortex during adolescence
synaptic pruning of rarely used connections
a general strengthening of every synapse in the cortex
the formation of myelin around every synapse

A decline in synapse density across adolescence reflects pruning, which removes connections that are rarely used. Neurogenesis would increase the number of neurons rather than reduce synapses, and myelin wraps axons rather than synapses.
psych12a1-neur-21
Which cells produce myelin in the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord)?
Schwann cells, which myelinate neurons throughout the central nervous system
astrocytes, which are the main source of neurotransmitters
oligodendrocytes, which form myelin sheaths around axons in the central nervous system
microglia, which carry nerve impulses along axons

Oligodendrocytes wrap their processes around axons in the brain and spinal cord to form myelin. Schwann cells perform this role in the peripheral nervous system, while astrocytes support neurons and microglia act as immune cells.
psych12a1-neur-22
When are most neurons in the cerebral cortex generated?
during the teenage years
in adulthood in response to learning
during the first week after birth
before birth

Most cortical neurons form during prenatal development, so later plasticity mainly involves changes in connections rather than large numbers of new neurons. Neurogenesis is not the main source of cortical neurons during adolescence or adulthood.
psych12a1-neur-23
What is the term for the creation of new neurons?
neurogenesis
sprouting
potentiation
myelination

Neurogenesis is the formation of new neurons, which occurs mainly before birth and to a limited extent in some adult regions. Sprouting refers to growth of new connections between existing neurons, potentiation strengthens synapses, and myelination adds insulation to axons.
psych12a1-neur-24
Which of the following would be least likely to promote adaptive neuroplasticity?
daily practice of a challenging new skill
a long period with little new sensory or mental stimulation
rehabilitation exercises after an injury
a varied environment with new learning opportunities

Challenging practice, rehabilitation and varied learning environments all promote plasticity, so they are tempting but incorrect answers. A prolonged lack of stimulation tends to reduce the strength and number of neural connections.
psych12a1-neur-25
Which statement best reflects current understanding of neuroplasticity across the lifespan?
plasticity ends at the end of adolescence
plasticity is confined to the first year of life
plasticity continues throughout life, although it is generally greatest in childhood
plasticity occurs only in areas damaged by injury
The brain keeps changing throughout life, though young brains are generally more plastic. Plasticity is not limited to the first year of life, to adolescence, or to damaged areas.
psych12a1-neur-26
State one way the adult brain can change after a skill is learned. (1 mark)
Frequently used synaptic connections can be strengthened, or new connections can form (sprouting) [1]
psych12a1-neur-27
A footballer stops training for a year after a knee injury and finds that their skills have declined. Explain, using neuroplasticity, why this may have occurred. (2 marks)

The neural pathways for the skill are used less, so their synaptic connections are weakened and some are pruned [1]; without repeated activation the network becomes less efficient, so movements are slower and less accurate [1]
psych12a1-neur-28
Explain how myelination during adolescence may improve the performance of a coordinated sporting skill, such as a volleyball spike. (2 marks)
Myelin insulates axons, which speeds the transmission of nerve impulses [1]; faster and more reliable signals between the brain and muscles improve the timing and coordination of the movement [1]
psych12a1-neur-29
Researchers found that London taxi drivers have a larger posterior hippocampus than non-drivers. Explain one limitation of concluding that navigation experience caused this difference. (2 marks)

The study is correlational, so it shows an association rather than proving that navigation experience caused the difference [1]; people with stronger spatial abilities may have been more likely to choose taxi driving, so pre-existing differences may explain the result [1]
psych12a1-neur-30
Compare adaptive and maladaptive neuroplasticity, using one example of each. (4 marks)

Adaptive plasticity is change that improves function or helps the brain adjust to experience [1], for example reorganisation that restores a lost ability after injury [1]; maladaptive plasticity is change associated with harmful or unhelpful outcomes [1], for example cortical reorganisation linked to persistent phantom limb pain [1]
psych12a1-neur-31

Explain why children exposed to a second language in early childhood may become more fluent than adults who learn the same language. Refer to the critical period and plasticity in your answer. (3 marks)

Early childhood is a critical (sensitive) period when the brain is especially responsive to language input [1]; children's greater plasticity allows language networks to form readily and efficiently [1]; adults have reduced plasticity and build new connections more slowly, so fluency develops more slowly [1]
psych12a1-neur-32
Describe how a lack of stimulation in childhood could affect later brain development, referring to synaptic pruning. (3 marks)

Connections that are not stimulated are less likely to be maintained, so they are pruned [1]; the networks that remain are those that were activated, which may limit the range of skills developed [1]; later enriched experiences can partly reorganise these networks, so the effects are not always permanent [1]
psych12a1-neur-33
Evaluate the claim that adolescents cannot make good decisions because their brains are not yet developed. Use two pieces of neuroscientific evidence in your response. (4 marks)

Evidence: the prefrontal cortex, which supports planning and impulse control, continues developing into the mid-20s [1]; the limbic system, involved in reward and emotion, is highly responsive during adolescence, which can increase risk-taking [1]; evaluation: the claim is overstated, as adolescents can make good decisions and outcomes depend on context, emotional state and peer presence [1]; neuroplasticity means experience and training can improve decision-making skills, so development is not fixed [1]
psych12a1-neur-34
Explain why the brain's capacity to replace lost neurons is limited, and why recovery after injury depends mainly on rewiring existing networks. (4 marks)

Most neurons are generated before birth, and neurogenesis in the adult brain is limited and restricted to a few regions [1]; neurons lost to injury are generally not replaced in large numbers [1]; recovery therefore depends on changes in existing networks, such as sprouting, rerouting and strengthening of surviving synapses [1]; rehabilitation that repeatedly uses the affected function encourages these changes [1]
psych12a1-neur-35
Explain why an older adult can still learn a new language, referring to neuroplasticity. (2 marks)

Neuroplasticity continues across the lifespan, so new synaptic connections can form and existing ones can be strengthened with practice [1]; learning is typically slower than in childhood because plasticity is generally greater earlier in life [1]
psych12a1-neur-36
A child with a squint has one eye covered by a patch for several months in early childhood. Later, the visual cortex responds less strongly to signals from that eye. This best illustrates
a fixed, innate wiring of the visual cortex that experience cannot change
neurogenesis that replaces the visual neurons of the covered eye
experience-dependent plasticity during a critical period, in which reduced input from one eye weakens its cortical representation
a reflex that protects the eye from bright light

Early visual experience shapes the visual cortex, and reduced input from one eye during the critical period weakens its connections, which is a form of experience-dependent plasticity. Fixed wiring ignores plasticity, neurogenesis does not replace visual neurons in this way, and a light reflex does not change cortical representation.
psych12a1-neur-37

A man who has been blind since birth is trained to use a device that converts camera images into patterns of pressure on his tongue. After months of practice he can recognise the shapes of objects using the device. The most likely explanation is that
his tongue has developed new sensory neurons that detect light
his myelin has been stripped from the nerves in his tongue, making signals faster
the device has permanently reactivated reflexes from his infancy
his brain has learned to interpret the new pattern of sensory input, which is a form of neuroplasticity

Neuroplasticity allows the brain to learn to interpret unfamiliar patterns of sensory input, even when they arrive through a different sense. Tongue neurons do not acquire sensitivity to light, myelin loss would slow rather than speed signals, and reflexes do not explain learning to recognise shapes.
psych12a1-neur-38
Explain why spaced, repeated practice is more likely than one long session to produce lasting changes in neural connections. (2 marks)

Lasting changes depend on repeated stimulation that strengthens synapses over time, through long-term potentiation [1]; spacing allows the changes to consolidate between sessions, whereas a single intense session produces only short-lived changes [1]
psych12a1-neur-39

A study finds that adolescents who practise juggling daily have more grey matter in motor regions than adolescents who do not. Explain why this finding is correlational, identify one reason it cannot show that juggling caused the difference, and describe one design that could test cause and effect. (3 marks)

The study measures an association between practice and brain structure without manipulating practice [1]; the groups may already differ, for example in motor ability or motivation, which could explain the difference [1]; randomly assigning adolescents to a juggling training group or a control group, and scanning both groups before and after training, would test cause and effect [1]
vce-psych12-np-c1
Adolescents are more likely than adults to take risks with friends watching. A brain-based explanation is that:
The prefrontal cortex develops before the amygdala, so their judgement is stronger than their emotions
Adolescents have no synaptic pruning, so they have too many connections to make clear decisions
The amygdala and reward systems develop earlier than the prefrontal cortex, which matures in the mid-20s
The cerebellum stops developing at 12, so adolescents cannot coordinate their decisions
Emotional and reward responses are strong while the regions for planning, judgement and impulse control are still developing.
vce-psych12-acquired-brain-injury-and-ne: psych12a1-acqu-1
Which of the following is an example of an acquired brain injury caused by a non-traumatic event?
A car accident causing concussion
A gunshot wound to the head
A fall that fractures the skull
A stroke caused by a blocked artery
Stroke is a non-traumatic acquired brain injury, as it results from a blockage or bleed. The other options are traumatic brain injuries caused by external force.
psych12a1-acqu-2
A man who had a stroke in his left hemisphere now has weakness on the right side of his body. This is best explained by
contralateral control of the body by each hemisphere
the left hemisphere controlling the left side of the body
damage to the corpus callosum
damage to the cerebellum
Each hemisphere mainly controls the opposite (contralateral) side of the body, so left motor cortex damage produces right-sided weakness.
psych12a1-acqu-3
Parkinson's disease involves the degeneration of neurons that produce which neurotransmitter?
GABA
Glutamate
Serotonin
Dopamine
Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons, leading to tremor, rigidity and slowed movement.
psych12a1-acqu-4
Which of the following is an impact of damage to the hippocampus resulting from an acquired brain injury?
Loss of vision
Difficulty forming new long-term memories
Loss of balance
Inability to produce speech
The hippocampus is critical for forming new explicit long-term memories. Speech production difficulty implies Broca's area, vision loss the occipital lobe, and balance the cerebellum.
psych12a1-acqu-5
Which statement about the effects of brain injury is most accurate?
Recovery is not possible because the brain cannot change
The effects depend on the location and severity of the injury
Effects are identical regardless of which area is damaged
Brain injury only affects physical functioning
Effects depend on location and extent, and can include physical, cognitive, emotional and behavioural changes. Neuroplasticity can support partial recovery.
psych12a1-acqu-6
A 45-year-old builder suffers a traumatic brain injury to the frontal lobes. Describe two possible changes to his behaviour or cognition. (2 marks)

Any two with justification: difficulty planning and making decisions; impulsivity or poor judgement; changes in personality or emotional regulation (e.g. irritability, aggression); reduced attention or problem solving; difficulty with voluntary movement (1 mark each).
psych12a1-acqu-7
Explain how neuroplasticity may assist recovery after a stroke. Include one example of a rehabilitation approach. (3 marks)

Neuroplasticity allows the brain to reorganise after damage (1); undamaged areas can take over function through rerouting and sprouting new synaptic connections (1); rehabilitation such as physiotherapy, speech therapy or repeated practice of lost skills strengthens the new pathways (1).
psych12a1-acqu-8
Distinguish between a traumatic and a non-traumatic acquired brain injury, giving one example of each. (3 marks)

Traumatic: caused by external physical force to the head, e.g. a fall or car accident (1+1 for definition and example); Non-traumatic: caused by internal factors such as a blockage, bleed, infection or lack of oxygen, e.g. stroke or tumour (1).
psych12a1-acqu-9
Damage to Broca's area in the left frontal lobe is most likely to cause which difficulty?
Slow, effortful speech with impaired grammar
Fluent speech that lacks meaning
Inability to understand the meaning of spoken words
Loss of colour vision

Broca's area is needed to produce speech, so damage causes non-fluent expressive aphasia while comprehension is largely preserved. Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension is the pattern of Wernicke's area damage, which is the tempting mistake here.
psych12a1-acqu-10
Damage to Wernicke's area is most likely to produce which pattern of language?
Halting, effortful speech with good understanding
Fluent, rapid speech that is often meaningless, with poor comprehension
Total deafness in both ears
Inability to write with the dominant hand

Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe is needed to understand language, so its damage produces fluent speech that is often nonsensical. Halting speech with good understanding is the reverse of the pattern caused by Broca's area damage.
psych12a1-acqu-11
Huntington's disease is an inherited disorder that causes degeneration of neurons in the basal ganglia. Which neurotransmitter is lost from these neurons?
Dopamine
Acetylcholine
GABA
Noradrenaline

The neurons of the striatum that degenerate in Huntington's disease release GABA, and their loss produces involuntary jerky movements called chorea. Dopamine is the neurotransmitter lost in Parkinson's disease, which is a common confusion.
psych12a1-acqu-12
The memory loss of Alzheimer's disease is most closely linked to a deficiency of which neurotransmitter?
Dopamine
GABA
Endorphin
Acetylcholine

Cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain, which supply acetylcholine to the hippocampus and cortex, degenerate early in Alzheimer's disease, and cholinesterase inhibitors are used to raise acetylcholine levels. Dopamine is the neurotransmitter associated with Parkinson's disease rather than with Alzheimer's memory loss.
psych12a1-acqu-13
Korsakoff syndrome, often associated with long-term alcohol misuse, is caused mainly by a deficiency of which vitamin?
Thiamine (vitamin B₁)
Vitamin C
Vitamin D
Vitamin K

Thiamine deficiency damages the thalamus and mammillary bodies, producing severe memory impairment and confabulation. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, which does not produce this type of memory loss.
psych12a1-acqu-14
Which statement about concussion is most accurate?
It always shows a visible bleed on a CT scan
It is a mild traumatic brain injury that can occur without loss of consciousness
It can only be caused by a fall from a height
Its symptoms always last for several years

A concussion is a mild traumatic brain injury that often occurs without loss of consciousness and usually shows no large structural bleed on standard scans. The claim that symptoms always last for years is wrong, because most symptoms resolve within days to weeks.
psych12a1-acqu-15
In a coup-contrecoup injury, which description is correct?
Damage occurs only at the site where the head was struck
Damage occurs only on the side of the brain opposite the impact
Damage occurs at the site of impact and on the opposite side, as the brain strikes the inside of the skull
The skull is fractured but the brain is unaffected

In a coup-contrecoup injury the brain moves within the skull and is bruised both at the point of impact (coup) and on the opposite side (contrecoup). Damage at the impact site alone is a common mistake, because it does not include the opposite-side injury.
psych12a1-acqu-16
Diffuse axonal injury most typically results from which mechanism?
A localised blood clot pressing on one small area of the brain
A blocked artery that cuts off blood supply to part of the brain
Several minutes without oxygen to the brain
Rapid acceleration and rotation of the head that stretches and tears axons

Rotational forces shear and tear axons across widespread white matter, producing diffuse damage. A localised clot, a blocked artery or oxygen deprivation each produce different types of injury, so they are common mistakes.
psych12a1-acqu-17
A man is resuscitated after a cardiac arrest, but his brain went without a normal oxygen supply for several minutes. He is at risk of which type of acquired brain injury?
Anoxic (hypoxic) brain injury
Traumatic brain injury
Subdural haematoma
Multiple sclerosis

Lack of oxygen can kill neurons across the brain, causing a non-traumatic anoxic brain injury. A traumatic brain injury and a subdural haematoma usually follow a blow to the head, and multiple sclerosis is an immune condition that is not caused by loss of oxygen.
psych12a1-acqu-18
Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks which part of nerve cells?
The cell body
The myelin sheath
The dendrites
The synaptic vesicles

In MS the immune system damages the myelin sheath around axons in the central nervous system, which slows or blocks nerve signals. The cell body and dendrites are not the main target, so they are tempting but incorrect.
psych12a1-acqu-19
Severing the corpus callosum would most directly disrupt which ability?
Regulating body temperature
Seeing the colour of objects in the visual field
Forming memories in the hippocampus
Transferring information between the two cerebral hemispheres

The corpus callosum is the large bundle of nerve fibres connecting the two cerebral hemispheres, so cutting it blocks information transfer between them. The other options depend on the hypothalamus, visual cortex and hippocampus, which the corpus callosum does not directly serve.
psych12a1-acqu-20
Which of the following best describes retrograde amnesia?
Inability to form new memories after the injury
Loss of memories for events that happened before the injury
Loss of the ability to recognise familiar objects
Loss of the ability to understand written words

Retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories formed before the injury, often for events shortly before it. Inability to form new memories describes anterograde amnesia, which is the tempting wrong answer.
psych12a1-acqu-21
Constraint-induced movement therapy is a rehabilitation approach used after stroke. What does it involve?
Surgically removing damaged brain tissue
Giving high doses of dopamine to the whole brain
Restraining the unaffected limb so the affected limb is used more intensively
Eating a diet high in vitamin C to repair neurons

Constraint-induced movement therapy restrains the stronger limb so the weaker, affected limb is used repeatedly, which strengthens the neural pathways controlling it. The other options describe surgery, drug treatment or diet, none of which is the basis of this therapy.
psych12a1-acqu-22
What is the key difference between an ischaemic stroke and a haemorrhagic stroke?
Ischaemic stroke involves a bleed, and haemorrhagic stroke involves a blocked artery
Ischaemic stroke affects only the cerebellum
Haemorrhagic stroke is always caused by a blow to the head
Ischaemic stroke results from a blocked blood supply, and haemorrhagic stroke from a burst blood vessel

An ischaemic stroke occurs when blood flow is blocked, while a haemorrhagic stroke occurs when a blood vessel ruptures and bleeds into the brain. The reversed option swaps the two definitions, which is a common mistake.
psych12a1-acqu-23
Damage to the occipital lobe is most likely to cause which problem?
Loss or impairment of vision
Difficulty with voluntary movement of the arm
Impaired ability to form new memories
Loss of balance when walking

The occipital lobe houses the primary visual cortex, so damage can cause visual loss or impairment. Arm movement is controlled by the motor cortex in the frontal lobe, memory relies on the hippocampus, and balance is coordinated by the cerebellum.
psych12a1-acqu-24
Epilepsy is best described as
a progressive loss of dopamine neurons in the midbrain
a tendency to have recurrent seizures caused by sudden, abnormal electrical discharges in the brain
a genetic disorder that causes involuntary jerky movements of the limbs
a permanent loss of myelin in the spinal cord

Epilepsy is a neurological disorder in which a person has recurrent seizures caused by abnormal, excessive electrical activity in the brain. The loss of dopamine neurons describes Parkinson's disease, and the jerky movements describe Huntington's disease.
psych12a1-acqu-25
Which of the following is a common early symptom of Alzheimer's disease?
Sudden loss of the ability to see colour
Loss of balance when walking on uneven ground
Progressive difficulty remembering recent events and new information
Involuntary jerky movements of the limbs

Difficulty remembering recent events is one of the earliest and most typical symptoms of Alzheimer's disease, due to damage in the hippocampus and cortex. Loss of balance suggests cerebellar damage, and involuntary jerky movements suggest Huntington's disease rather than Alzheimer's.
psych12a1-acqu-26
Describe two features of Huntington's disease. (2 marks)

Any two, [1] each: inherited, autosomal dominant genetic disorder; involuntary, jerky movements (chorea) caused by degeneration of neurons in the basal ganglia; progressive cognitive decline and changes in mood or personality.
psych12a1-acqu-27
Explain how amyloid-β plaques and tau tangles may disrupt communication between neurons in Alzheimer's disease. (3 marks)

Amyloid-β plaques build up between neurons, interfering with synaptic signalling and triggering inflammation [1]; tau tangles form inside neurons and disrupt the internal transport of nutrients along axons [1]; the resulting neuronal death causes brain atrophy and memory loss [1].
psych12a1-acqu-28
Name the condition in which a person cannot recognise familiar objects by sight even though their vision is intact. (1 mark)
Visual agnosia [1]
psych12a1-acqu-29
Explain why a stroke in the left middle cerebral artery territory may produce different effects from a stroke on the right side of the brain. (4 marks)

The left hemisphere is usually dominant for language, so a left-sided stroke may cause aphasia, such as difficulty speaking or understanding [1]; the right hemisphere is more involved in spatial awareness and attention, so right-sided damage may cause neglect of the left side of space [1]; each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body, so a left stroke causes right-sided weakness and a right stroke causes left-sided weakness [1]; the size and location of the damage determine the severity and the specific deficits [1].
psych12a1-acqu-30
Explain why people with Korsakoff syndrome often confabulate, that is, produce invented memories to fill gaps. (2 marks)
Their damaged memory system cannot accurately store or retrieve past events [1]; the brain fills the gaps with plausible but false information, which the person may believe is true [1].
psych12a1-acqu-31
Explain why repeated concussions may have a more serious effect than a single concussion. (2 marks)

Each concussion can disrupt neuronal function and cause further damage before the brain has recovered from the previous one [1]; repeated injury can lead to longer-lasting cognitive, emotional or behavioural problems [1].
psych12a1-acqu-32
Levodopa (L-dopa) is a common treatment for Parkinson's disease, but it does not cure the condition. Explain why. (3 marks)

Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted into dopamine in the brain, which relieves movement symptoms [1]; it replaces some of the lost dopamine rather than stopping the degeneration of dopamine neurons [1]; the neurons continue to die, so the disease progresses and treatment does not cure it [1].
psych12a1-acqu-33
Describe what happens in the brain during an epileptic seizure. (2 marks)

A group of neurons produces sudden, excessive and abnormal electrical discharges [1]; the abnormal activity spreads or synchronises across brain regions, disrupting normal function and causing altered consciousness, movement or sensation [1].
psych12a1-acqu-34
Explain why a person who nearly drowned may have widespread problems with memory and attention rather than deficits in one localised area. (3 marks)

Neurons need a continuous oxygen supply and begin to die within minutes without it [1]; reduced oxygen affects the whole brain rather than a single localised area, so damage is diffuse [1]; the hippocampus and cortex are particularly vulnerable, which can cause memory and attention deficits [1].
psych12a1-acqu-35
Identify two causes of non-traumatic acquired brain injury other than stroke. (2 marks)
Any two, [1] each: brain tumour; infection such as encephalitis or meningitis; toxic exposure, such as long-term alcohol or drug misuse.
psych12a1-acqu-36
Explain how damage to myelin in multiple sclerosis affects the transmission of nerve signals. (3 marks)

Myelin is the fatty insulating sheath around axons that allows impulses to travel quickly by jumping between nodes [1]; in MS the immune system attacks and destroys myelin, a process called demyelination [1]; without myelin, signals are slowed or blocked, causing symptoms such as weakness, numbness, fatigue or vision problems [1].
psych12a1-acqu-37

A woman who lost language ability after a left hemisphere stroke is referred to a speech pathologist. Describe two rehabilitation strategies the pathologist could use and explain how neuroplasticity supports them. (4 marks)

Repeated structured practice of word-finding or naming tasks [1]; melodic intonation therapy, which uses singing and rhythm to engage intact right-hemisphere areas [1]; neuroplasticity allows repeated practice to strengthen existing or newly formed connections [1]; reorganisation can shift some language function to undamaged regions, including the right hemisphere [1].
psych12a1-acqu-38
A slow-growing tumour presses on the frontal lobe of a man over several years. Which change is most likely to be seen first?
Loss of colour vision
Difficulty recognising faces, with speech preserved
Changes in personality, planning and self-control
Uncontrolled breathing and heart rate

The frontal lobe supports planning, judgement and self-control, so a growing tumour there often changes personality and behaviour. Colour vision and face recognition relate to the occipital and temporal lobes, and breathing is controlled by the medulla, so those options are less likely.
psych12a1-acqu-39
Explain why the effects of a stroke can appear suddenly, whereas the effects of Alzheimer's disease develop gradually over many years. (2 marks)

A stroke is caused by a sudden blockage or bleed that deprives brain cells of oxygen, so neurons die within minutes or hours [1]; Alzheimer's disease involves progressive degeneration of neurons and connections over years, so symptoms emerge slowly [1]
vce-psych12-ab2-c1
The tremor and slowed movement of Parkinson's disease are mainly caused by:
Loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra
Too much dopamine in the cerebellum
Damage to Broca's area
Sudden bursts of electrical activity in the cortex
Low dopamine disrupts the circuits that control smooth voluntary movement. Bursts of abnormal electrical activity describe epilepsy.
vce-psych12-nature-nurture-and-the-biops: psych12a1-natu-1
A psychologist argues that a child's shyness is largely inherited from her parents. This view emphasises
nature
the social factor of the biopsychosocial approach
cultural learning
nurture
Nature refers to inherited genetic and biological factors. Nurture refers to environmental influences such as parenting, culture and experience.
psych12a1-natu-2
The biopsychosocial approach to understanding behaviour proposes that
social factors are unimportant for mental health
behaviour is caused only by biological factors
behaviour results from the interaction of biological, psychological and social factors
psychological factors outweigh biological factors
The biopsychosocial approach treats biological, psychological and social factors as interacting influences on behaviour and mental processes.
psych12a1-natu-3
Which of the following is a psychological factor in the biopsychosocial approach?
Neurotransmitter levels
Peer pressure
Pattern of negative thinking
Genetic predisposition
Psychological factors include thinking, emotion, coping and learning. Genetics and neurotransmitters are biological; peer influence is social.
psych12a1-natu-4
Identical twins raised apart are found to have very similar personality traits. This finding is most likely used to support the influence of
culture
schooling
genetics
parenting style
Identical (monozygotic) twins share 100% of their genes, so similarity despite different environments suggests genetic influence. Twin studies cannot rule out all environmental effects.
psych12a1-natu-5
A student who has a family history of anxiety (genetic predisposition) develops an anxiety disorder after a stressful family move and an unsupportive school environment. This best demonstrates that
nature alone causes mental disorder
nurture alone causes mental disorder
biological, psychological and social factors can interact
social factors are irrelevant
Both biological predisposition and environmental stressors contributed, consistent with the biopsychosocial approach.
psych12a1-natu-6
Explain the difference between nature and nurture, using the example of a child's language development. (3 marks)

Nature: genetic and biological factors that influence development, e.g. inherited capacity for language/brain structures (1); Nurture: environmental influences, e.g. exposure to language, interaction with caregivers (1); both interact, as a child needs both the biological capacity and exposure to language to develop speech (1).
psych12a1-natu-7
Using the biopsychosocial approach, describe one biological, one psychological and one social factor that may contribute to a teenager developing depression. (3 marks)

Biological: genetic predisposition, imbalance of neurotransmitters, or hormonal changes (1); Psychological: negative thought patterns, low self-esteem or poor coping skills (1); Social: bullying, family conflict, social isolation or lack of support (1).
psych12a1-natu-8
Explain one limitation of using twin studies to investigate the influence of nature and nurture. (2 marks)

Identical twins raised together share both genes and environment, so it is hard to separate the two influences (1); twins raised apart are rare, giving small samples, and they may still share prenatal or similar environments, limiting generalisability (1). Accept another valid limitation.
psych12a1-natu-9
Adoption studies investigate nature and nurture by comparing an adopted child's traits with those of
their biological parents and their adoptive parents
only their adoptive parents, because genes have no influence on behaviour
other children raised in the same adoptive home
identical twins raised apart, because adopted children cannot be studied

Similarity to biological parents points to genetic influence, while similarity to adoptive parents points to environmental influence. Comparing only with adoptive parents ignores genes, which is the common mistake of treating the home environment as the sole cause.
psych12a1-natu-10
