The person is showing a temporary, typical response that does not stop them functioning

Brief distress that does not impair functioning is a common response to ordinary stress and is not, on its own, a sign of disorder. The distractors wrongly treat all distress as disorder or as proof of impaired functioning.
psych12a1-typi-13
Which feature would most strongly suggest that a person's sadness after the death of a family member has moved beyond a typical grief response?
The sadness is severe, has lasted for many months and interferes with daily functioning
The person cries at the funeral
The person prefers to spend a few weeks alone
The person feels sad on the anniversary of the death
Severity, persistence and interference with functioning are signs that a response may be a cause for concern. The other options describe expected grief responses that are common and temporary.
psych12a1-typi-14

Direct eye contact is usual in many Australian conversations, but in some other cultures prolonged direct eye contact with an elder is considered disrespectful. What does this example best illustrate?
Eye contact is a universal sign of confidence and honesty
Whether behaviour is typical depends on the cultural norms of the group in which it occurs
Cultural differences have little effect on how behaviour is judged
The same behaviour always has the same meaning across societies

The same behaviour can be typical in one culture and atypical in another, so judgements must consider the group's norms. The options claiming universal meaning or minimal cultural effect contradict this.
psych12a1-typi-15
What is the key difference between a mental health problem and a mental disorder on the mental wellbeing continuum?
A mental health problem is always more serious than a mental disorder
There is no meaningful difference, and the two terms are used interchangeably
A mental disorder is a diagnosable condition, usually with persistent and significant effects on functioning, while a mental health problem may be less severe, shorter-lived or less disabling
A mental disorder occurs only in people who have experienced a traumatic event

Mental disorders are defined by diagnostic criteria and usually involve persistent, significant impairment, whereas mental health problems can be milder and less enduring. The option claiming problems are more serious reverses the relationship, and trauma is not a requirement for disorder.
psych12a1-typi-16
Which statement about typical and adaptive behaviour is correct?
Behaviour that is atypical is always maladaptive
Behaviour that is typical is always adaptive, because most people do it
Behaviour can only be adaptive if it is typical for the person's culture
Typical behaviour can be maladaptive, and atypical behaviour can be adaptive

Typical and adaptive are different ideas: common behaviours such as heavy sugar consumption can harm wellbeing, while uncommon talents or lifestyles can be beneficial. Judging behaviour requires considering its effect on functioning, not just how common it is.
psych12a1-typi-17
Why do psychologists caution against labelling a person as disordered on the basis of a single atypical behaviour?
A single atypical behaviour does not show whether the distress, impaired functioning or persistence criteria are met
Disorders can only be diagnosed in people over 65
Atypical behaviour is never harmful, so it never needs attention
Only a family member is permitted to judge a person's behaviour

Judging a behaviour as a concern requires looking at several criteria over time and in context, so one behaviour is not enough. The other options are false claims about diagnosis or about who may judge behaviour.
psych12a1-typi-18
Which example best illustrates atypical behaviour that is adaptive rather than harmful?
A person who avoids all social contact and feels distressed whenever others are near
A person who shouts at colleagues and has lost several jobs
A person who can memorise long strings of numbers accurately and uses this ability successfully in their work
A person who checks the door lock repeatedly until their hands are sore
An unusual ability that the person uses to function well is atypical but adaptive. The other options describe behaviours that cause distress or impair work and relationships, so they are maladaptive.
psych12a1-typi-19
Which of the following is an example of a behaviour judged atypical because it violates a social norm, rather than because it is statistically uncommon?
Having a rare blood type
Having naturally red hair
Having an exceptionally high IQ
Wearing a swimsuit to a formal wedding ceremony
Wearing a swimsuit to a formal ceremony breaks the expectations of that setting, whereas a rare blood type, red hair and a very high IQ are judged atypical by how rare they are.
psych12a1-typi-20
Which statement about social norms is correct?
Social norms are shared expectations about how people should behave in a group, and they can differ between groups and change over time
Social norms are fixed and identical in every society
Social norms apply only to children and adolescents
Social norms are the same as laws, so breaking one is always illegal
Social norms are shared, group-based expectations that vary across cultures and over time. The distractors describe norms as universal, limited to young people, or as legal rules.
psych12a1-typi-21
When judging whether a behaviour is a cause for concern, which combination of information is most useful?
Only the person's own opinion of the behaviour
How the behaviour compares with the person's age, culture and context, and whether it causes distress or impairs functioning
How rare the behaviour is in the general population, regardless of its effects
Whether the behaviour matches the observer's personal preferences

Psychologists consider the context and the effects on the person rather than a single source of information. Relying only on the person's opinion, rarity alone or the observer's preferences ignores key criteria.
psych12a1-typi-22
A teenager spends most evenings reading alone and has only a few close friends. However, the teenager is happy, does well at school and reports no distress. Which conclusion is best supported?
The behaviour is unusual, but it is not maladaptive or a cause for concern on the criteria given
The behaviour is a mental disorder, because it is uncommon among teenagers
The behaviour must be treated, because the teenager has few friends
The behaviour is maladaptive, because it differs from what most teenagers do

Being uncommon and being a concern are different things, and this teenager is functioning well with no reported distress. The other options treat rarity or difference from others as enough to label behaviour a problem.
psych12a1-typi-23
A child is shy with new people but makes friends over time, enjoys school and copes with new routines. Which conclusion is best supported?
The child is showing maladaptive behaviour because they avoid new people
The child has a mental disorder, because shyness is atypical for children
The child's behaviour falls within the typical range of temperament, with no clear sign of concern
The child's behaviour is atypical and harmful to their development, so it needs treatment

Shyness that does not stop a child forming friendships, enjoying school or coping with routines falls within normal variation. The other options treat a single trait as evidence of disorder or harm without considering functioning.
psych12a1-typi-24
Identify the term for judging the behaviour of people from other cultures only by the standards of one's own culture. (1 mark)
Ethnocentrism [1]
psych12a1-typi-25

A survey of 500 people finds that 15 of them show a particular behaviour. Calculate the percentage of people who show the behaviour and state what this indicates about its statistical status in this group. (2 marks)
15 ÷ 500 × 100 = 3% [1]; the behaviour is statistically uncommon (infrequent) in this group [1]
psych12a1-typi-26
Explain why the duration of a behaviour is considered when deciding whether it is a cause for concern. (2 marks)

A brief response to a stressful event is usually expected, whereas a behaviour that continues for a long time is more likely to indicate an ongoing problem [1]; persistence suggests the behaviour may be affecting functioning beyond the situation that triggered it [1]
psych12a1-typi-27
A six-year-old who cannot yet read fluently is typical for their age, but the same difficulty in a sixteen-year-old may be atypical. Explain why. (2 marks)

Typical behaviour is judged against age-based developmental expectations, so the same ability is expected at different ages [1]; a sixteen-year-old is expected to read fluently, so the difficulty is unusual for their age [1]
psych12a1-typi-28
Explain why labelling a person as having a mental disorder on the basis of a single atypical behaviour can be harmful. (3 marks)

A single atypical behaviour does not show distress, impaired functioning or persistence, so the label may not be accurate [1]; labels can lead to stigma and discrimination from others [1]; a label may change how the person sees themselves and affect their relationships, self-esteem or opportunities [1]
psych12a1-typi-29
Explain how the mental wellbeing continuum can describe a person whose functioning changes over time. (3 marks)

The continuum shows a range of states rather than a simple healthy or unhealthy split [1]; a person can move along it over time, for example from flourishing to a mental health problem after a stressful event [1]; with support they can move back towards wellbeing [1]
psych12a1-typi-30
Explain how the same behaviour can be adaptive for one person and maladaptive for another. Use an example in your answer. (3 marks)

Whether a behaviour is adaptive depends on the person's circumstances, goals and context [1]; e.g., working long hours may be adaptive for a person whose job requires it and who has time for rest, but maladaptive for a person who is exhausted and neglecting their health [1]; judgements should focus on the effect on the person's functioning and wellbeing [1]
psych12a1-typi-31
Explain why distress alone does not establish that a behaviour is atypical or a cause for concern. (3 marks)

Distress can be a typical response to events such as loss, illness or exam stress [1]; a behaviour is a concern when distress is combined with other criteria such as impaired functioning, persistence or severity [1]; whether it is atypical also depends on the person's age, culture and context [1]
psych12a1-typi-32

Mia, aged 16, has become withdrawn over the past three months. She has stopped playing netball, her grades have dropped, and she reports feeling sad and tired most days. Using at least three criteria, assess whether her behaviour is a cause for concern. (4 marks)

Her behaviour is a marked change from her usual pattern and atypical for her age [1]; she reports distress, feeling sad and tired most days [1]; it interferes with her functioning at school and in sport [1]; it has persisted for three months, so it is a cause for concern and warrants support from a professional [1]
psych12a1-typi-33
A pattern of distress or behaviour that is recognised as a condition within one cultural group, but is not recognised as a disorder in other cultures, is described as a
culture-bound syndrome
statistical outlier
ethnocentric judgement
criterion of dysfunction

A culture-bound syndrome is a condition defined within a particular cultural context, so it cannot be fully judged by the standards of other cultures. A statistical outlier is judged by rarity, an ethnocentric judgement is a biased way of evaluating other cultures, and dysfunction refers to impaired functioning.
psych12a1-typi-34
Which example best illustrates the criterion of harm to self or others when judging whether a behaviour is atypical?
A left-handed child who writes with her left hand
A teenager who reads for hours each evening
A woman who sleeps for ten hours after a long week
A man who shouts at a referee, leading to a physical fight in which someone is injured

Behaviour that puts the person or others at risk of physical harm is a stronger cause for concern, regardless of how common it is. The other examples are harmless even though some are unusual or uncommon.
psych12a1-typi-35
A school uses a standardised test and labels any student scoring in the bottom 5 per cent as atypical. What is the main limitation of this statistical approach?
It assumes that every student in the bottom 5 per cent is in distress
It does not show whether a low score causes distress or impairment in the student's daily life
It assumes that all students are equally capable
It requires a sample of at least 1000 students
Statistical infrequency shows how rare a score is, but not whether it is distressing or impairs everyday functioning. The other options are not the central limitation of the approach.
psych12a1-typi-36
Identify one criterion used to judge whether a behaviour is atypical, and explain why it is more useful than statistical infrequency alone. (2 marks)

A criterion such as harm, dysfunction or distress [1]; it considers the impact on the person and others, rather than only how rare the behaviour is, so harmless rare behaviours are not labelled as problems [1]
psych12a1-typi-37

A client reports that she does not discuss her feelings with family members present, because privacy norms in her culture discourage this. Explain how a clinician should consider cultural context before judging this behaviour as atypical. (3 marks)

The clinician should consider whether the behaviour is typical within the client's cultural group rather than judging it by the clinician's own norms [1]; the behaviour may be adaptive and expected within her family norms, so it should not be labelled atypical without further context [1]; the clinician should still assess whether it causes distress or impairment in her daily life [1]
psych12a1-typi-38
A child has refused to attend school for five weeks and can no longer join family outings. Using two criteria, explain why this behaviour may be a cause for concern. (2 marks)
Duration: the behaviour has lasted five weeks, which is longer than a temporary reaction [1]; dysfunction: it prevents the child from attending school and taking part in family life [1]
vce-psych12-ta-c1
Using only a statistical approach, a person with an IQ of 140 would be described as atypical. This highlights a limitation of the approach because:
Statistics cannot measure intelligence, so IQ scores are not valid data
Being statistically rare is not the same as being maladaptive or a problem
Most people have an IQ of 140, so the statistical approach is unreliable
The statistical approach considers only cultural norms, not frequency
Each approach (statistical, socio-cultural, functional, historical, situational) has limits; combining them gives a fuller judgement.
vce-psych12-mental-wellbeing-and-categor: psych12a2-mw-1
Which statement best describes mental wellbeing?
The absence of any diagnosable mental disorder
A state of emotional, social and cognitive functioning in which a person can cope with normal stressors and contribute to their community
A permanent personality trait that does not change across the lifespan
The ability to avoid all negative emotions

Mental wellbeing is a positive state of emotional, social and cognitive functioning. It is not merely the absence of disorder (A), it can change over time (C), and it does not require avoiding negative emotions (D).
psych12a2-mw-2
On the mental health continuum, a person who reports frequent positive emotions, feels they contribute to society and has a sense of purpose would most likely be described as
having a dimensional deficit
languishing
flourishing
experiencing a categorical disorder
Flourishing is the high end of the continuum, with high emotional, psychological and social wellbeing. Languishing is the opposite end.
psych12a2-mw-3
A clinician diagnoses a client with generalised anxiety disorder because the client meets a set number of specified symptoms from a diagnostic manual. This is an example of
a categorical approach
a biopsychosocial approach
a cultural relativist approach
a dimensional approach

A categorical approach classifies a person as either having or not having a disorder based on meeting criteria, as in the DSM-5-TR. A dimensional approach rates symptoms along a continuum of severity.
psych12a2-mw-4
A key criticism of the categorical approach to classifying mental disorders is that it
relies on a continuum of severity only
does not use any diagnostic criteria
cannot be used by clinicians
may ignore variation in symptom severity and treat people just below the threshold as having no disorder
Categorical systems use cut-offs, so a person with significant but sub-threshold symptoms may be classed as 'no disorder'. A dimensional approach addresses this by recording severity.
psych12a2-mw-5
Which of the following is a feature of the dimensional approach to mental disorders?
Disorders are either present or absent
Symptoms are rated on a continuum of severity
Each disorder has a single biological cause
Classification does not consider the person's behaviour
The dimensional approach places people along a spectrum of severity rather than in discrete categories.
psych12a2-mw-6
Distinguish between the categorical approach and the dimensional approach to classifying mental disorders. (3 marks)

Categorical approach: a disorder is diagnosed as present or absent when a person meets a set of specified criteria (e.g. DSM-5-TR); dimensional approach: symptoms are rated along a continuum of severity, so people differ in degree rather than kind; one valid difference in use, e.g. categorical gives a clear diagnosis that guides treatment, while dimensional captures severity and sub-threshold cases.
psych12a2-mw-7

Mia reports that she sleeps well, has close friends, copes with exam stress and feels she is learning and growing. Her friend Jo reports feeling empty, isolated and unmotivated most days, though he has no diagnosis. Using the mental health continuum, describe where each person is likely to sit and explain why. (3 marks)

Mia is likely flourishing; she shows positive emotional, social and psychological functioning (social connection, coping, personal growth); Jo is likely languishing; low emotional and social wellbeing even without a diagnosed disorder shows that mental health is not just the absence of disorder.
psych12a2-mw-8
Explain why a person can have a diagnosed mental disorder yet still experience a relatively high level of mental wellbeing at times. (2 marks)

Mental health is a continuum and wellbeing varies over time and across emotional, social and cognitive domains; with effective treatment, supports and coping strategies, a person with a disorder can function well and report positive wellbeing, so disorder and wellbeing are not opposites.
psych12a2-mw-9
On Keyes' mental health continuum, which category lies between flourishing and languishing?
moderately mentally healthy
mentally unwell with a diagnosed disorder
in remission
dimensionally deficient

Keyes' continuum has three categories: flourishing, moderately mentally healthy and languishing. A diagnosed disorder is classified separately from wellbeing, so 'mentally unwell' is not a category on the continuum.
psych12a2-mw-10
A person who meets the diagnostic criteria for both major depressive disorder and generalised anxiety disorder at the same time is an example of
a provisional diagnosis
comorbidity
a dimensional rating
a specifier

Comorbidity is the co-occurrence of two or more disorders in the same person. A provisional diagnosis is used when criteria are nearly but not fully met, a dimensional rating measures severity, and a specifier adds detail to a single diagnosis.
psych12a2-mw-11
A clinician believes a client meets most, but not all, of the criteria for a disorder and needs more information before confirming it. The clinician may record
a comorbid diagnosis
a remission specifier
a provisional diagnosis
a dimensional severity score

A provisional diagnosis is recorded when a disorder is strongly suspected but there is insufficient information to confirm all criteria. A comorbid diagnosis refers to two disorders together, and a remission specifier applies to a disorder that has already been diagnosed.
psych12a2-mw-12
Which requirement, in addition to a set number of symptoms, is included in most DSM-5-TR disorder criteria?
A brain scan showing structural abnormality
A minimum duration of ten years
Diagnosis made only by a psychiatrist
Clinically significant distress or impairment in important areas of functioning

Most DSM-5-TR criteria require clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas. Brain scans are not a general requirement, durations vary by disorder, and diagnosis can be made by other trained clinicians.
psych12a2-mw-13
Inter-rater reliability in the classification of mental disorders refers to
the extent to which different clinicians reach the same diagnosis for the same person
the extent to which a classification accurately describes the disorder it names
the stability of a diagnosis over a person's lifetime
the proportion of people who recover from a disorder
Inter-rater reliability is consistency between clinicians. Accuracy in describing the disorder is validity, while diagnostic stability over time and recovery rates are different concepts.
psych12a2-mw-14
A diagnostic system has high validity when it
is applied in the same way by every clinician
accurately identifies the condition it claims to describe
can be administered at a low cost
relies only on self-report

Validity is the accuracy with which a system identifies the condition it describes. Consistent application across clinicians is reliability, and cost or the source of information does not determine validity.
psych12a2-mw-15
Which feature of the DSM-5-TR helps clinicians consider a client's cultural background when assessing symptoms?
Removal of all symptom criteria for people from non-Western backgrounds
A rule that cultural background must not be recorded
The Cultural Formulation Interview
A requirement that only family members may give a diagnosis

The Cultural Formulation Interview helps clinicians understand how culture shapes a person's experience and presentation of symptoms. The other options either remove culture from assessment or are not features of the manual.
psych12a2-mw-16
Which example best reflects psychological wellbeing in Keyes' model, rather than emotional or social wellbeing?
Frequent positive emotions
High satisfaction with life overall
A sense of belonging to a community
A clear sense of purpose and direction in life

Psychological wellbeing includes purpose in life, self-acceptance, personal growth, autonomy and environmental mastery. Positive emotions and life satisfaction are emotional wellbeing, and belonging to a community is social wellbeing.
psych12a2-mw-17
What is the minimum number of the nine listed symptoms of major depressive disorder required for a diagnosis under the DSM-5-TR?
Five
Two
Nine
Three
At least five symptoms must be present during the same two-week period, and one of them must be depressed mood or loss of interest. Two or three symptoms are too few, and all nine are not required.
psych12a2-mw-18
The DSM-5-TR is best described as
a fully dimensional system that rates every disorder on a continuum
a manual that classifies disorders mainly by criteria, with some severity specifiers
a biological test that confirms brain damage
a measure of a person's overall wellbeing

The DSM-5-TR is largely categorical, using criteria and specifiers, although it includes some dimensional elements. It is not a biological test for brain damage, and it does not measure overall wellbeing.
psych12a2-mw-19
Which is a potential negative consequence of a diagnostic label?
It guarantees that the person's wellbeing will improve
It removes all stigma attached to the condition
It can lead to stigma and self-fulfilling expectations about what a person can do
It makes further treatment unnecessary
Labels can attract stigma from others and create self-fulfilling expectations. A diagnosis does not guarantee improved wellbeing, remove stigma or end the need for treatment.
psych12a2-mw-20
Which statement best reflects the biopsychosocial view of mental wellbeing?
Wellbeing is determined entirely by genetic inheritance
Wellbeing depends only on a person's income
Wellbeing is fixed at birth and cannot change
Wellbeing is shaped by biological, psychological and social factors together, such as sleep, relationships and coping

The biopsychosocial view holds that biological, psychological and social factors interact to shape wellbeing. The other options each name a single factor or claim that wellbeing cannot change, which the view rejects.
psych12a2-mw-21
Keyes' two-continuum model proposes that
mental health and mental illness are related but separate continua
mental health and mental illness are opposite ends of one continuum
mental illness can only occur when wellbeing is low
a person cannot have a diagnosed disorder and high wellbeing at the same time

The two-continuum model treats mental illness and positive mental health as related but separate dimensions, so a person can have a disorder and still have high wellbeing. The single-continuum view is the one the model rejects.
psych12a2-mw-22
A specifier such as 'with anxious distress' added to a diagnosis is used to
confirm that a biological cause is present
describe an additional feature of the diagnosed disorder
indicate that the person has no other disorders
replace the symptom threshold for the disorder
Specifiers give further detail about a diagnosis, such as particular features or course. They do not confirm a cause, rule out other disorders or change the diagnostic threshold.
psych12a2-mw-23
Which is a main purpose of classifying mental disorders into diagnostic categories?
to predict exactly how every person will respond to treatment
to remove the need for clinical assessment
to allow clinicians to communicate, guide treatment and support research
to prove that a behaviour has a single cause
Shared categories help clinicians communicate, guide treatment decisions and support research. They do not predict individual outcomes perfectly, replace assessment or establish a single cause.
psych12a2-mw-24
Which is an example of a dimensional measure of depression?
A yes/no checklist that determines whether a person has major depression
A clinical interview that records whether five symptoms are present
A diagnosis of 'no disorder' for scores below a cut-off
A rating scale that scores symptom severity on a continuum
A rating scale that scores severity on a continuum is dimensional. The other options rely on yes/no judgements or cut-offs, which are categorical.
psych12a2-mw-25
Which factor belongs to social wellbeing in Keyes' model?
social contribution
life satisfaction
purpose in life
self-acceptance

Social wellbeing includes social contribution, social integration, social acceptance, social coherence and social actualisation. Life satisfaction is emotional wellbeing, while purpose in life and self-acceptance are psychological wellbeing.
psych12a2-mw-26
Which classification system is published by the World Health Organization?
DSM-5-TR
ICD-11
a biological test for depression
the Cultural Formulation Interview

The International Classification of Diseases, 11th edition (ICD-11), is published by the WHO. The DSM-5-TR is published by the American Psychiatric Association, and the other options are not classification systems.
psych12a2-mw-27
Diagnostic manuals are revised across editions. Which best explains why the diagnostic criteria for a disorder may change?
the number of clinicians working in the field changes
the cost of treatment changes over time
research and clinical evidence about the symptoms and course of a disorder changes
patients request different labels

Criteria are revised as research improves understanding of a disorder's symptoms and course. Changes in clinician numbers, treatment costs or patient requests are not the basis for revising diagnostic criteria.
psych12a2-mw-28
Define comorbidity in the context of mental disorders. (1 mark)
The co-occurrence of two or more mental disorders in the same person at the same time [1]
psych12a2-mw-29
Explain what is meant by a provisional diagnosis and give one situation in which a clinician might use it. (2 marks)

A provisional diagnosis is recorded when a disorder is strongly suspected but there is insufficient information to confirm all criteria [1]; for example, symptoms are present but their duration cannot yet be established [1]
psych12a2-mw-30
Give an example of each of two components of psychological wellbeing in Keyes' model. (2 marks)
Self-acceptance, e.g. holding a positive view of oneself and one's past [1]; purpose in life, e.g. having goals that give one's life direction and meaning [1]
psych12a2-mw-31
Explain why both reliability and validity are important when classifying mental disorders. (3 marks)

Reliability means different clinicians reach the same diagnosis for the same person [1]; validity means the classification accurately describes the disorder it names [1]; without both, people may receive inconsistent or inaccurate diagnoses and inappropriate treatment [1]
psych12a2-mw-32
Discuss two advantages and two limitations of a categorical approach to classifying mental disorders. (4 marks)

Advantage: clear criteria give a diagnosis that supports consistent communication between clinicians [1]; advantage: a clear diagnosis can guide treatment decisions and eligibility for services [1]; limitation: people just below the threshold may be excluded, so their severity is ignored [1]; limitation: labels can oversimplify a complex experience and may create stigma [1]
psych12a2-mw-33
Explain what a dimensional rating can capture that a categorical diagnosis cannot. (2 marks)
The degree or severity of symptoms along a continuum [1]; changes over time, such as improvement or worsening, including people below a diagnostic cut-off who still have significant difficulties [1]
psych12a2-mw-34

Jade has been feeling low for three weeks. She has lost interest in activities, sleeps poorly and has little energy, and she has four of the nine symptoms listed for major depressive disorder. Explain whether a categorical approach would diagnose her, and describe how a dimensional approach would represent her presentation. (3 marks)

A categorical approach would not diagnose major depressive disorder, because Jade has four symptoms and five are required [1]; a dimensional approach would rate the severity of her symptoms, for example as mild to moderate [1]; this captures her real difficulties and allows her progress to be tracked over time [1]
psych12a2-mw-35
Give two reasons why a clinician should consider a client's cultural background before diagnosing a mental disorder. (2 marks)
Symptoms and distress may be expressed differently across cultures [1]; some beliefs or idioms of distress are culturally normal, so a clinician may mistake them for a disorder or miss a disorder [1]
psych12a2-mw-36
Identify the type of wellbeing that includes life satisfaction and frequent positive emotions. (1 mark)
Emotional wellbeing [1]
psych12a2-mw-37

Mohammed has strong emotional wellbeing, but he reports that he does not belong to any community and feels he has nothing useful to offer others. Identify the dimension of wellbeing most affected and explain using two examples from his situation. (3 marks)

Social wellbeing is most affected [1]; he lacks social integration, as he does not feel he belongs to any community [1]; his social contribution is low, as he believes he has nothing useful to offer others [1]
psych12a2-mw-38
Explain how categorical and dimensional approaches can be used together in clinical practice, and identify one benefit of doing so. (4 marks)

A categorical diagnosis gives a clear classification for communication, service access and treatment guidelines [1]; a dimensional rating captures the severity of symptoms and how they change over time [1]; used together, the clinician can diagnose and also track severity for the same client [1]; benefit: a fuller picture guides treatment choices and allows progress to be monitored [1]
psych12a2-mw-39
In mental health research, prevalence is best defined as
the number of new cases of a disorder that begin during a set time period
the consistency with which two clinicians agree on the same diagnosis
the extent to which a diagnostic test measures what it claims to measure
the proportion of a population who have a disorder at a particular point in time or period

Prevalence describes how many people in a population currently have a disorder, expressed as a proportion of the whole population. New cases are described by incidence, agreement between clinicians is reliability, and validity is about whether a test measures what it claims to measure.
vce-psych12-mc-c1
Which is a common criticism of categorical systems such as the DSM-5-TR and ICD-11?
They assume a clear boundary between 'disordered' and 'normal', and labels can lead to stigma
They have no diagnostic criteria, so clinicians must diagnose using their own judgement
They are used only for physical illnesses, so they miss many mental disorders
They describe disorders on a continuum, so no diagnosis can ever be made
Categorical approaches give a yes/no diagnosis; dimensional approaches describe symptoms on a continuum.
vce-psych12-person-perception-and-attrib: psych12a2-pp-1
Person perception refers to
an enduring set of beliefs about a social group
the tendency to avoid people who are different
the process of forming impressions and making judgements about other people
the unconscious urge to behave like a majority

Person perception is the process of forming impressions of others, influenced by factors such as the halo effect and physical appearance. B describes conformity, C stereotypes, D is not a standard definition.
psych12a2-pp-2
A new teacher assumes a student who is neatly dressed and attractive is also intelligent and hard-working. This is an example of
the halo effect
the fundamental attribution error
the self-serving bias
confirmation bias
The halo effect is the tendency to let one positive trait (e.g. attractiveness) influence judgements about other, unrelated traits.
psych12a2-pp-3
Sam is late to a meeting and his manager concludes he is lazy, without considering that there was a train breakdown. This is best described as
the self-serving bias
a stereotype threat
a situational attribution
the fundamental attribution error
The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to overemphasise dispositional (internal) factors and underestimate situational factors when explaining others' behaviour.
psych12a2-pp-4
After winning a trophy, a netballer says it was due to her hard training. After losing a final, she blames the umpiring. This pattern is called
the self-serving bias
the fundamental attribution error
cognitive dissonance
the halo effect
The self-serving bias attributes successes to internal factors and failures to external factors, protecting self-esteem.
psych12a2-pp-5
Which of the following is an example of an external (situational) attribution?
'She failed the test because she is not clever.'
'He yelled at the waiter because he has a bad temper.'
'I was late because the road was closed for repairs.'
'They won because they are naturally talented.'
Situational attributions explain behaviour by factors outside the person, such as road closures. A, B and D are dispositional.
psych12a2-pp-6
Describe the difference between a dispositional attribution and a situational attribution, using one example of each. (3 marks)

Dispositional attribution: behaviour explained by internal characteristics such as personality, ability or attitudes; situational attribution: behaviour explained by external factors such as circumstances, other people or the environment; two appropriate examples, e.g. 'he is rude' (dispositional) vs 'he was stressed by a deadline' (situational).
psych12a2-pp-7

Priya sees a stranger snap at a shop assistant and concludes the stranger is an unpleasant person. Later, when Priya snaps at someone herself, she explains it was because she was exhausted. Identify the attribution bias illustrated and explain what it shows. (3 marks)

Actor-observer bias (a form of the fundamental attribution error when judging others); we explain others' behaviour dispositionally (unpleasant person); we explain our own behaviour situationally (being exhausted); we have more access to our own situational context than to others'.
psych12a2-pp-8
Explain one way in which the halo effect could disadvantage a job applicant in an interview. (2 marks)

An interviewer's unfavourable first impression of one trait (e.g. appearance, nervousness or accent) can generalise to unrelated traits; the applicant may be rated as less competent or reliable than their actual skills warrant, so they are unfairly judged.
psych12a2-pp-9
The primacy effect in person perception refers to
the tendency for information presented first to carry more weight in forming an impression than later information
the tendency for the most recent information to be remembered and weighted most heavily
the tendency to judge people more favourably when they share our attitudes
the belief that people generally get what they deserve in life

The primacy effect means early information shapes the overall impression more strongly than later information, which is then interpreted in its light. The recency effect is the reverse, where the latest information dominates, while the other options describe similarity bias and the just world belief.
psych12a2-pp-10
Which of the following is the best description of a schema in person perception?
a single, specific memory of meeting someone at a party
a mental framework of organised knowledge about a type of person or situation that guides expectations
a visible physical trait, such as height or hair colour, used to judge a person
a sudden emotional reaction to a stranger's appearance

A schema is an organised body of knowledge and expectations that helps people interpret and predict what they encounter. A single memory is an episode rather than a framework, while physical traits and emotional reactions are inputs or responses, not the schema itself.
psych12a2-pp-11
In Kelley's covariation model, which combination of information would most strongly lead an observer to make a situational attribution?
low consensus, low distinctiveness, high consistency
high consensus, low distinctiveness, low consistency
high consensus, high distinctiveness, high consistency
low consensus, high distinctiveness, low consistency

A situational attribution is most likely when many others behave the same way (high consensus), the person behaves this way only in this situation (high distinctiveness) and does so reliably (high consistency). The first option points to a dispositional attribution, while the other two give mixed signals.
psych12a2-pp-12
Which of the following best describes a self-fulfilling prophecy?
a belief that a person's personality is fixed and cannot change over time
the tendency to remember predictions that turned out correct and forget those that were wrong
a prediction that is accurate only because the predictor has more information
an expectation about someone that leads that person to behave in a way that confirms the expectation

In a self-fulfilling prophecy, a perceiver's expectation changes how they treat someone, which elicits the expected behaviour and so appears to confirm the belief. The other options describe fixed-trait beliefs, selective memory and accurate prediction, none of which involves the expectation causing its own confirmation.
psych12a2-pp-13
Research comparing cultures suggests that the fundamental attribution error is
generally more pronounced in individualist cultures than in many collectivist cultures
absent entirely in collectivist cultures, where people never explain behaviour through personal traits
a universal bias that affects all cultures to exactly the same degree
found only in people with a high level of formal education

Individualist cultures place more emphasis on personal traits and independence, so dispositional explanations are typically more common there, while collectivist cultures attend more to context. The 'absent entirely' and 'exactly the same degree' options overstate the findings, and education is not the explanatory factor.
psych12a2-pp-14
The horns effect refers to
the tendency to remember the first person met in a group
a negative impression formed from one unfavourable trait, which then colours judgements of other, unrelated traits
a positive impression formed from one favourable trait, which then colours judgements of other, unrelated traits
the belief that a person's appearance reveals their hidden character

The horns effect is the negative counterpart of the halo effect: one unfavourable trait generalises to unrelated judgements. The positive version describes the halo effect itself, while the other options describe primacy-type memory and a belief that appearance reveals character.
psych12a2-pp-15
Which of the following best illustrates the just world hypothesis?
A manager promotes the candidate who scored highest in the selection tests.
A driver who cut someone off is assumed to be careless, rather than rushed by an emergency.
A colleague says a worker who was dismissed must have deserved it, because bad things only happen to people who do something wrong.
A team member credits a win to their own skill but blames a loss on the referee.

The just world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve, so misfortune must be the victim's fault. The driver example is a fundamental attribution error and the team example is the self-serving bias, while the promotion decision is simply a fair outcome rather than an attribution.
psych12a2-pp-16
Stereotype threat refers to
a fear of being physically harmed by members of an outgroup
the tendency to agree with a majority opinion in order to avoid conflict
a belief that one's own group is superior to all others
a concern that one's performance will confirm a negative stereotype about one's group, which can itself reduce performance

Stereotype threat is the pressure felt when a person worries that their performance will confirm a negative stereotype, and this anxiety can lower performance. The other options describe fear of physical harm, conformity and ingroup bias, which are related to prejudice but are different concepts.
psych12a2-pp-17
After deciding her new neighbour is unfriendly, Mia notices every brief, abrupt moment and overlooks the friendly waves they give her. This best illustrates
confirmation bias, the tendency to seek out and interpret information in ways that support an existing belief
the primacy effect, the tendency for early information to be remembered best
the halo effect, where one positive trait shapes judgements about other traits
cognitive dissonance, the discomfort created by holding conflicting beliefs or behaviours

Confirmation bias leads Mia to notice evidence that fits her view and discount evidence that does not. The primacy and halo effects describe different impression-forming errors, and cognitive dissonance concerns conflicting beliefs or actions rather than how information is selected.
psych12a2-pp-18
The ultimate attribution error describes the tendency to
rate every member of one's own group as more similar to one another than members of other groups
explain negative behaviour of outgroup members in terms of their character, but explain the same behaviour by ingroup members as the result of circumstances
assume that the behaviour of others is always caused by their situation rather than their personality
remember more information about outgroup members than about ingroup members

The ultimate attribution error extends the fundamental attribution error to groups: outgroup wrongdoing is seen as dispositional, while the same behaviour by ingroup members is excused as situational. The other options describe related but different biases, such as ingroup perceptions, the reverse of the fundamental attribution error and selective memory.
psych12a2-pp-19
Which of the following is an example of a non-verbal cue that can shape a first impression?
the content of a job applicant's résumé
the length of time a person has worked in their previous job
the tone of voice and eye contact an applicant uses during an interview
the wording of references written by former employers

Non-verbal cues such as tone of voice, eye contact and posture strongly influence first impressions, often within seconds. The other options are verbal or written information, which can be assessed separately from how a person communicates in person.
psych12a2-pp-20
A person judges how common a trait is among members of a group by how easily examples come to mind. This best illustrates
the availability heuristic
the representativeness heuristic
the anchoring effect
the gambler's fallacy

The availability heuristic bases judgements on how easily examples come to mind, which can be skewed by vivid or recent cases. The representativeness heuristic judges by how closely something matches a prototype, anchoring relies on an initial reference value, and the gambler's fallacy wrongly expects reversals in random events.
psych12a2-pp-21
Which of the following statements about first impressions is most accurate?
First impressions form only after a long period of interaction, once a person has enough evidence.
First impressions form within seconds and can be difficult to change, even when new information contradicts them.
First impressions are always accurate because they are based on objective evidence.
First impressions are formed only from what a person says, not from how they look or behave.

Research suggests people form impressions within seconds, and these can persist because of primacy and confirmation bias. The other statements are inaccurate, since impressions form quickly, are not always correct and draw heavily on non-verbal cues as well as words.
psych12a2-pp-22
Impression management refers to
the tendency to form impressions of others from first meetings
a bias in which people overestimate how much others notice their appearance and behaviour
the deliberate effort to control the image that others form of us
the process of changing one's own beliefs to match those of a group

Impression management involves deliberately shaping how others see us, for example through dress, behaviour or the information we choose to share. The spotlight effect is the overestimation of how much others notice us, while the other options describe impression formation and conformity.
psych12a2-pp-23
Which statement correctly distinguishes a stereotype from prejudice?
A stereotype is a negative feeling towards a group; prejudice is a belief about the characteristics of that group.
Stereotypes and prejudice are the same thing, and both always involve overt discrimination.
A stereotype is a feeling of dislike; prejudice is the action of treating a group unfairly.
A stereotype is a belief about the characteristics of a group; prejudice is a negative attitude or feeling towards members of that group.

A stereotype is a cognitive belief about a group's characteristics, while prejudice is an affective, usually negative, attitude towards its members. Discrimination is the behaviour that can follow from either, so the option describing prejudice as an action confuses the two, and the others swap or merge the definitions.
psych12a2-pp-24
The tendency to see members of an outgroup as more alike than members of one's own group is called
the outgroup homogeneity effect
the false consensus effect
the ingroup favouritism effect
the spotlight effect

The outgroup homogeneity effect leads people to perceive outgroup members as all alike, while they see their own group as more diverse. The false consensus effect is overestimating how many others share one's views, while the other two describe favouritism towards one's group and self-focus.
psych12a2-pp-25
The belief that certain personality traits tend to occur together, so that knowing one trait allows an observer to predict others, is known as
the spotlight effect
implicit personality theory
the actor-observer bias
cognitive dissonance

Implicit personality theory is a lay belief about how traits cluster together, which can produce the halo effect when one trait is used to predict others. The spotlight effect, actor-observer bias and cognitive dissonance describe different processes.
psych12a2-pp-26
Which of the following is an example of the representativeness heuristic?
remembering a dramatic plane crash and overestimating the risk of air travel
accepting the first price offered as a reference point for negotiations
assuming a quiet, bookish person is more likely to be a librarian than a salesperson, because they match the librarian prototype
believing a coin is due to land tails after five heads in a row

The representativeness heuristic judges the likelihood of a category by how closely a person matches its prototype, while ignoring base rates. The plane crash example is the availability heuristic, the price example is anchoring, and the coin example is the gambler's fallacy.
psych12a2-pp-27

After hearing several news reports about accidents involving one car brand, a driver concludes that drivers of that brand are reckless. Explain how the availability heuristic could lead to this inaccurate belief. (2 marks)

Vivid, widely reported accidents come to mind easily, so the driver overestimates how common such accidents are among the brand's drivers [1]; the judgement ignores base rates, so it is biased and inaccurate [1].
psych12a2-pp-28

A teacher believes a Year 9 student is unlikely to succeed in mathematics and gives the student fewer challenging questions and less feedback. Over the term the student's confidence and results decline. Explain how this scenario illustrates a self-fulfilling prophecy, and identify one way the cycle could be broken. (4 marks)

The teacher's expectation shapes how they treat the student, reducing opportunities and feedback [1]; the student responds to these cues with lower confidence and effort, so their results decline [1]; the decline appears to confirm the original expectation, creating a self-reinforcing cycle [1]; the cycle could be broken by the teacher giving the student challenging tasks and feedback, or by the student being shown evidence that contradicts the expectation [1].
psych12a2-pp-29

A marker reads a strong opening paragraph of a student's essay, then a weaker body, and awards a higher mark than the rest of the essay deserves. Explain how the primacy effect could account for this. (3 marks)

The strong opening is early information, which is given more weight in forming the overall impression [1]; the marker interprets the later, weaker paragraphs in light of that favourable first impression, so their weaknesses are underweighted [1]; the mark therefore does not accurately reflect the whole essay [1].
psych12a2-pp-30
Explain how stereotype threat could reduce the test performance of a student who is aware of a negative stereotype about their group's maths ability. (2 marks)
The student worries that poor performance will confirm the stereotype, which creates anxiety and pressure [1]; this anxiety uses up attention and working memory, lowering performance on the test [1].
psych12a2-pp-31
Explain how the just world hypothesis could lead an observer to blame the victim of a robbery. (2 marks)

The observer believes people get what they deserve, so the victim must have done something to bring the robbery on [1]; blaming the victim protects the observer's belief that the world is fair and that similar misfortune can be avoided [1].
psych12a2-pp-32
Identify one non-verbal cue an interviewer might use to form a first impression of a job applicant, and explain how it could affect that impression. (2 marks)
A non-verbal cue such as eye contact or tone of voice [1]; steady eye contact may lead the interviewer to judge the applicant as confident and honest, making the impression more favourable [1].
psych12a2-pp-33
A coach believes a player is careless. Explain how confirmation bias could affect how the coach evaluates the player's performance across a season. (3 marks)

The coach notices and remembers the player's mistakes because they fit the belief [1]; the coach overlooks or discounts good plays that contradict it [1]; the belief is therefore maintained despite balanced evidence, so the evaluation is biased [1].
psych12a2-pp-34
Explain how the outgroup homogeneity effect and the ultimate attribution error can work together to maintain prejudice against an outgroup. (4 marks)

Outgroup homogeneity: members of the outgroup are seen as all alike, so one negative example is generalised to the whole group [1]; ultimate attribution error: negative behaviour by outgroup members is attributed to their dispositions, while the same behaviour by ingroup members is excused as situational [1]; negative outgroup behaviour is therefore seen as typical and inherent, while ingroup failings are explained away [1]; individual counter-examples are dismissed as exceptions, so the prejudice resists contrary evidence [1].
psych12a2-pp-35
Explain how a person's mood at the time of meeting a stranger could influence their first impression. (2 marks)

A positive mood can lead the person to interpret the stranger's ambiguous behaviour more favourably [1]; a negative mood can lead to more unfavourable judgements, so the impression reflects the perceiver's state as well as the stranger's behaviour [1].
psych12a2-pp-36

A manager notices that employees from one social group make more mistakes than others, so concludes that the group is less capable. Records show that the groups make errors at the same rate, but the manager remembers the mistakes of this group more easily. This is an example of
the fundamental attribution error
the self-serving bias
illusory correlation
the halo effect

An illusory correlation occurs when people perceive a link between two things that is not present in the data, often because distinctive or memorable events stand out. The fundamental attribution error concerns explaining others' behaviour in terms of personality, the self-serving bias concerns explaining one's own success or failure, and the halo effect concerns generalising a positive trait.
psych12a2-pp-37
Explain the self-serving bias, and give one example of how it could affect a student's explanation of an exam result. (2 marks)

The tendency to attribute successes to internal, dispositional factors and failures to external, situational factors, which protects self-esteem [1]; for example, a student who does well credits her ability, but blames an unfair test when she does poorly [1]
psych12a2-pp-38

A small business owner rejects an applicant for an accounting role because he has a tattoo and plays in a band, and believes people like this are rarely good with numbers. Identify the heuristic involved and explain how it could lead to an unfair judgement. (3 marks)

The representativeness heuristic, in which a person is judged by how closely they match a stereotype or prototype of a group [1]; the owner ignores the applicant's qualifications and work history, which are better evidence of ability [1]; this could lead to rejecting a capable applicant for irrelevant reasons [1]
vce-psych12-pp-c1
A classmate arrives late and you assume they are lazy, without considering that the trains were cancelled. This is an example of:
A situational (external) attribution
The halo effect
Cognitive dissonance
The fundamental attribution error
We tend to overestimate personal (internal) causes and underestimate situational (external) causes of other people's behaviour.
vce-psych12-attitudes-and-cognitive-diss: psych12a2-ad-1
In the tri-component model of attitudes, the 'affective' component is
a person's beliefs about an object
a person's feelings about an object
a person's behaviour towards an object
a person's habits of thought
The affective component is the emotional response (e.g. 'I love dogs'). The cognitive component is beliefs and the behavioural component is actions or intentions.
psych12a2-ad-2
Cognitive dissonance is best described as
the tendency to conform to group norms
the tendency to attribute success to internal factors
a pleasant feeling when attitudes and behaviours match
an uncomfortable mental tension that arises when a person holds inconsistent cognitions or when behaviour conflicts with attitudes
Festinger's cognitive dissonance is the psychological discomfort from inconsistent cognitions, which motivates the person to reduce it.
psych12a2-ad-3
A smoker who believes smoking is harmful keeps smoking and tells himself 'the risk is overstated and I'll quit later'. He is reducing dissonance by
changing his behaviour
changing or minimising the importance of his attitude or belief
obeying an authority figure
applying the halo effect
He is rationalising and minimising the belief about harm rather than changing his behaviour, which reduces dissonance.
psych12a2-ad-4
Which of the following strategies would reduce cognitive dissonance by changing behaviour?
Deciding the environment doesn't really matter
Ignoring information that conflicts with the attitude
A person who values the environment starts cycling instead of driving
Adding a new belief that driving is necessary
Changing behaviour to match the attitude (cycling) removes the inconsistency. B and D change or protect cognition, and A trivialises the attitude.
psych12a2-ad-5
Researchers find that people who are paid a small amount to tell others a boring task was interesting later rate the task as more enjoyable than those paid a large amount. This result is explained by
greater cognitive dissonance in the small payment group, resolved by changing their attitude
greater conformity in the large payment group
the self-serving bias
greater external justification in the small payment group
With little external justification for lying, dissonance is higher and is reduced by changing the attitude to match the behaviour (Festinger and Carlsmith).
psych12a2-ad-6
Describe the three components of the tri-component model of attitudes, using an example about recycling. (3 marks)

Cognitive: beliefs or thoughts about the object (e.g. recycling reduces landfill); affective: feelings about it (e.g. feeling proud or good about recycling); behavioural: how the person acts or intends to act (e.g. sorting rubbish into the recycling bin).
psych12a2-ad-7

Leila values honesty but tells a friend she loves a gift she actually dislikes. Using cognitive dissonance, explain what Leila is likely to experience and outline one way she might reduce it. (3 marks)

She experiences dissonance (psychological discomfort) because her behaviour conflicts with her attitude about honesty; reduction by changing the attitude (e.g. 'white lies are kind'), adding a new cognition (it avoided hurting her friend) or changing behaviour (telling the friend the truth); one strategy clearly linked to the scenario.
psych12a2-ad-8
Explain why attitudes do not always predict behaviour. (2 marks)

Behaviour can be shaped by situational factors such as social pressure, cost or convenience; attitudes may be weak or conflicting across components, or the person may not have the opportunity or ability to act on them.
psych12a2-ad-9
Which of the following is an example of the behavioural component of an attitude?
Signing a petition to ban single-use plastic bags
Believing that single-use plastic bags harm marine life
Feeling angry whenever a plastic bag is littered
Thinking reusable bags are more convenient to carry
Signing a petition is an observable action, so it is the behavioural component. Believing that bags harm marine life is cognitive and feeling angry is affective, so both are tempting but wrong.
psych12a2-ad-10
Which of the following makes an attitude most likely to predict a person's behaviour?
The attitude is held weakly and the person rarely thinks about it
The attitude is strong, based on direct personal experience and often thought about
The attitude is held only because the person's friends share it
The attitude is about a topic the person has never encountered

Strong attitudes formed through direct experience are more accessible in memory, so they guide behaviour more consistently. Weak or borrowed attitudes, and attitudes about unfamiliar topics, are less likely to predict what a person actually does.
psych12a2-ad-11
After years of hearing her older brother describe a certain sport as boring and pointless, Mia now dislikes the sport, even though she has never played it. Her attitude is most likely formed through
operant conditioning, because she is rewarded each time she agrees with her brother
cognitive dissonance, because her beliefs about sport conflict with each other
observational learning from a trusted model
the mere exposure effect, because she has heard about the sport often

Mia has learned her attitude by observing and modelling a person she trusts, without any personal experience of the sport. Mere exposure would tend to produce liking rather than dislike, and operant conditioning depends on consequences of her own behaviour, which are not described.
psych12a2-ad-12
Which statement best defines an attitude?
A temporary mood caused by the immediate environment
A fixed personality trait that is present from birth
A behaviour a person performs automatically without conscious thought
A learned and relatively enduring evaluation of a person, object or issue
An attitude is a learned evaluation, positive or negative, that tends to last over time. A mood is temporary, a trait is largely inborn, and an automatic behaviour is not an evaluation at all.
psych12a2-ad-13
Which situation is most likely to produce cognitive dissonance?
A person who believes regular exercise is important skips every training session and then feels guilty
A person who enjoys swimming goes to the pool on a hot day
A person who likes pizza orders pizza for dinner
A person who thinks the sky is blue looks outside and sees a blue sky
Dissonance arises when a held belief and a behaviour conflict, and the guilt signals that tension. The other options all show beliefs and behaviour that match, so no tension arises.
psych12a2-ad-14
Recruits who endure a severe, painful initiation to join a club often come to rate the club more highly than recruits who had an easy entry. This is best explained by
conformity, because the recruits copy the views of existing members
dissonance reduction, because the recruits increase the value they place on the club to justify their suffering
the self-serving bias, because the recruits credit their entry to their own ability
the halo effect, because the club's members seem attractive

Enduring pain for a club they do not value highly would create tension, so the recruits resolve it by valuing the club more. Conformity and the self-serving bias do not involve resolving this inconsistency, and the halo effect is a judgement bias rather than a dissonance process.
psych12a2-ad-15
After choosing between two equally attractive job offers, Rahul begins to rate the job he accepted as more appealing and the one he rejected as less appealing. This is best explained by
the foot-in-the-door technique
dissonance reduction after a decision, by changing how the options are evaluated
the bystander effect
the fundamental attribution error

Having rejected an attractive option creates tension, which Rahul reduces by making his choice look better and the alternative look worse. The foot-in-the-door technique, bystander effect and fundamental attribution error do not explain this post-decision shift.
psych12a2-ad-16
Which factor is most likely to weaken the link between a person's attitude and their behaviour?
The behaviour is easy and inexpensive to perform
The attitude is specific to the behaviour in question
The person has had direct personal experience with the issue
Strong social pressure from peers to act against the attitude
Strong social pressure to act against an attitude can override it, weakening the attitude-behaviour link. Ease of action, specificity and direct experience all tend to strengthen that link.
psych12a2-ad-17
Which statement about attitudes and behaviour is correct?
Attitudes always fully determine behaviour, so behaviour never affects attitudes
Attitudes and behaviour are unrelated, so changing one never affects the other
Behaviour can change attitudes only in childhood, after which attitudes are fixed
Attitudes can influence behaviour, and behaviour can also change attitudes, so the influence can run in both directions
Dissonance research shows that acting in a certain way can shift attitudes, while attitudes also guide behaviour. The other options are absolute claims that the evidence does not support.
psych12a2-ad-18

A child feels uneasy every time she hears the whirr of a dentist's drill. Later she feels uneasy at the sight of any dental clinic, even before anything painful happens. Her attitude towards dentists is best explained by
classical conditioning, because a neutral stimulus has been repeatedly paired with an unpleasant experience
operant conditioning, because she is punished for going to the dentist
observational learning from her parents
cognitive dissonance, because her beliefs about dentists conflict with her feelings

The drill sound was neutral but became associated with pain, so it now triggers the emotional response on its own. Operant conditioning depends on the consequences of her own behaviour, which are not described, and cognitive dissonance is about inconsistent cognitions.
psych12a2-ad-19
A teenager receives praise from friends each time he speaks positively about a political party. Over time he begins to hold that view himself. This change is best explained by
classical conditioning, because the party's name is paired with a neutral sound
operant conditioning, because positive reinforcement strengthens the expressed view
cognitive dissonance, because he is uncomfortable with his views
the mere exposure effect, because he hears the party's name often

Praise following his statements is a reinforcer that increases the likelihood he repeats them, which can lead to holding the attitude. Classical conditioning involves an involuntary response to paired stimuli, and mere exposure involves no reward.
psych12a2-ad-20
Which statement reflects the affective component of an attitude towards a new school uniform policy?
The policy costs families more money than the previous one
Uniforms have been part of this school's tradition for fifty years
I feel frustrated every time I have to put on the uniform
I wrote to the principal to ask for the policy to be reviewed
Frustration is an emotional response, so it is the affective component. The cost and tradition statements are beliefs (cognitive) and the letter is an action (behavioural).
psych12a2-ad-21
According to Festinger's theory, cognitive dissonance is strongest when
a person is pressured by an authority figure to do something they dislike
two trivial beliefs that the person rarely thinks about are inconsistent
a person is unaware of any inconsistency between their beliefs and actions
a valued belief conflicts with an action the person freely chose to take

Dissonance is greatest when a freely chosen action clashes with an important belief, because there is no outside reason for the action. Pressure from an authority gives external justification and reduces dissonance, while trivial or unnoticed inconsistencies create little discomfort.
psych12a2-ad-22
Which of the following is an example of an attitude formed through direct personal experience?
Reading a news article about a flood in another state
Hearing a friend describe a flood from years ago
Living through a flood and losing property
Watching a documentary about flooding
Losing property in a flood is first-hand experience, which tends to produce strong, lasting attitudes. The other options are second-hand information from the media or from other people.
psych12a2-ad-23
What is the main difference between a belief and an attitude?
Beliefs are always true, whereas attitudes can be false
There is no difference, as beliefs and attitudes are the same thing
Attitudes include an evaluation of something as good or bad, whereas beliefs are information a person holds about it
Beliefs include feelings of like or dislike, whereas attitudes are purely factual

An attitude is an evaluation (positive or negative) of an object, while a belief is what a person thinks is true about it. Beliefs are not guaranteed to be true, and beliefs do not carry the like-or-dislike evaluation that attitudes do.
psych12a2-ad-24
Ravi believes that flying is much safer than driving, yet feels intense fear every time he boards a plane. Which statement best describes this situation?
The cognitive and affective components of his attitude are inconsistent
His attitude is consistent because all of its components are positive
His belief about safety is the affective component, while the fear is the behavioural component
His attitude is consistent because he never acts on his fear
His belief that flying is safe is cognitive, while his fear is affective, and these clash. The other options either deny the inconsistency or mislabel the components.
psych12a2-ad-25
A new band's name appears on posters around campus many times. Without ever hearing their music, a student comes to like the band more. This is best explained by
the mere exposure effect
cognitive dissonance, because the student's beliefs about the band are inconsistent
the foot-in-the-door technique
the self-serving bias, because the student credits their taste to their own judgement

Repeated exposure to a neutral stimulus alone can increase liking, which is the mere exposure effect. The other options describe processes that involve inconsistency, compliance or attribution, none of which are present here.
psych12a2-ad-26
After a friend criticises Lena's decision to leave her job, Lena spends time with colleagues who agree the move was sensible. Which dissonance-reduction strategy is she using?
Changing her attitude towards her friend
Changing her behaviour by returning to her old job
Adding consistent cognitions by seeking support for her decision
Ignoring the criticism completely

Seeking colleagues who agree adds supporting cognitions, which reduces the conflict created by the criticism. Returning to the old job would be a behavioural change, and changing her attitude towards her friend does not address the decision itself.
psych12a2-ad-27
Explain why an advertisement that appeals to feelings may be more effective at changing behaviour than one that only presents facts. Use the tri-component model in your answer. (3 marks)

A message that only presents facts engages only the cognitive component, which may be insufficient because attitudes are also driven by emotion [1]; an appeal to feelings such as guilt or fear engages the affective component and can motivate action [1]; a stronger affective response makes it more likely that the behavioural component (intention to act) will change [1].
psych12a2-ad-28

Ana believes hunting is cruel. After her grandfather asks her, she spends a weekend helping at a hunting-club fundraiser. Describe the dissonance she may experience and outline two ways she could reduce it. (4 marks)

Her behaviour (helping) conflicts with her belief that hunting is cruel, creating cognitive dissonance [1]; the family request provides external justification, which may ease the tension somewhat [1]; she could change her attitude, e.g. by deciding that hunting is a tradition that is not truly cruel [1]; or she could change her behaviour or add a new cognition, e.g. by telling herself she helped only to support her family and declining future events [1].
psych12a2-ad-29
Explain what is meant by 'external justification' in cognitive dissonance. (1 mark)
A reason outside the person, such as a reward or pressure from others, that explains why they acted against their attitude, so less dissonance is felt [1].
psych12a2-ad-30
Sofia buys a new phone, then reads reviews saying a competitor's model is better. Describe the dissonance she may feel and outline one way she could reduce it. (2 marks)
She feels tension because the new information conflicts with her decision to buy the phone [1]; she could reduce it by focusing on the strengths of her phone and devaluing the competitor's model [1].
psych12a2-ad-31
Outline why a person's cognitive and affective components of an attitude towards public transport might be inconsistent, using an example. (2 marks)

The person may hold beliefs that public transport is cheap and efficient (cognitive) [1]; while also feeling anxious or annoyed about crowded trains (affective), so the two components do not match [1].
psych12a2-ad-32
Describe how a person's behaviour can change the cognitive component of their attitude. Use an example. (2 marks)

Acting in a way that conflicts with a belief creates dissonance, so the person may change the belief to match the action [1]; e.g. someone who spends heavily on a brand comes to believe its products are superior to those of other brands [1].
psych12a2-ad-33
Describe how observational learning can contribute to a child developing a positive attitude towards reading. (2 marks)

The child watches and imitates models, such as parents or teachers, who read enthusiastically [1]; the child sees reading valued or enjoyed and so adopts the attitude (e.g. wanting to read because a parent visibly enjoys books) [1].
psych12a2-ad-34
Name the component of an attitude that consists of a person's actions or intentions to act towards an object. (1 mark)
Behavioural component [1].
vce-psych12-ac-c1
A smoker knows smoking is harmful but keeps smoking, saying 'My grandfather smoked and lived to 90.' The smoker is:
Showing an attitude that has no affective component at all
Reducing cognitive dissonance by changing a belief to fit the behaviour
Making the fundamental attribution error about his grandfather
Showing obedience to his grandfather as an authority figure
Conflicting thoughts and actions cause discomfort; people reduce it by changing the behaviour, the belief, or adding justifying beliefs.
vce-psych12-stereotypes-prejudice-and-di: psych12a2-sp-1
A stereotype is best defined as
a negative feeling directed at a group
a generalised belief about the characteristics of members of a social group
an unfair action taken against a group
a belief formed through direct experience with every member of a group
Stereotypes are cognitive generalisations about a group. Negative feelings are prejudice (A) and unfair actions are discrimination (C).
psych12a2-sp-2
A landlord refuses to rent a flat to a family because of their ethnic background. This behaviour is an example of
discrimination
the halo effect
a stereotype
prejudice
Discrimination is the unfair treatment of people based on group membership. Prejudice is the attitude and stereotype is the belief.
psych12a2-sp-3
Which statement correctly identifies the components of prejudice, stereotypes and discrimination?
Stereotype: behavioural; prejudice: cognitive; discrimination: affective
Stereotype: cognitive; prejudice: affective; discrimination: behavioural
Stereotype: affective; prejudice: behavioural; discrimination: cognitive
All three are cognitive
Stereotypes are beliefs (cognitive), prejudice is a feeling or attitude (affective) and discrimination is action (behavioural).
psych12a2-sp-4

An employer who believes older workers cannot learn new technology reads a CV of a skilled 60-year-old and still hires a younger applicant. Which cognitive process most helps maintain the employer's stereotype?
Actively adopting a dimensional approach
Ignoring or discounting information that disconfirms it
Seeking out disconfirming evidence
Reducing dissonance by changing the belief
Stereotypes persist because people attend to information that confirms them and discount contradictory cases.
psych12a2-sp-5
Which of the following would be most likely to reduce prejudice between two groups, according to contact research?
Isolating the groups from each other
Cooperative contact between groups working towards shared goals on an equal footing
Highlighting differences between the groups
Competition between groups for limited resources
Cooperative contact on equal status towards superordinate goals reduces prejudice. Competition (D) tends to increase it.
psych12a2-sp-6
Distinguish between prejudice and discrimination, using an example of each in a workplace. (3 marks)

Prejudice: an unjustified, usually negative, attitude or feeling towards people because of their group membership; discrimination: unfair behaviour or treatment of people because of their group membership; examples, e.g. disliking colleagues who wear a hijab (prejudice) vs. not promoting them because of it (discrimination).
psych12a2-sp-7

A study finds that identical CVs with names suggesting different ethnic backgrounds receive different numbers of interview offers. Identify what this shows about the relationship between stereotypes and discrimination, and propose one strategy to reduce it. (3 marks)

Stereotypes and prejudice can lead to discriminatory behaviour even when applicants' qualifications are identical; the employers' beliefs affected who was selected; strategy, e.g. blind CV screening, cooperative contact, or diversity training that challenges stereotypes.
psych12a2-sp-8
Explain how a stereotype can be self-perpetuating. (2 marks)

People notice and remember information that supports the stereotype (confirmation of belief) while ignoring exceptions; this reinforces the belief and may shape behaviour towards the group in ways that elicit stereotype-consistent responses.
psych12a2-sp-9
Prejudice is best defined as
a generalised belief about the characteristics of a social group
an unjustified, usually negative, attitude towards members of a group because of their group membership
unfair treatment of people because of their group membership
an accurate judgement about the typical behaviour of a group

Prejudice is the affective component: a usually negative attitude or feeling held because of group membership. A generalised belief describes a stereotype, and unfair treatment describes discrimination.
psych12a2-sp-10
Which term describes the tendency to evaluate and treat members of one's own group more favourably than members of other groups?
out-group homogeneity
illusory correlation
in-group favouritism
fundamental attribution error

In-group favouritism is the tendency to favour one's own group over others. Out-group homogeneity is the perception that members of other groups are all alike, illusory correlation is a perceived link between two things that are not actually related, and the fundamental attribution error explains behaviour by personality rather than situation.
psych12a2-sp-11

A student says, 'All the people from that suburb are the same; I can't tell any of them apart,' yet describes the members of their own school as individuals with different personalities. Which bias does the first statement most clearly illustrate?
out-group homogeneity effect
in-group favouritism
the halo effect
