self-serving bias

The out-group homogeneity effect is the tendency to see members of other groups as more alike than members of one's own group. In-group favouritism concerns favourable evaluation of one's own group, the halo effect is a general positive impression spreading across unrelated traits, and self-serving bias is attributing success to oneself.
psych12a2-sp-12

A teacher notices that two rare, unusual misbehaviours both occurred among students from a minority group, and concludes the two behaviours are linked to that group. Which cognitive error most likely explains this conclusion?
self-fulfilling prophecy
just-world hypothesis
fundamental attribution error
illusory correlation

An illusory correlation is the perception of a relationship between two things that the data do not support, often when rare, distinctive events happen together. A self-fulfilling prophecy changes behaviour to match expectations, the just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve, and the fundamental attribution error explains behaviour in terms of personality rather than circumstances.
psych12a2-sp-13

When a person meets a member of a stereotyped group who does not fit the stereotype, they may treat that person as a rare exception and keep the stereotype for the rest of the group. This process is known as
subtyping
conformity
scapegoating
realistic group conflict

Subtyping creates a separate sub-category for the exception so that the broader stereotype is protected. Conformity is changing behaviour to match a group norm, scapegoating blames a group for problems it did not cause, and realistic group conflict arises from competition over scarce resources.
psych12a2-sp-14

A teacher expects a student from a particular group to struggle with maths, so gives them easier tasks and less feedback. The student's results decline and the teacher concludes the expectation was right. This is an example of
fundamental attribution error
in-group favouritism
self-fulfilling prophecy
realistic group conflict

A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when an expectation changes behaviour so that the expected outcome occurs, which then appears to confirm the expectation. The other options describe different processes: attributing behaviour to personality, favouring one's own group, and competing over scarce resources.
psych12a2-sp-15

A company requires all staff to attend full-time meetings during business hours. This excludes many people with caring responsibilities, most of whom are women, even though the company does not intend to disadvantage them. This is best described as
prejudice
institutional discrimination
a stereotype
in-group favouritism

Institutional discrimination occurs when rules or practices that appear neutral disadvantage a group, regardless of intent. Prejudice and stereotypes are attitudes and beliefs held by people, and no such attitude or belief is described here, while in-group favouritism concerns favouring one's own group.
psych12a2-sp-16
Which statement about stereotypes is correct?
Stereotypes are always negative
Stereotypes are feelings rather than beliefs
Stereotypes can only be formed through direct experience with a group
Stereotypes can be positive or negative, and may be accurate, partly accurate or inaccurate

Stereotypes are cognitive generalisations that can be positive or negative and vary in accuracy. Feelings describe prejudice rather than stereotypes, and people often form stereotypes indirectly through the media, family and culture.
psych12a2-sp-17

In a laboratory study, participants are randomly placed into two groups using a meaningless criterion. When asked to allocate rewards between members of the two groups, they consistently give more to their own group. What does this finding best show?
Prejudice requires a long history of conflict between groups
Simply being categorised into a group can produce in-group favouritism
Stereotypes are only formed through direct contact with group members
Discrimination requires a negative attitude towards the other group

This is the minimal group effect: categorisation alone, with no conflict or contact, is enough to produce in-group favouritism. The other options describe conditions that are not necessary for these processes to occur.
psych12a2-sp-18
During an economic downturn, a community blames a small immigrant group for rising unemployment, even though there is no evidence the group caused it. This is an example of
scapegoating
the contact hypothesis
self-serving bias
out-group homogeneity

Scapegoating directs hostility at a group that is blamed for problems it did not cause, often when people feel frustrated. The contact hypothesis describes ways to reduce prejudice, self-serving bias is attributing success to oneself, and out-group homogeneity is perceiving other groups as alike.
psych12a2-sp-19
Which statement best describes implicit prejudice?
An openly stated negative attitude that a person is willing to report
An automatic, often unintentional negative association with a group that a person may not consciously endorse
A stereotype that a person has deliberately chosen to adopt
Discrimination that is carried out in secret

Implicit prejudice operates automatically and may be unconscious, so a person can hold it without agreeing with it when they reflect. Explicit prejudice is consciously held and openly reported, while deliberately chosen beliefs and secret actions do not describe implicit prejudice.
psych12a2-sp-20
Which strategy most directly targets the cognitive component of prejudice?
Enforcing laws that prohibit discriminatory hiring
Providing education that challenges inaccurate stereotypes
Separating groups to avoid conflict
Repeating media images that show the group in typical roles

Education that challenges inaccurate stereotypes works on beliefs, which are the cognitive component. Anti-discrimination laws act on behaviour, separating groups reduces the contact that can weaken prejudice, and repeating typical media images reinforces stereotypes.
psych12a2-sp-21
A woman feels anger whenever she hears about a particular group, but has never treated any member of that group unfairly. Which statement is correct?
She holds prejudice, the affective component, without having discriminated
She shows discrimination because she feels anger
She holds a stereotype, the cognitive component, without any prejudice
She holds no prejudice because she has not acted on her feelings

Prejudice is an attitude and can exist without any unfair behaviour. Discrimination requires an action that treats people unfairly, and the scenario describes feelings rather than a belief about the group's characteristics.
psych12a2-sp-22
In social identity theory, which process involves sorting people, including oneself, into groups such as 'us' and 'them'?
social categorisation
social comparison
social identification
conformity

Social categorisation is the first step, sorting people into in-groups and out-groups. Social identification involves adopting the identity of a group, and social comparison involves evaluating one's own group against others, usually favourably. Conformity is changing behaviour to match group norms and is not one of the theory's processes.
psych12a2-sp-23
Which of the following is an example of discrimination rather than prejudice?
A manager privately believes women are less committed to their careers
A manager feels uneasy whenever a female colleague joins a meeting
A manager promotes a less qualified male colleague over a female colleague because of gender
A manager describes people from one ethnic group as loud and disorganised

Discrimination is an unfair action based on group membership, here the promotion decision. The other options describe beliefs or feelings, which are the cognitive and affective components of prejudice, and do not in themselves involve an unfair action.
psych12a2-sp-24
Which statement best describes the role of stereotypes in social cognition?
They are behaviours that result directly from prejudice
They always reflect accurate knowledge, so they should never be challenged
They are only held by people who are prejudiced
They simplify information processing about groups, but can lead to errors

Stereotypes are a cognitive shortcut that speeds up judgements about groups, but they overgeneralise and can be wrong. Stereotypes are beliefs rather than behaviours, and people without prejudice can still hold them.
psych12a2-sp-25
Which change would most effectively reduce a self-fulfilling prophecy in a classroom where teachers expect some students to struggle?
Telling teachers in advance which students are expected to struggle
Grouping students by their expected ability
Lowering expectations for all students
Giving every student the same challenging tasks and the same quality of feedback

Equal challenge and feedback removes the differential treatment that drives the expected outcome. Telling teachers about expectations reinforces them, grouping by expected ability can produce the same effect, and lowering expectations for all students still limits what everyone is asked to achieve.
psych12a2-sp-26
Which term describes judging a person by their unique characteristics rather than by the group they belong to?
social facilitation
deindividuation
individuation
reactance

Individuation means attending to a person's unique attributes, which reduces reliance on stereotypes. Social facilitation is improved performance in the presence of others, deindividuation is loss of self-awareness in a crowd, and reactance is a response to a threat to personal freedom.
psych12a2-sp-27
State what is meant by an out-group. (1 mark)
A social group that a person does not belong to, which is often perceived as different from, and less favourably than, their own in-group. [1]
psych12a2-sp-28
Explain how an illusory correlation can lead to the formation of a stereotype. (2 marks)

People overestimate the link between rare, distinctive behaviours and a minority group, because such pairings stand out in memory. [1] This leads people to believe the group is associated with that behaviour, which becomes a stereotype. [1]
psych12a2-sp-29
Outline how the out-group homogeneity effect can contribute to prejudice. (2 marks)

Members of an out-group are seen as more alike than members of the in-group, so individual differences are overlooked. [1] This makes it easier to apply one negative belief to all out-group members, supporting prejudice. [1]
psych12a2-sp-30
Distinguish between direct discrimination and institutional discrimination, giving one example of each. (3 marks)

Direct discrimination: a person or organisation deliberately treats someone less favourably because of their group membership, e.g. refusing to hire someone because of their religion. [1] Institutional discrimination: a policy or practice that appears neutral disadvantages a group regardless of intent, e.g. a roster that excludes people with caring responsibilities. [1] Both produce unfair outcomes based on group membership; the key difference is intent. [1]
psych12a2-sp-31
Explain why individuating information about a member of a stereotyped group can reduce the influence of the stereotype on judgements of that person. (3 marks)

Individuating information gives specific personal details that the stereotype does not describe. [1] Because a stereotype is a generalisation, this makes it less likely to be applied to the person. [1] Judgements then rely on the person's own characteristics rather than their group membership. [1]
psych12a2-sp-32
Explain how a common in-group identity could reduce prejudice between two groups. (3 marks)

Recategorisation places members of both groups within a shared, superordinate category, so they are seen as one in-group. [1] Former out-group members are then evaluated more favourably as part of the shared group. [1] This weakens the us-versus-them boundary, reducing prejudice and in-group bias. [1]
psych12a2-sp-33
Explain how social identity theory accounts for in-group favouritism. Refer to categorisation, identification and comparison in your answer. (3 marks)

Categorisation: people sort themselves and others into groups, creating in-groups and out-groups. [1] Identification: people adopt their group's identity, which becomes part of their self-concept. [1] Comparison: people compare their in-group with out-groups and evaluate their own group more positively to protect self-esteem, leading to favouritism. [1]
psych12a2-sp-34
Using the terms cognitive, affective and behavioural, explain why a law banning discriminatory hiring may not eliminate prejudice. (4 marks)

Laws target the behavioural component by making discriminatory actions illegal. [1] Prejudice also has affective (feelings) and cognitive (stereotype) components, which laws do not directly change. [1] A person may stop discriminating while still holding negative feelings and stereotypes, so prejudice can persist. [1] Interventions that change beliefs and feelings, such as education and positive contact, are needed to address these components. [1]
psych12a2-sp-35

A community experiences conflict between two groups competing for limited jobs. Using realistic group conflict theory, explain how this competition may increase prejudice, and outline one strategy that could reduce it. (4 marks)

Competition for scarce resources creates real conflicts of interest between the groups. [1] Groups come to see each other as rivals, increasing hostility and negative stereotypes of the out-group. [1] Realistic group conflict theory predicts that prejudice increases as competition intensifies. [1] A strategy such as introducing superordinate goals that require both groups to cooperate can reduce the conflict. [1]
psych12a2-sp-36
Explain how the just-world hypothesis can encourage prejudice against a disadvantaged group. (2 marks)

Believing that people get what they deserve leads people to see members of a disadvantaged group as responsible for their own misfortune. [1] This justifies unfair treatment or indifference towards the group, supporting prejudice and discrimination. [1]
vce-psych12-sp-c1
Which condition is most important for intergroup contact to reduce prejudice?
The groups are simply placed together in the same room for a long period of time
One group is given more status, so the other group learns to respect it
The groups work cooperatively, with equal status, towards a shared goal supported by authority
The groups compete for a prize, so they get to know each other's strengths
Contact alone can increase hostility; cooperation and equal status (as in the jigsaw classroom) are needed.
vce-psych12-heuristics-and-cognitive-bia: A heuristic is best described as
a systematic, step-by-step method that guarantees the correct answer
a mental shortcut that allows quick judgements and decisions but may lead to errors
Heuristics are rules of thumb that speed up judgement, sacrificing some accuracy.
After seeing news reports of several shark attacks, Tom decides swimming at the beach is very dangerous, even though attacks are rare. Which heuristic is Tom using?
The availability heuristic judges probability by how easily examples come to mind, and vivid news stories make shark attacks seem common.
Ayesha assumes a quiet, bookish person at a party is more likely to be a librarian than a salesperson, ignoring that there are far more salespeople. This is the
The representativeness heuristic judges likelihood by how well something matches a prototype, ignoring base rates.
Which of the following best describes confirmation bias?
Seeking, interpreting and remembering information that supports existing beliefs while overlooking contradictory evidence
Attributing one's failures to external causes
Judging an event as likely because it is easy to recall
Confirmation bias is a cognitive bias in which we favour information consistent with our beliefs. D describes the availability heuristic.
A voter reads only articles that support her preferred party and dismisses opposing articles as unreliable. This is an example of
She is selecting and interpreting information to fit her existing view, which is confirmation bias.
Define a cognitive bias and explain how it differs from a heuristic. (3 marks)

Cognitive bias: a systematic error in thinking or judgement that can affect decisions; heuristic: a mental shortcut or rule of thumb used to make quick decisions; heuristics are the strategies and biases are the systematic errors that can result, e.g. availability heuristic causing overestimation of vivid events.
After a plane crash is widely covered in the news, Ben cancels his flight and drives 800 km instead. Identify the heuristic involved and explain why his decision may be poorly reasoned. (3 marks)

Availability heuristic; the vivid crash coverage makes plane crashes easy to recall, so he overestimates their probability; statistically driving is riskier per distance travelled, so the decision relies on a biased estimate rather than actual risk.
Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using heuristics in everyday decision making. (2 marks)

Advantage: fast and efficient, saving time and cognitive effort when information is limited; disadvantage: can lead to errors or biased judgements, e.g. ignoring base rates or overestimating vivid events.
A shopper sees a jacket labelled 'Was $300, now $120'. Even though $300 was never a real selling price, the figure makes $120 seem like a bargain. Which bias is most directly involved?

The original price acts as an anchor, and the shopper's judgement of value is not adjusted sufficiently away from it. The availability heuristic depends on how easily examples come to mind, and hindsight bias concerns judging past events as predictable.

Most people judge the sequence H T H T T H as more likely to come from a fair coin than the sequence H H H H H H, even though both sequences have the same probability. Which heuristic best explains this judgement?

The mixed sequence looks more like people's idea of a random sequence, so it is judged as more representative of a fair coin. The affect heuristic relies on emotional reactions, and anchoring relies on an initial reference value, so neither explains a judgement about how a sequence looks.
Eli rejects a new medicine without reading the trial results because he dislikes the company that makes it. Which heuristic is he most likely using?

The affect heuristic involves judging an option by the emotional response it provokes, here dislike of the company. The availability heuristic would depend on how easily negative examples come to mind, not on feelings about the company.
After a team loses a grand final, a fan says, 'The signs were there all along; I knew they would lose.' Which bias does this statement show?

Hindsight bias is the tendency to believe, once an outcome is known, that it was predictable beforehand. Confirmation bias concerns seeking and interpreting information that supports existing beliefs, which is not what the fan is doing here.
Liam is sure that most students at his school prefer online lectures, because all his friends do. A survey later finds only 35% agree. Which bias is Liam showing?

The false consensus effect is the tendency to overestimate how many others share our own views, here based on a small circle of friends. Optimism bias concerns underestimating personal risk, which is not the issue in this scenario.
A teacher is told that a student's gifted test results were fabricated, yet still believes the student is gifted because of those results. Which bias is involved?

Belief perseverance is the tendency to keep a belief after the evidence that created it has been discredited. The halo effect involves one positive trait shaping overall impressions, which does not describe a belief that survives discredited evidence.
Most drivers rate their own driving as better than average. Which bias best explains this?

Overconfidence, or illusory superiority, is the tendency to overrate one's own abilities relative to others. The gambler's fallacy involves wrongly expecting chance outcomes to balance out, which has nothing to do with self-assessment.

A treatment is described as having a '90% survival rate' rather than a '10% mortality rate'. People are more willing to choose it when framed this way, though the facts are identical. Which bias is at work?

The framing effect is the tendency for the same information, presented in different ways, to change decisions. The availability heuristic depends on how easily examples come to mind, not on how information is worded.

A screening test correctly identifies a condition 95% of the time. The condition affects 1 in 100 people. Maya tests positive and concludes she has a 95% chance of having the condition, without considering how rare the condition is. Which error is she making?

Base rate neglect is ignoring how common a condition is in the population when judging the probability for an individual. Anchoring involves being pulled towards a starting figure, which is not the main error in Maya's reasoning.
A gambler believes that blowing on a pair of dice before rolling them will make a high score more likely. Which bias is shown?

The illusion of control is the belief that one can influence outcomes that are actually determined by chance. The gambler's fallacy is the mistaken expectation that a random outcome is 'due' after a run of other outcomes, which is a different error.
After six reds in a row on a roulette wheel, Jin bets heavily on black because black is 'due'. Which error is Jin making?

Each spin is independent, so a run of reds does not raise the chance of black, yet the gambler's fallacy expects a balancing outcome. Illusion of control would involve believing one can influence the spin, which Jin does not claim.
Ruby keeps watching a film she finds dull because she has already paid for the ticket. Which bias is she showing?

The sunk cost fallacy is continuing a course of action because of resources already spent, even though those costs cannot be recovered. Confirmation bias concerns seeking information that supports existing beliefs, which does not fit this decision about how to spend time.
Most smokers believe they are less likely than other smokers to develop lung disease. Which bias is this?

Optimism bias is the tendency to believe that negative events are less likely to happen to oneself than to others. Self-serving bias concerns explaining one's own outcomes, not forecasting one's own future risk.
Asked which of two cities has the larger population, a person chooses the one they have heard of and knows nothing else about. Which heuristic is being used?

The recognition heuristic chooses the recognised option when only one option is familiar. The availability heuristic judges by ease of recalling examples, which is a different process from simply recognising a name.
Which statement about cognitive biases is accurate?
They are deliberate choices people make after careful reasoning
They are systematic errors in thinking that can occur without the person being aware of them
They only affect people with low levels of intelligence
They can be removed completely by making one conscious decision

Cognitive biases are systematic patterns of error that often operate automatically and outside awareness. The other options are wrong because biases are not deliberate, affect people across all levels of intelligence, and cannot be eliminated by a single decision.
A teacher rates a student's essays highly on every criterion because the student is polite and well presented. Which bias is most evident?

The halo effect is when one positive trait shapes judgements about unrelated qualities. Confirmation bias would involve seeking evidence for an existing belief, rather than forming a general impression from a single trait.

Linda is described as outspoken and concerned with social justice. Most people judge 'Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement' as more probable than 'Linda is a bank teller', although the first can never be more likely than the second. Which error is this?

The conjunction fallacy is judging a combination of two events as more probable than one of them alone, because the combined description seems more representative of Linda. Base rate neglect involves ignoring how common a category is, which is not the error in this pairing.
Explain how the anchoring effect could influence the final salary agreed in a job negotiation. (2 marks)

The first salary figure offered acts as an anchor or reference point [1]; later offers and the final agreement are adjusted insufficiently away from that figure, so the outcome is pulled towards it [1].
Name the bias in which people believe, once an outcome is known, that it was predictable all along. (1 mark)

A doctor diagnoses a patient whose symptoms closely match her textbook description of a rare virus, without considering how uncommon the virus is in the community. Identify the heuristic involved and explain the error. (3 marks)

Representativeness heuristic: the diagnosis is judged by how closely the symptoms resemble the doctor's prototype of the virus [1]; base rate (prevalence) information is ignored, so the likelihood of this rare virus is overestimated [1]; the judgement relies on resemblance rather than the statistical probability of the illness [1].
Jade has kept investing in a failing business because she has already spent a large amount of money on it. Name the bias, explain why it is an error, and suggest one strategy to reduce it. (4 marks)

Sunk cost fallacy [1]; her decision is driven by past, unrecoverable costs rather than the expected future costs and benefits [1]; past investment should be irrelevant to whether further investment is worthwhile [1]; a strategy such as evaluating only future prospects or seeking an independent, objective review [1].
Explain how the recognition heuristic can lead to a correct judgement, and describe one situation in which it would fail. (3 marks)

When only one option is recognised, that option is chosen [1]; this can be accurate because recognition often correlates with the quantity being judged, such as a city's population [1]; it fails when recognition reflects factors unrelated to the judged criterion, such as a small town being well known because of a famous sporting team [1].
Define the term base rate. (1 mark)
The overall frequency or proportion of a condition or event in a population, which should inform judgements about an individual case [1].
Define the false consensus effect and describe how it could affect a person's judgement of others. (4 marks)

The tendency to overestimate how many other people share one's own beliefs, attitudes or behaviours [1]; the person treats their own views as typical of the majority [1]; this can lead to misperceiving social norms, such as believing most people support a policy simply because the person does [1]; it can also lead to inaccurate predictions of others' behaviour and a reduced understanding of differing views [1].
Explain the illusion of control and give an example. (2 marks)
The belief that one can influence outcomes that are actually determined by chance [1]; e.g. a player who believes that choosing 'lucky' numbers improves their chance of winning a lottery [1].
Explain how the availability heuristic and the representativeness heuristic differ. Give a different example for each. (4 marks)

Availability heuristic: likelihood is judged by how easily examples come to mind [1]; e.g. a resident who recalls several recent local burglaries overestimates the crime rate in their suburb [1]; representativeness heuristic: likelihood is judged by how closely something matches a prototype or category [1]; e.g. judging an unfamiliar man who is neatly dressed and punctual to be an accountant because he matches that stereotype [1].
After heavy news coverage of a plane crash, a person decides flying is more dangerous than driving. This reflects:
The anchoring bias: the first figure heard sets the estimate of risk
The false-consensus bias: assuming others share the same fear of flying
The halo effect: one bad feature makes the whole airline seem unsafe
The availability heuristic: vivid, easily recalled examples seem more common
Judgements of how likely something is are distorted by how easily examples come to mind. Driving is statistically far more dangerous per trip.
vce-psych12-obedience: psych12a2-ob-1
Obedience is best defined as
following the orders or commands of an authority figure
agreeing with a group in public but not in private
copying the behaviour of a role model
changing behaviour to match the behaviour of a majority
Obedience is a form of social influence where a person complies with directions from an authority figure. A describes conformity.
psych12a2-ob-2
In Milgram's obedience study, about what percentage of participants delivered the maximum 450-volt shock?
Around 95%
Around 10%
Around 25%
Around 65%
In the baseline study 65% of participants delivered the maximum shock, a far higher proportion than psychiatrists had predicted.
psych12a2-ob-3
In Milgram's variations, obedience dropped significantly when
the experimenter left the room and gave instructions by telephone
the study was held at Yale University
the participant was paid more
the learner was in a different room from the teacher
Obedience fell when the authority figure was physically absent. The Yale setting added prestige and did not reduce obedience.
psych12a2-ob-4
Which ethical concern was most strongly raised about Milgram's original study?
Participants were not randomly assigned to groups
The sample was too large
Lack of a control group
Participants experienced psychological distress and were deceived about the true purpose
Deception and the distress caused to participants raised concerns about informed consent and protection from harm. Debriefing was provided after the study.
psych12a2-ob-5
Which factor would most likely increase obedience?
The authority figure wears a uniform and appears legitimate
The presence of another person who refuses to obey
The authority figure being far away
The person taking responsibility for their actions
Legitimacy and symbols of authority such as a uniform increase obedience. B and C reduce it, and D (taking personal responsibility) also reduces it.
psych12a2-ob-6
Outline two situational factors that increased obedience in Milgram's research. (2 marks)

Authority figure physically present/close to the participant; prestigious or legitimate setting (e.g. Yale), lab coat; learner at a distance from the participant; gradual escalation of shocks (any two, each described).
psych12a2-ob-7

A junior nurse administers a dose of medication that she suspects is too high because the senior doctor insists it is correct. Using obedience research, explain two reasons she might comply. (3 marks)

Perceived legitimacy and expertise of the authority figure (doctor in a hospital setting); diffusion of responsibility, believing the doctor is responsible for the outcome; a third factor such as the pressure of hierarchy or gradual escalation; at least two reasons linked to the scenario.
psych12a2-ob-8
Describe one ethical guideline that Milgram's study may have breached and explain how a modern researcher could address it. (3 marks)

Breach identified, e.g. informed consent (participants were deceived), or protection from harm/withdrawal rights (participants were pressed to continue); explanation of how it is breached; modern approach, e.g. full debriefing, ethics committee approval, risk assessment, stopping at lower shock levels, or allowing withdrawal without pressure.
psych12a2-ob-9
In Milgram's original study, what was the role of the 'learner'?
an actor who pretended to receive the shocks and gave scripted responses
a fellow volunteer who was randomly assigned the teacher role
a researcher who secretly operated the shock generator
a student who had agreed to take part in a separate memory test

The learner was a confederate who received no real shocks and followed a script of protests, while teachers believed he was a real volunteer. A genuine fellow volunteer in that role would have meant a real person receiving shocks, which Milgram avoided.
psych12a2-ob-10
How were participants assigned to the 'teacher' role in Milgram's study?
They chose their own role after reading a description of each task
The draw was rigged so the real participant always became the teacher and the confederate the learner
The experimenter selected teachers using a personality test
A computer assigned roles at random, giving each person an equal chance of either role

The draw looked random but was fixed, so the real participant was always the teacher and the confederate always the learner. Genuine random allocation would have given each person an equal chance of either role, so the computer option misses what actually happened.
psych12a2-ob-11
Milgram's shock generator labelled switches from 15 volts to 450 volts in 15-volt steps. How many switches did it have?
Dividing 450 by 15 gives 30 switches, one for each 15-volt step. Choosing 15 confuses the number of switches with the lowest voltage on the generator.
psych12a2-ob-12
Who were the participants in Milgram's original baseline study?
120 Yale undergraduate students who received course credit
40 psychiatric patients referred by hospital staff
400 volunteers recruited from military training camps
40 men aged 20 to 50 from a range of occupations, recruited through newspaper advertisements
The baseline sample was 40 men aged 20 to 50 from varied occupations, recruited through newspaper advertising. The other options describe samples that Milgram did not use.
psych12a2-ob-13
In Hofling et al.'s (1966) hospital study, what did the researchers find?
21 of the 22 nurses were prepared to give an unauthorised dose on the phone order of an unknown doctor
Most nurses refused the order because the drug label clearly stated the maximum dose
All 22 nurses checked the dose with a pharmacist before administering it
Nurses only obeyed when the doctor was physically present on the ward

21 of 22 nurses were prepared to give twice the stated maximum dose when a doctor they did not know ordered it by telephone. The refusal and pharmacist options contradict the finding, and the physical presence option is wrong because the doctor was not on the ward.
psych12a2-ob-14
Milgram explained obedience using the idea of an 'agentic state'. Which description best fits this state?
feeling personally responsible for every outcome of one's actions
seeing oneself as the agent of an authority figure, so responsibility is shifted to that authority
copying the behaviour of the majority to avoid standing out
refusing orders that conflict with one's personal moral values

In an agentic state a person acts as the instrument of another's wishes and feels less responsible for what follows. Feeling personally responsible for every outcome describes the autonomous state, which Milgram contrasted with the agentic state.
psych12a2-ob-15
A student changes her answer on a multiple-choice quiz to match the answer most of her classmates gave. This is best described as
obedience, because she is following the group's instructions
compliance, because she responded to a direct request
conformity, because she changed her behaviour to match the majority
identification, because she wants to be like her classmates
Conformity is changing behaviour to match a group majority without a direct order. Obedience requires a command from an authority figure, and no one in this scenario gives one.
psych12a2-ob-16
Milgram later tested female participants in a similar procedure. His results showed that
women obeyed far less, with only about one in five going to 450 volts
women refused to continue beyond 150 volts in every case
women could not be tested because they refused to take the teacher role
women obeyed at roughly the same rate as men
Milgram found that women obeyed at roughly the same rate as men, which challenged the idea that gender strongly affects obedience. The other options contradict this finding.
psych12a2-ob-17
A modern researcher in Australia planning an obedience study must first have the proposal approved by which body?
a human research ethics committee (HREC), which reviews a study before it begins
the Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority, which reviews all research
a university's marketing department, which checks the study's appeal to participants
the researcher's own supervisor alone, with no external review

Research involving humans in Australia is normally reviewed by a human research ethics committee before it begins, to assess risks and the consent process. The other bodies do not approve research ethics, and supervisor review alone is not independent.
psych12a2-ob-18
A bus driver is told by a dispatcher to skip a scheduled stop and is assured that the company will take full responsibility. According to obedience research, what effect does this assurance have?
It reduces obedience, because the driver feels more personal responsibility for the outcome
It increases obedience, because the driver may feel less responsible for the outcome
It has no effect, because only the driver's personality determines compliance
It makes the driver more likely to refuse, because the assurance makes the instruction seem unsafe

Shifting responsibility to an authority encourages an agentic state, so people feel less personally responsible and comply more. The option that reduces obedience reverses this effect, and the no-effect option ignores the situational factors Milgram identified.
psych12a2-ob-19
Milgram reported that many teachers showed visible signs of stress while continuing to administer shocks. Which signs were reported?
calm, detached acceptance with no visible reaction
immediate refusal to continue after the first protest
nervous laughter, trembling and sweating
cheering when the learner stopped answering

Many teachers showed distress through nervous laughter, trembling and sweating, yet most continued. The calm acceptance and cheering options misrepresent the observations, and immediate refusal was not the typical response.
psych12a2-ob-20
In Milgram's baseline study, how was obedience measured?
the number of questions the teacher answered correctly
how long the teacher waited before pressing the switch
the number of times the teacher asked the experimenter for advice
the highest shock level the teacher was willing to administer
Obedience was measured as the highest shock level a teacher was prepared to administer, with 450 volts representing full obedience. The other options are not the measure Milgram used.
psych12a2-ob-21
Which individual-difference explanation of obedience did Adorno and colleagues (1950) propose?
the authoritarian personality, a set of traits linked to submission to authority
the agentic personality, a tendency to shift responsibility to others
the conformist personality, a tendency to match the majority
the Machiavellian personality, a tendency to manipulate others

Adorno and colleagues proposed the authoritarian personality, a dispositional explanation linking submission to authority with a set of traits. The agentic state is Milgram's situational concept, not a personality type.
psych12a2-ob-22
A key strength of Milgram's research procedure was that it
had high ecological validity because it used real-world authority figures
used over 1000 participants, making the results generalisable
was highly standardised, which allowed it to be replicated
removed all ethical concerns through full debriefing

Standardised procedures, such as scripted prods and set shock levels, allowed other researchers to replicate the study. The other options are either false or describe weaknesses rather than strengths.
psych12a2-ob-23
Explain why many of Milgram's teachers kept administering shocks even while showing signs of conflict. (2 marks)

Teachers experienced conflict between their own values (not harming another person) and the experimenter's instructions [1]; continuing despite this shows that the authority's demands can override personal conscience, a key finding of the study [1].
psych12a2-ob-24
Describe the difference between obedience and conformity, giving one example of each. (3 marks)

Obedience is following a direct order or command from an authority figure [1]; conformity is changing behaviour to match a group or majority without a direct order [1]; valid examples of each, e.g. a soldier following a commander's order (obedience) and a teenager adopting the clothing style of friends (conformity) [1].
psych12a2-ob-25
Evaluate the strengths and limitations of Milgram's obedience research. (4 marks)

Strength: the standardised procedure (set shock levels, scripted prods and a confederate learner) allowed the study to be replicated [1]; strength: later replications have supported the general finding that ordinary people obey strongly, adding reliability [1]; limitation: the original sample was small and all male, limiting generalisability [1]; limitation: deception and psychological distress raise serious ethical concerns [1].
psych12a2-ob-26
Explain the purpose of the experimenter's standard verbal prods in Milgram's study. (2 marks)

The prods were scripted instructions to continue (e.g. 'The experiment requires that you continue') [1]; they standardised the pressure so every participant received the same instructions, allowing fair comparison [1].
psych12a2-ob-27
Burger (2009) replicated Milgram's procedure but stopped at 150 volts. Explain why he stopped at this point and what the replication showed. (3 marks)

The study was stopped for ethical reasons, to reduce the risk of psychological harm to participants [1]; 150 volts is where the learner first protests and asks to be released, so the most distressing shocks were avoided [1]; obedience up to that point was similar to Milgram's original results, supporting the replicability of the findings [1].
psych12a2-ob-28
Define 'legitimate authority' as it applies to obedience. (1 mark)
An authority figure whose power is seen as rightful or accepted, for example because of their position, expertise or the institution they represent [1].
psych12a2-ob-29
Explain how the gradual increase in shock levels in Milgram's study may have increased obedience. (2 marks)

Each step was only slightly higher than the last, so refusing at any point felt inconsistent with having already complied [1]; once teachers had continued through earlier levels they were committed to going on, a foot-in-the-door effect [1].
psych12a2-ob-30
Explain one advantage and one limitation of conducting obedience research in a controlled laboratory. (2 marks)

Advantage: variables such as shock levels and prods can be controlled, so cause-and-effect conclusions and replication are possible [1]; limitation: the artificial setting may reduce ecological validity, so results may not generalise to everyday situations [1].
psych12a2-ob-31
Explain how Milgram's research suggests that obedience depends on the situation rather than on fixed personality traits. (3 marks)

Participants were ordinary people from varied occupations, and most obeyed to the maximum, suggesting obedience is common rather than limited to unusual personalities [1]; obedience changed substantially when situational features changed, such as the authority figure's presence or the learner's proximity, which fixed traits cannot explain [1]; so the situation is a key determinant of obedience [1].
vce-psych12-ob-c1
In variations of Milgram's obedience study, which change led to a large drop in obedience?
The 'learner' was moved to a separate room, out of the teacher's sight
The study was run in a university building with an official appearance
The experimenter wore a grey lab coat and spoke in a firm, calm voice
The experimenter gave instructions by telephone instead of in person
Obedience fell when the authority figure was absent; the original set-up (learner in another room, at Yale) gave about 65% full obedience.
vce-psych12-conformity-and-group-influen: psych12a2-cg-1
Conformity refers to
refusing to change one's opinion
doing the opposite of what a group does
obeying a direct order from an authority figure
adjusting one's behaviour or beliefs to match those of a group or social norm
Conformity is changing behaviour or attitudes in response to real or imagined group pressure. A is obedience.
psych12a2-cg-2
In Asch's line-judgement experiments, a participant tended to give an incorrect answer when
alone in a room
all other group members, who were confederates, gave the same incorrect answer
one confederate gave the correct answer
the task was very difficult
The majority's unanimous incorrect responses led about a third of responses to be incorrect; having an ally who gave the right answer reduced conformity.
psych12a2-cg-3
A teenager starts wearing a style of shoes because everyone in the group does, even though she privately dislikes them. This is an example of
informational influence
obedience
internalisation
normative influence leading to compliance
Normative influence is the desire to be liked or accepted, producing outward conformity without private acceptance.
psych12a2-cg-4
Which of the following would most likely reduce conformity in an Asch-type task?
Having the participant respond publicly in front of the group
Having at least one other person disagree with the majority
Making the task more ambiguous
Increasing the size of the majority to 15 people
Dissent from even one other person breaks unanimity and reduces conformity. Ambiguity increases conformity.
psych12a2-cg-5
Social loafing occurs when
a group makes riskier decisions than individuals
individuals put in less effort when working in a group than when working alone
individuals put in more effort when in a group
people follow orders blindly
Social loafing is reduced individual effort in a group, often because contributions are not individually identifiable.
psych12a2-cg-6
Describe two factors that influence the level of conformity to a group. (2 marks)

Group size (conformity increases up to a point, e.g. 3 or 4 members); unanimity (a dissenter reduces conformity); also task ambiguity, group status or whether responses are public/private (any two, each described).
psych12a2-cg-7

Zoe is in a group project in which the marks are given to the whole group only. She does less work than she would on her own. Identify the concept shown and suggest two ways a teacher could reduce it. (3 marks)
Social loafing; make individual contributions identifiable or assess them individually; use smaller groups or give each member a defined role; (any two strategies, linked to the concept).
psych12a2-cg-8
Distinguish between normative influence and informational influence, using an example for each. (3 marks)

Normative influence: conforming to be accepted or avoid rejection by the group (e.g. wearing a brand because friends do); informational influence: conforming because the group is seen as having correct information in an ambiguous situation (e.g. copying others' choice of exit in an unfamiliar building); clear difference in motivation (belonging vs accuracy).
psych12a2-cg-9

In Sherif's (1935) autokinetic experiments, a single point of light in a dark room appeared to move. When participants heard others' estimates, their own estimates converged towards a shared figure. This is an example of
normative influence, where people conform to be accepted by the group
informational influence, where people look to others to judge an ambiguous situation
obedience to an authority figure
social loafing, where individuals reduce their effort in a group

The light gave no objective reference point, so the situation was ambiguous and participants used others' estimates as a guide to accuracy. Normative influence is wrong because the aim was to be right, not to be accepted by the group.
psych12a2-cg-10
A meta-analysis of Asch-type conformity studies carried out in many countries (Bond & Smith, 1996) found that conformity rates tended to be higher in
individualist cultures, which emphasise personal independence and self-expression
urban populations, which have more anonymous contact with others
collectivist cultures, which emphasise group harmony and belonging
every culture equally, because conformity is entirely innate

Collectivist cultures value group harmony and interdependence, so their members are more inclined to align with the group. Individualist cultures tend to show lower conformity, so a similar rate in every culture is also wrong.
psych12a2-cg-11

In Latané, Williams and Harkins's (1979) study, participants made as much noise as they could by clapping or shouting, either alone or in groups. As group size increased, the noise produced by each person
increased, because people feel more energised in a crowd
stayed the same, showing that group size makes no difference
increased only when the participants could see one another
decreased, showing social loafing

Output per person fell as group size grew, which is the reduction in individual effort known as social loafing. An increase in per-person output would be the opposite of loafing, and no change would mean group size had no effect.
psych12a2-cg-12
Group polarisation refers to the tendency for
groups to always reach a compromise between the most extreme positions held by members
group discussion to strengthen members' initial shared views, so the group decision becomes more extreme than the average individual decision
members to become less confident in their views after hearing others
groups to split into two equal factions when they cannot agree

Discussion pushes the group towards a more extreme version of the view its members already shared, whether that view was cautious or risky. A compromise between extremes is a different process and is not what polarisation describes.
psych12a2-cg-13
Which of the following is a symptom of groupthink, as described by Janis?
an illusion of invulnerability, in which members believe the group cannot make a serious mistake
members deliberately seeking criticism from outside experts
a leader inviting open disagreement before a decision is made
decision makers repeatedly testing alternative options against evidence

Groupthink includes an illusion of invulnerability, in which members believe the group cannot make a serious mistake. The other options describe open, critical decision making, which is the opposite of groupthink.
psych12a2-cg-14
Deindividuation is most likely to occur when people
are asked to state their own names and identify themselves to the group
work on a task alone with a clear personal goal
are anonymous in a large crowd and feel less personally accountable
are paid individually for each contribution they make

Anonymity in a crowd reduces self-awareness and personal accountability, which can weaken normal restraint. Being identifiable or working alone with personal goals increases self-awareness, so these options describe conditions that reduce deindividuation.
psych12a2-cg-15
In a variation of Asch's study, participants wrote their answers privately instead of stating them aloud in front of the group. Conformity in this condition was
higher, because participants felt more pressure to appear consistent
lower than when answers were given publicly
unchanged, because the group could still hear the other answers
eliminated entirely, because private responses removed all social pressure

Responding publicly increases conformity because participants fear disapproval, and private responding removes some of that pressure. Private responding reduces conformity but does not remove it entirely, so 'eliminated entirely' is a common overstatement.
psych12a2-cg-16
According to Moscovici's research on minority influence, a minority is most likely to change the majority's view when it
is made up of high-status members of the group
gives different answers on every trial so that its position is unpredictable
is consistent and confident in its position over time
gives the same answer as the majority in public but a different answer in private

Consistency over time makes a minority appear confident and can lead the majority to reconsider its view. Random or inconsistent answers reduce the minority's credibility, so they are a common mistake.
psych12a2-cg-17
In Asch's (1951) line-judgement experiment, each participant completed 18 trials. How many of these trials were critical trials, in which the confederates gave the same incorrect answer?

Asch used 18 trials, of which 12 were critical trials with unanimous incorrect answers from confederates and 6 were neutral. Using all 18 trials, or counting only the 6 neutral ones, are the common errors.
psych12a2-cg-18
In an Asch-type study, a participant conformed on 4 of the 12 critical trials. What percentage of the critical trials did the participant conform on?
4 ÷ 12 = 0.33, so 33%. Dividing by all 18 trials gives 22%, which wrongly includes the neutral trials where conformity could not occur.
psych12a2-cg-19
On a crowded train, a passenger collapses. Other passengers look around, see that no one is responding, and conclude that the situation is not serious. This is best explained by
normative influence, as passengers want to avoid standing out
informational influence, as passengers use others' inaction as evidence about the situation
obedience, as passengers are following a driver's instructions
social loafing, as individuals reduce effort when working in a group

Passengers treat others' lack of response as evidence about how serious the situation is, which is informational influence in an ambiguous setting. Normative influence would apply if the main concern were being judged by others rather than finding out what is happening.
psych12a2-cg-20
In Asch's post-experiment interviews, some participants who had given the group's wrong answer said that
they had not been paying attention to the task at all
they had been told in advance that the confederates would give wrong answers
they knew the correct answer but gave the group's answer to avoid looking foolish
their answers had been recorded for a later study on memory

Asch's interviews revealed that some participants knew the correct answer but gave the group's answer to avoid looking foolish. This shows that conformity can occur without any change in private belief.
psych12a2-cg-21
Which of the following conditions is most likely to reduce social loafing in a team?
a task that team members see as meaningful and important
a task in which only the group's total output is measured
a larger team in which each member's role is undefined
a reward shared equally by all members, regardless of individual effort

People loaf less when the task matters to them, because their own motivation rises. Measuring only the group total and sharing rewards regardless of effort encourage loafing, so they are the wrong direction.
psych12a2-cg-22
A factory worker wears safety goggles only when the supervisor is on the floor. Privately, he thinks the rule is unnecessary. This is an example of
internalisation
compliance
identification
informational influence

Compliance is changing behaviour to gain a reward or avoid punishment without private acceptance, and here the goggles are worn only when observed. Internalisation would mean genuinely accepting the rule, and informational influence would apply only if the worker were unsure what was safe.
psych12a2-cg-23
Deutsch and Gerard (1955) proposed that conformity is driven by two needs. These are the need for accurate information and
the need for independence and self-expression
the need to obey legitimate authority
the need to win arguments within the group
the need to be liked and accepted by others

The need to be liked and accepted underlies normative influence, while the need for accurate information underlies informational influence. Independence and obedience are not the second need in this model, so they are tempting but wrong.
psych12a2-cg-24
Approximately what proportion of Asch's (1951) participants conformed at least once on the critical trials?
about 25%
about 50%
about 75%
about 100%
Asch found that about three-quarters of participants conformed at least once, even though on average only about a third of critical responses were incorrect.
psych12a2-cg-25
According to Janis, groupthink is most likely to develop when a group is
highly cohesive, isolated from outside opinions and under time pressure
made up of members with very different backgrounds who are encouraged to debate freely
led by a leader who asks for independent written opinions before discussion
small, with clearly defined roles and an outside facilitator

Janis linked groupthink to high cohesion, isolation from outside views, a directive leader and time pressure, which together discourage members from voicing doubts. The other options describe conditions that promote critical thinking, so they are tempting but wrong.
psych12a2-cg-26
Outline the procedure of Asch's (1951) line-judgement experiment. (3 marks)

A naive participant was seated among confederates who had been instructed in advance to give answers [1]; the group judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard line over 18 trials [1]; on the 12 critical trials the confederates unanimously gave the same incorrect answer, and the participant usually answered last [1].
psych12a2-cg-27
Outline how compliance, identification and internalisation differ as processes of social influence. (4 marks)

Compliance: changing behaviour to gain a reward or avoid punishment, without private acceptance [1]; identification: adopting behaviour to maintain a satisfying relationship with a respected person or group, with private beliefs possibly unchanged [1]; internalisation: genuinely accepting the belief or behaviour, so it is maintained even when no one is watching [1]; the key difference is motivation and permanence, as compliance and identification depend on the social context while internalisation depends on the person's own values [1].
psych12a2-cg-28
Explain why an individual is less likely to help a person in distress when other people are present. (2 marks)

Diffusion of responsibility: each bystander feels less personally responsible for acting, so responsibility is shared among those present [1]; informational influence: bystanders look to one another, see no one acting, and conclude that help is not needed [1].
psych12a2-cg-29
Explain how deindividuation can lead to antisocial behaviour in a crowd. (3 marks)

Anonymity in a crowd reduces a person's sense of individual identity and accountability [1]; lower self-awareness weakens normal self-restraint and personal moral standards [1]; the crowd's emotional arousal and norms can then encourage behaviour, such as vandalism, that the person would not normally perform [1].
psych12a2-cg-30

A company board unanimously approves a risky plan. Two directors privately have doubts but say nothing, and the chair describes anyone who questions the plan as disloyal. Identify three symptoms of groupthink shown in this scenario. (3 marks)
Self-censorship: the directors with doubts keep quiet [1]; pressure on dissenters: the chair labels critics as disloyal [1]; illusion of unanimity: the board treats silence as agreement [1].
psych12a2-cg-31
Explain the difference between conformity and obedience, using one example of each. (4 marks)

Conformity: changing behaviour or beliefs to match a group or social norm, without a direct order [1]; obedience: following a direct order from an authority figure [1]; example of conformity: a student wears the same style of clothing as her friends to fit in [1]; example of obedience: a nurse gives a patient a medication dose because a doctor instructs it [1].
psych12a2-cg-32
Describe what Sherif's (1935) autokinetic studies showed about the persistence of group norms. (3 marks)

An estimate formed through group interaction continued to be used by participants when they were later tested alone [1]; this showed the norm had been accepted privately, not just displayed for others [1]; participants relied on the group's estimate as a guide to accuracy because the task was ambiguous [1].
psych12a2-cg-33
Define the term 'confederate' as used in Asch's research. (1 mark)
An actor who secretly works with the researcher and gives pre-arranged answers [1].
psych12a2-cg-34

Four students each produce 10 units of work when working alone. When they work together on a group task, the group produces 28 units in total. Calculate the average output per student in the group, and explain whether this shows social loafing. (3 marks)
Average output = 28 ÷ 4 = 7 units per student [1]; this is less than the 10 units each student produced alone [1]; the reduction in individual effort in a group is consistent with social loafing [1].
psych12a2-cg-35
Evaluate Asch's line-judgement experiment as a measure of conformity in everyday life. (4 marks)

Limitation: the task was artificial and low-stakes, so it has low ecological validity [1]; limitation: the sample was an all-male group of American college students, so the findings may not generalise to women or other cultures [1]; strength: the controlled procedure and clear measure of incorrect answers allowed reliable comparison across conditions [1]; limitation: participants were deceived by confederates and may have experienced stress, raising ethical concerns [1].
psych12a2-cg-36
Describe two strategies a team leader could use to reduce groupthink, and explain how each would work. (4 marks)

Appointing a devil's advocate to challenge the proposal [1], which encourages critical discussion and reduces the pressure to agree [1]; asking members to form and record independent views before the group discusses the issue [1], so that doubts are voiced rather than suppressed [1].
vce-psych12-cg-c1
In Asch's line-judgement experiments, conformity dropped sharply when:
The group was made larger than 15
The lines were made easier to see
One other group member (a confederate) gave the correct answer
Participants wrote answers in front of the group
A single dissenter breaks the group's unanimity, reducing normative pressure. Answering privately also reduces conformity.
vce-psych12-sensation-and-the-visual-sys: psych12a2-sv-1
Sensation is best defined as
the storage of information in memory
the selection of which stimuli to pay attention to
the interpretation and organisation of sensory information
the detection and initial registration of stimulus energy by sensory receptors
Sensation involves receptors detecting stimulus energy and converting it into neural signals; perception is the interpretation of those signals.
psych12a2-sv-2
Which structure of the eye contains the photoreceptors that detect light?
Cornea
Lens
Retina
Optic nerve
The retina contains the photoreceptors (rods and cones). The cornea and lens focus light and the optic nerve carries signals to the brain.
psych12a2-sv-3
Compared with cones, rods are
responsible for sharp detail and colour vision
absent from the retina
concentrated in the fovea and detect colour
more sensitive to low light and found mainly in the periphery of the retina
Rods function in dim light and are concentrated in the periphery; cones are concentrated in the fovea and are responsible for colour and detail.
psych12a2-sv-4
The process by which the lens changes shape to focus light from objects at different distances onto the retina is called
transduction
adaptation
convergence
accommodation
Accommodation is the adjustment of the lens shape. Transduction is the conversion of light energy to neural signals.
psych12a2-sv-5
A person walks from bright sunlight into a dark cinema and initially cannot see, but gradually their vision improves. This is best explained by
accommodation of the lens
dark adaptation as rods become more sensitive
light adaptation as cones become more active
a damaged optic nerve
Dark adaptation involves increased sensitivity of rods, taking several minutes. Light adaptation is the reverse.
psych12a2-sv-6
Trace the pathway of light from the cornea to the visual cortex, naming the key structures involved. (4 marks)

Light enters through the cornea and passes through the pupil and lens (focused by accommodation); falls on the retina where rods and cones detect it (transduction into neural signals); signals travel via bipolar and ganglion cells through the optic nerve; to the thalamus and then the visual cortex in the occipital lobe.
psych12a2-sv-7
Explain why a person with damage to the fovea would have difficulty reading but could still detect movement at the edge of their visual field. (3 marks)

The fovea contains a high density of cones, which provide sharp detail and colour vision, so reading is impaired; the periphery of the retina has mostly rods, which remain intact; rods detect motion and low-light stimuli in the periphery.
psych12a2-sv-8
Distinguish between sensation and perception, using the visual system as an example. (2 marks)
Sensation: detection of light by photoreceptors and conversion into neural signals; perception: the brain's organisation and interpretation of these signals, e.g. recognising a face.
psych12a2-sv-9
Which structure is the transparent, curved layer at the front of the eye that provides most of the eye's focusing power?
cornea
lens
pupil
retina
The cornea bends incoming light and supplies about two-thirds of the eye's focusing power. The lens makes fine adjustments, the pupil is only an opening, and the retina is where light is detected.
psych12a2-sv-10
The pupil is best described as
the coloured muscular ring that changes the shape of the lens
the opening in the iris through which light passes into the eye
the layer of photoreceptors at the back of the eye
the transparent jelly that fills the eyeball

The pupil is the opening in the centre of the iris, and the iris muscles change its size to regulate the light entering the eye. The coloured ring is the iris itself, and lens shape is changed by the ciliary muscles, not by the iris.
psych12a2-sv-11
The blind spot exists because
the lens casts a shadow on part of the retina
the fovea contains many rods, which are insensitive to detail
the optic nerve leaves the eye at a point with no photoreceptors
the retina is thickest at the centre of the eye

The optic disc, where the optic nerve leaves the eye, has no rods or cones, so light falling there is not detected. A tempting wrong answer is the claim about the fovea, but the fovea is made up of cones rather than rods.
psych12a2-sv-12
Which layer of the eyeball is the tough white outer coat that protects the eye and helps maintain its shape?
choroid
iris
retina
sclera
The sclera is the tough white outer layer of the eyeball. The retina is the light-sensitive inner layer, the iris controls pupil size, and the choroid is the layer that carries blood to the retina.
psych12a2-sv-13
A person looks at a book held close to their eyes. Which change in the ciliary muscles and lens is needed to focus the image on the retina?
the ciliary muscles contract, making the lens thicker and more curved
the ciliary muscles relax, making the lens thinner and flatter
the ciliary muscles contract, making the lens thinner and flatter
the ciliary muscles relax, causing both eyes to turn inward

Contracting the ciliary muscles slackens the suspensory ligaments, so the lens rounds up and gains focusing power for near objects. Relaxed ciliary muscles flatten the lens for distant objects, and turning both eyes inward is convergence, not a change in the lens.
psych12a2-sv-14
The fovea is best described as
an area of the retina with a high density of rods, giving high sensitivity in dim light
the central region of the retina with the highest concentration of cones and the sharpest vision
an area at the edge of the retina that contains mostly rods
a region at the back of the eye that contains no photoreceptors and is where the lens is attached

The fovea is a small central region packed with cones, which gives the sharpest vision and colour detail. Rods are concentrated in the periphery rather than the fovea, which is why a faint object is often seen better when looked at slightly to one side.
psych12a2-sv-15
Walking into a kitchen, you notice the hum of the fridge for a few minutes, then stop noticing it even though it is still running. This is an example of
transduction
accommodation
sensory adaptation
perceptual constancy

Sensory adaptation is a decline in responsiveness to a constant, unchanging stimulus, so the hum fades from awareness. Transduction is the conversion of energy into neural signals, accommodation is a change in lens shape, and perceptual constancy describes stable perception of objects despite changes in the sensory input.
psych12a2-sv-16
What distinguishes the three types of cone photoreceptors from one another?
the size of the cell body
the location of the cell within the retina
the speed at which they adapt to darkness
the wavelengths of light each type responds to most strongly

The three cone types respond most strongly to short, medium and long wavelengths (roughly blue, green and red), which underlies trichromatic colour vision. Size, location and adaptation speed do not separate the cone types.
psych12a2-sv-17
At the optic chiasm, which of the following occurs?
fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross to the opposite side of the brain
all fibres from each eye travel to the same side of the brain
the signal is converted from neural activity back into light energy
fibres from the fovea are sent directly to the frontal lobe

At the optic chiasm, nasal fibres from each retina cross over, so each hemisphere receives signals from the opposite visual field. A tempting wrong answer is that each eye sends all its fibres to the same side, which ignores this crossing.
psych12a2-sv-18
A person who lacks functional medium-wavelength cones would most likely have difficulty distinguishing
blue from yellow
red from green
light from dark
sharp from blurry images

Medium-wavelength (green-sensitive) cones are needed to separate red from green signals, so losing them causes red-green colour deficiency. Losing short-wavelength cones affects blue-yellow discrimination, and rods detect light intensity rather than colour.
psych12a2-sv-19
Which statement about light adaptation is correct?
It takes about 30 minutes to complete, as rods slowly lose sensitivity.
It occurs when the pupil enlarges to let in more light.
It occurs quickly, as photoreceptors reduce their sensitivity in bright light.
It is the same process as dark adaptation, only slower.

Light adaptation is a reduction in photoreceptor sensitivity in bright conditions, and it happens within minutes, much faster than dark adaptation. The pupil does change size, but that reflex is separate and does not define light adaptation.
psych12a2-sv-20
Many rods in the periphery of the retina may send their signals through a single ganglion cell, whereas a cone at the fovea often has its own ganglion cell. What is the most likely consequence?
greater detail in the periphery but reduced sensitivity to dim light
better colour perception in the periphery than at the fovea
faster dark adaptation at the fovea than in the periphery
greater sensitivity to dim light but poorer detail in the periphery

Pooling signals from many rods makes the periphery very sensitive to dim light, but the pooled signal cannot show fine detail. The foveal cones have more direct connections, giving detailed vision that needs brighter light.
psych12a2-sv-21
In the retina, bipolar cells
receive signals from photoreceptors and pass them on to ganglion cells
carry signals from the brain back to the photoreceptors
produce the photopigment that is bleached by bright light
send visual information straight to the thalamus

Bipolar cells form the middle relay layer, passing signals from the photoreceptors forward to the ganglion cells. The photopigment is contained in the photoreceptors themselves, and the thalamus receives visual signals through the optic nerve rather than directly from bipolar cells.
psych12a2-sv-22
The primary visual cortex, where visual information first arrives in the cerebral cortex, is located in the
frontal lobe
occipital lobe
temporal lobe
parietal lobe

The primary visual cortex lies at the back of the brain in the occipital lobe. The temporal and parietal lobes contain other visual processing areas, while the frontal lobe is mainly involved in planning and movement.
psych12a2-sv-23
Before reaching the primary visual cortex, signals from the optic nerve are relayed through which structure?
hypothalamus
hippocampus
lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
cerebellum

Visual signals synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus before being sent on to the primary visual cortex. The hypothalamus, hippocampus and cerebellum are involved in other functions such as regulation, memory and coordination.
psych12a2-sv-24
The inward turning of both eyes so that the images of a near object fall on corresponding points of each retina is called
accommodation
transduction
adaptation
convergence

Convergence is the inward turning of both eyes for a near object. Accommodation is the lens changing shape, transduction is the conversion of light energy into neural signals, and adaptation is a change in sensitivity.
psych12a2-sv-25
Which statement about the arrangement of the retina is correct?
Light must pass through the ganglion and bipolar cell layers before reaching the photoreceptors.
Photoreceptors lie in front of the other retinal layers, closest to the incoming light.
The optic nerve is made up of the axons of rod cells.
Bipolar cells are found only in the fovea.

In the retina, light passes through the ganglion and bipolar cell layers before reaching the photoreceptors, which lie at the back next to the pigment layer and choroid. Students often assume light hits the photoreceptors first, which is not the case.
psych12a2-sv-26
The clear, jelly-like substance that fills the large chamber behind the lens and helps maintain the shape of the eyeball is the
aqueous humour
vitreous humour
choroid
cornea

The vitreous humour fills the main chamber behind the lens and supports the eyeball's shape. The aqueous humour fills the chamber in front of the lens, while the choroid and cornea are tissue layers rather than fluids.
psych12a2-sv-27
Which of the following describes the function of the optic nerve?
converts light into neural signals
focuses light onto the retina
carries neural signals from the retina to the brain
controls how much light enters the eye

The optic nerve is a bundle of ganglion cell axons that transmits visual signals from the retina to the brain. Transduction occurs in the photoreceptors, focusing is done by the cornea and lens, and light entry is controlled by the iris.
psych12a2-sv-28
Describe how the iris and pupil regulate the amount of light that enters the eye. (2 marks)
The iris contracts or relaxes its muscles to change the size of the pupil [1]; the pupil constricts in bright light to limit the light entering, and dilates in dim light to admit more [1].
psych12a2-sv-29
Explain how the cornea and lens work together to focus an image on the retina. (3 marks)

The cornea bends incoming light and provides most of the eye's focusing power [1]; the lens makes fine adjustments to the focus [1]; the ciliary muscles change the shape of the lens so that light from objects at different distances is focused on the retina [1].
psych12a2-sv-30
Explain why most people do not notice the blind spot in their everyday vision when both eyes are open. (2 marks)

The blind spot in each eye falls in a different part of the visual field, so the other eye detects that region [1]; the brain also fills in the gap using information from the surrounding visual field [1].
psych12a2-sv-31
A faint star is often easier to see when looked at slightly to one side rather than directly. Explain why. (3 marks)

Faint light is detected mainly by rods [1]; rods are concentrated in the periphery of the retina and are largely absent from the fovea [1]; looking to the side places the image of the star on the rod-rich periphery, increasing sensitivity [1].
psych12a2-sv-32
A person has damage to the right primary visual cortex. Explain which part of the visual field is affected, referring to the optic chiasm. (3 marks)

The right visual cortex receives information from the left visual field of both eyes [1]; at the optic chiasm, fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross to the opposite hemisphere, sending left visual field signals to the right hemisphere [1]; damage therefore causes loss of vision in the left visual field of both eyes [1].
psych12a2-sv-33
Distinguish between transduction and accommodation in the eye. (2 marks)

Transduction is the conversion of light energy into neural signals by photoreceptors in the retina [1]; accommodation is the change in lens shape that allows light from objects at different distances to be focused on the retina [1].
psych12a2-sv-34
Define the term 'visual field'. (1 mark)
The area of the external world that can be seen at one moment when the eyes are fixed on a single point [1].
psych12a2-sv-35
A person has no functional cones but has normal rods. Describe two effects this would have on their vision. (2 marks)
Loss of colour vision, because cones are required to detect colour [1]; reduced visual acuity and detail, because cones are concentrated in the fovea and are needed for sharp vision [1].
psych12a2-sv-36
A student claims: 'You can see colours at night because your rods detect colour in the dark.' Evaluate this claim. (3 marks)

The claim is incorrect [1]; rods do not detect colour, as colour vision requires cones [1]; in low light cones are much less active, so colours appear faded and the scene is seen mainly in shades of grey [1].
psych12a2-sv-37

When moving from a bright room into a dim one, the pupil changes quickly but overall sensitivity takes much longer to adjust. Explain why, referring to the iris and pupil and to the photoreceptors. (4 marks)

The iris muscles dilate the pupil within seconds, letting more light reach the retina [1]; this is a fast reflex that changes the amount of light entering the eye [1]; rods and cones increase their sensitivity through regeneration of photopigment, which takes minutes to around 30 minutes [1]; so overall sensitivity adjusts much more slowly than the pupil does [1].
vce-psych12-sv-c1
Which order correctly describes the stages of visual sensation and perception?
Transduction, reception, organisation, transmission, selection, interpretation
Reception, transduction, transmission, selection, organisation, interpretation
Selection, reception, transduction, interpretation, organisation, transmission
Reception, selection, transduction, transmission, interpretation, organisation
Sensation: light is received, converted (transduced) by rods and cones, and transmitted along the optic nerve. Perception: the brain selects, organises and interprets.
vce-psych12-top-down-and-bottom-up-proce: psych12a2-td-1
Bottom-up processing begins with
the raw sensory input from a stimulus
a decision about what to attend to
stored memories only
a person's expectations and prior knowledge
Bottom-up (data-driven) processing builds perception from sensory input. Top-down (conceptually driven) processing begins with prior knowledge and expectations.
psych12a2-td-2
A person reading a sentence with a missing letter easily understands it because of the context of the surrounding words. This is mostly an example of
transduction
bottom-up processing
top-down processing
