sensory adaptation
Using context and prior knowledge to interpret ambiguous input is top-down processing.
psych12a2-td-3
A researcher shows participants an unfamiliar abstract pattern and asks them to describe exactly what they see, line by line. This task relies mostly on
bottom-up processing, because there is little prior knowledge to guide interpretation
perceptual set
confirmation bias
top-down processing, because participants use prior expectations
For unfamiliar stimuli, perception is driven mainly by the sensory features themselves (bottom-up).
psych12a2-td-4
Which factor is most likely to influence top-down processing?
The number of photoreceptors in the retina
The intensity of the stimulus
The wavelength of the light
The person's expectations, motivation and past experience
Top-down processing is shaped by cognitive factors such as expectation, motivation, culture and context. Stimulus features influence bottom-up processing.
psych12a2-td-5
A woman sees a blurry shape in the dark and perceives it as a burglar because she is anxious about break-ins. A calmer friend sees it as a coat on a hook. The difference is best explained by
different sensory receptors in the eye
top-down processing influenced by expectation and emotion
bottom-up processing only
damage to the optic nerve
Identical sensory input was interpreted differently owing to expectations and emotional state, a top-down effect.
psych12a2-td-6
Distinguish between top-down processing and bottom-up processing in perception, using one example of each. (4 marks)

Bottom-up: perception built from the sensory features of the stimulus upward to recognition; example, e.g. noticing the shapes, edges and colours of an unfamiliar object; top-down: perception guided by prior knowledge, context and expectation; example, e.g. reading messy handwriting by using context.
psych12a2-td-7
Two people look at the same ambiguous drawing. One sees a duck and the other sees a rabbit. Explain how top-down processing may account for this. (2 marks)

Their perception is influenced by expectations, prior experience or context (e.g. recent priming or interests) rather than only the stimulus; this leads to different interpretations of the same sensory input.
psych12a2-td-8
Explain why both top-down and bottom-up processing are usually needed to perceive a familiar object accurately in a cluttered room. (3 marks)

Bottom-up processing registers the visual features of the object (shape, colour, edges); top-down processing uses knowledge and context (e.g. a kitchen setting) to interpret the features and recognise it quickly; together they allow efficient, accurate perception, especially when input is incomplete.
psych12a2-td-9
A listener hears a recording in which a speech sound has been replaced by a cough, yet reports hearing the complete word as normal. This best illustrates
top-down processing filling in missing sensory information using knowledge of the word
transduction converting the cough into a neural signal at the cochlea
sensory adaptation making the cough seem quieter than the speech
bottom-up processing in which the cough is registered as a speech sound

Knowledge of the word lets the listener fill in the missing sound, which is top-down processing. Registering the cough as a sound describes bottom-up processing, and transduction and adaptation do not explain the completed word.
psych12a2-td-10
An experienced chess player glances at a mid-game board and quickly recognises a familiar opening pattern, while a novice sees only scattered pieces. The difference mainly reflects
stronger bottom-up processing in the novice, who registers every piece
more efficient transduction of light in the expert's eyes
top-down processing based on stored knowledge of chess patterns
sensory adaptation to the board in the novice

The expert's stored knowledge of patterns organises the same board into meaningful units, which is top-down processing. The idea that the novice's piece-by-piece processing is superior reverses the actual difference, since the novice lacks the expectations that group the pieces.
psych12a2-td-11
The same shape is read as the letter B in the sequence A, B, C and as the number 13 in the sequence 12, 13, 14. Which statement best explains this?
The shape has different physical features in each sequence, so bottom-up processing gives different results
Surrounding context leads to top-down processing that resolves the ambiguous shape differently in each sequence
Transduction converts each sequence into a different set of neural signals
Sensory adaptation to the first sequence makes the shape look different in the second

The shape is identical in both sequences, so the difference comes from expectations set by the surrounding characters rather than from the physical input. Options suggesting different physical features or different sensory processes miss the role of context.
psych12a2-td-12
A listener with no knowledge of a language notices its individual sounds and pitch patterns before understanding any words. This is an example of
top-down processing, because the listener uses meaning to predict the next word
perceptual set, because the listener expects the language to be unfamiliar
bottom-up processing, because perception starts from the sensory features of the sounds
sensory adaptation, because the listener becomes used to the sounds over time

Recognition here is built from the sound features with no stored meaning to guide it, so it is bottom-up. The top-down option is tempting because listeners often predict words, but this listener has no knowledge of the language to make predictions.
psych12a2-td-13
Which statement about top-down processing is accurate?
It draws on stored knowledge, expectations and context to interpret sensory input
It begins in the cortex and sends signals down to the eye's receptors
It operates only when a stimulus is unclear, and not when it is clear
It is the process by which light energy is converted into neural signals

Top-down processing draws on prior knowledge, expectation and context, and it contributes to perception even when input is clear. The 'cortex down to receptors' reading misunderstands the term, and transduction is a separate process.
psych12a2-td-14
Two groups drink the same wine. One group is told it is expensive and rates it as tastier than the other group, who is told nothing about its price. The difference is best attributed to
bottom-up processing, because the wine's chemical features differed between the groups
transduction in the taste buds being more sensitive in the first group
sensory adaptation, because the expensive label was noticed before the taste
top-down processing, because the price expectation shaped how the taste was interpreted

The wine was identical, so the difference must come from the price expectation shaping how the taste was interpreted, which is top-down processing. Options that point to the wine's chemistry or to taste receptors ignore that the input was the same.
psych12a2-td-15
A writer proofreads their own essay and misses a repeated word, as in 'the the'. Which explanation best accounts for this?
Bottom-up processing registers each letter so precisely that repeats are always noticed
Top-down expectation of a grammatical sentence makes the second word seem to belong, so the repeat goes unnoticed
Transduction fails for common words, so the repeat is not sent to the brain
Sensory adaptation makes the second instance of the word invisible

Expecting a grammatical sentence makes the repeated word seem to fit, so the reader perceives the text as they expect it to be, which is top-down processing. Careful bottom-up reading of each letter would be more likely to catch the repeat.
psych12a2-td-16
A radiologist told that a patient has a particular condition looks at an X-ray and reports a shadow that a colleague with no such information did not notice. Which statement best describes this?
Top-down processing is shaping how the same sensory input is interpreted, which can make expected features more likely to be seen
Bottom-up processing has been reduced because the radiologist is looking for a specific condition
The X-ray has been converted into different neural signals for an informed observer
Sensory adaptation has made the shadow stand out more to the radiologist

Prior information creates an expectation that influences what is perceived from the same image, a top-down effect. The idea that bottom-up processing switches off is a misconception, because the sensory features are still registered.
psych12a2-td-17
A computer program can identify letters from their edges and strokes, but it has trouble with a smudged word that a person reads easily from the surrounding sentence. This contrast best illustrates
the superiority of bottom-up feature analysis over top-down processing
top-down processing being confined to the cortex of the brain
the value of combining bottom-up feature analysis with top-down use of context
transduction being the cause of the program's errors

Human reading combines the detail of the stimulus with context and expectation, which is why a smudged word is easy to read in a sentence. Claims that bottom-up analysis is superior, or that transduction causes the errors, do not explain the contrast.
psych12a2-td-18
Which condition is least likely to increase the influence of top-down processing on a perceptual judgement?
The stimulus being presented clearly and for a long time
A strong expectation about what will be shown
Context that makes one interpretation more likely
A high level of anxiety about what might be seen

A clear, prolonged stimulus gives strong bottom-up information, which reduces reliance on expectation. The other conditions all increase the role of prior knowledge, expectation or emotion in interpretation.
psych12a2-td-19
Participants shown the word 'doctor' are faster to recognise the word 'nurse' than participants who saw an unrelated word first. Which type of processing is most directly involved?
bottom-up processing, because the word 'nurse' is a physical stimulus
transduction of the printed word into neural signals
sensory adaptation to repeated letters in the words
top-down processing, because prior exposure creates an expectation that speeds recognition

The earlier word creates a context that makes a related word easier to recognise, which is a top-down effect. Bottom-up options describe the stimulus itself, and sensory adaptation to letters has nothing to do with meaning.
psych12a2-td-20
A student argues that bottom-up processing is more accurate than top-down processing because it avoids the influence of expectation. Which response best corrects this claim?
Bottom-up processing is always more accurate, so the student is correct
Neither type is more accurate in general; each has strengths, and perception usually combines them
Top-down processing is always accurate because it uses stored knowledge
Expectation has no effect on perception, so accuracy depends only on the stimulus

Perception usually combines sensory features with context and expectation, and each contributes strengths. Top-down processing can mislead when expectations are wrong, but neither type is always more accurate, so the student's claim is not correct.
psych12a2-td-21
Which order of events best matches a bottom-up account of recognising an unfamiliar shape?
recognition of the object, then detection of its edges, then a guess about its context
an expected object, then sensory input that confirms the expectation, then recognition
a memory search, then the sensory input being ignored, then recognition
detection of edges and features, then combining them into a shape, then recognition as an object

Bottom-up processing builds perception upwards from the features of the stimulus to the whole object. The other orders begin with recognition, memory or expectation, which are features of top-down processing.
psych12a2-td-22
Why might people from different cultures perceive the same scene differently?
Prior experience and cultural expectations shape how the same sensory input is interpreted
People from different cultures have different wavelength sensitivities in their eyes
Culture changes the number of photoreceptors each person has
Some cultures lack bottom-up processing, so they rely only on expectation

Cultural background shapes expectations and interpretation of the same input, which is a top-down influence. Eye structure and receptor counts are largely shared across people, and all people use bottom-up processing.
psych12a2-td-23
A road sign is partly covered by snow, but a driver recognises it as a stop sign because of its octagonal outline and the sight of an intersection. Which part of the recognition is top-down?
Detecting the red colour and octagonal outline of the sign
Using the context of an intersection to expect a stop sign
Transduction of light into neural signals by photoreceptors
Registering the edges of the snow-covered sign
Expecting a stop sign because of the intersection draws on context and prior knowledge, which is top-down. The colour, outline and edges are sensory features, so they are bottom-up.
psych12a2-td-24
Which statement about perception is most accurate?
Perception is a passive recording of sensory input that is unaffected by expectation
Perception is the same for everyone who receives identical sensory input
Perception combines sensory input with prior knowledge, expectation and context
Perception takes place entirely in the eye's receptors

Perception is an interpretation of sensory input that draws on both bottom-up and top-down processes. The 'passive recording' and 'receptors only' ideas ignore the role of knowledge and context in what is perceived.
psych12a2-td-25
Which example best illustrates top-down processing in hearing?
Converting sound waves into nerve impulses in the cochlea
Detecting a sudden loud bang as a rapid rise in air pressure
Locating a sound's direction from timing differences between the ears
Recognising a familiar song from its first few notes because the listener knows the whole tune

Knowledge of the song lets the listener recognise it from very little sensory input, which is top-down processing. The other options describe the physical or neural processing of sound, which is transduction or bottom-up analysis.
psych12a2-td-26
A shopper sees a familiar cereal brand's logo partly hidden behind a shelf label, and identifies the product immediately. Explain how top-down processing contributes to this identification. (2 marks)
Stored knowledge of the brand and its logo fills in the hidden part of the image [1]; the shopper's expectation of finding that product guides how the visible features are interpreted [1].
psych12a2-td-27
A degraded black-and-white image looks like meaningless blotches until a viewer is told it contains a face, after which the face is clearly seen. Explain this using top-down processing. (3 marks)

The sensory input is ambiguous, so the bottom-up features alone do not form a recognised face [1]; being told there is a face creates an expectation that is used to organise the blotches [1]; the same input is now interpreted differently, so the perception changes [1].
psych12a2-td-28
Describe one situation in which bottom-up processing is more useful than top-down processing, and explain why. (3 marks)

An unfamiliar stimulus with no relevant prior knowledge, such as encountering a new object or species [1]; perception must then be built from the sensory features themselves [1]; relying on expectations could lead to a misperception because the wrong expectations would be applied [1].
psych12a2-td-29
A child learns to read by first sounding out letters and later reads whole words at a glance. Describe how bottom-up and top-down processing change as the child becomes a skilled reader. (4 marks)

Early reading relies mainly on bottom-up processing, decoding each letter and sound from its sensory features [1]; as skill develops, stored knowledge of words and spelling patterns allows top-down processing [1]; the skilled reader uses context and expectation to recognise words quickly [1]; bottom-up features are still used for unfamiliar or misspelt words [1].
psych12a2-td-30

A tourist in a foreign city reads a bus sign as showing their hotel's route, because they expect the bus to go there. Identify the type of processing involved and explain how the error could be reduced. (3 marks)

Top-down processing, because the tourist's expectation shapes the interpretation of the sign [1]; the expectation overrides the sensory detail, so the misreading occurs [1]; the error could be reduced by attending more closely to the sensory features of the sign, such as reading each word carefully [1].
psych12a2-td-31
Explain why a perceptual error can occur even when the sensory input is clear and accurate. (2 marks)

Perception also depends on expectations, prior experience and context, which can influence the interpretation of clear input [1]; so the brain may interpret the input in a way that does not match what is actually present, for example by seeing what is expected [1].
psych12a2-td-32
Describe how context contributes to top-down processing. Give one everyday example. (3 marks)

Context provides extra information about the likely meaning of an ambiguous stimulus [1]; it narrows the range of possible interpretations, so the most likely one is perceived [1]; e.g. reading the word 'bank' as a river bank when it appears beside a picture of water [1].
psych12a2-td-33

A pilot approaching a runway in fog sees faint lights and edges, and expects to see a landing strip. Explain how bottom-up and top-down processing could both contribute to the pilot's perception, and how an error could arise. (4 marks)

Bottom-up: the faint lights and edges are registered from the sensory input [1]; top-down: the pilot's expectation of a landing strip guides the interpretation of those features [1]; both combine to form the perception [1]; an error could arise if the expectation leads the pilot to perceive a runway where the lights do not show one [1].
psych12a2-td-34
Define bottom-up processing. (1 mark)
Perception built up from the raw sensory features of a stimulus, without relying on prior knowledge or expectation [1].
vce-psych12-td-c1
You read a scrawled word in a friend's note because the rest of the sentence makes its meaning clear. This is mainly:
Top-down processing, using context and expectations
Bottom-up processing, using only the features of the letters
Transduction
Binocular depth perception
Top-down processing uses prior knowledge and context to interpret incomplete sensory information.
vce-psych12-depth-cues-and-gestalt-princ: A photograph of a long straight road shows the two edges of the road appearing to meet at a point on the horizon. This monocular depth cue is best described as
Linear perspective is the apparent convergence of parallel lines with distance. Texture gradient refers to a change in the density of surface detail, not converging lines.
Which of the following depth cues is binocular?
Retinal disparity depends on the slightly different images received by each eye. The other three are monocular cues that can be used with one eye.
Sarah sees a row of identical trees in a park. The trees in the distance look smaller than the nearby ones, so she judges them to be further away. She is using

Relative size: when objects are known or assumed to be the same size, the one casting the smaller retinal image is judged to be further away. Interposition would require one object to partially block another.
A scrapbook page shows a set of dots in the shape of a circle, with small gaps between some dots. Viewers still see a complete circle. This is best explained by the Gestalt principle of
Closure is the tendency to fill in gaps to perceive a complete, whole object. Proximity concerns grouping by nearness.
In a grid, columns of red squares alternate with columns of blue squares. Viewers perceive vertical stripes rather than rows. Which Gestalt principle best explains this?
Similarity: elements that look alike (here, colour) are grouped together. If the squares were grouped because they were close together, it would be proximity.
Distinguish between monocular and binocular depth cues, and give one example of each. (3 marks)

Monocular cues require input from only one eye (1); binocular cues require input from both eyes and depend on their different positions (1); example of monocular: relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient; example of binocular: retinal disparity or convergence (1 for both examples correct).
Explain what is meant by the Gestalt principle of figure-ground and describe how it might be used in the design of a company logo. (3 marks)

Figure-ground is the tendency to organise a visual scene into a distinct object (the figure) that stands out against its background (1); we perceive the figure as having a defined form and the ground as extending behind it (1); a logo could use contrasting colours so that the shape or lettering clearly stands out as the figure, or deliberately use ambiguity so that the negative space forms a second image (1).
A photographer takes a picture in which a mountain partly hides a second, more distant mountain. Identify the depth cue that makes the viewer judge which is closer and explain how it works. (2 marks)
Interposition (overlap) (1); the object that partially blocks the view of another is perceived as closer, and the partly hidden object as further away (1).
A student holds a pencil close to her nose and focuses on it. Her eyes turn inwards so that their lines of sight meet at the pencil. Which depth cue is this?

Convergence is the inward turning of both eyes to focus on a near object, and the muscle effort signals its distance. Accommodation is a change in lens shape, and retinal disparity is the difference between the two retinal images rather than the eye movement itself.
A reader covers one eye and looks at a book held 30 cm away. The muscles around the lens tighten so that the lens becomes thicker, bringing the page into focus. Which depth cue is being used?

Accommodation is the change in lens shape for focusing, and the muscle tension signals distance; it works with one eye. Convergence needs both eyes turning inwards, and the reader is not moving, so motion parallax is not involved.
Pebbles on a beach look large and widely spaced close to the viewer, but small and tightly packed near the horizon. Which depth cue is shown?

Texture gradient is the change in the size and density of surface detail with distance. Relative size judges the size of whole objects, and aerial perspective depends on haze rather than surface detail.
On a train platform, people stand in tight groups of three or four, with wide gaps between groups. Viewers see the groups rather than one evenly spread crowd. Which Gestalt principle explains this?

Proximity is the tendency to group elements that are close together. Similarity groups elements that look alike, and common fate groups elements that move together, so neither explains grouping by spacing.

The classic vase image can be seen either as a white vase on a black background or as two black faces facing each other on a white background, but not both at the same time. Which Gestalt principle explains this?

Figure-ground organisation separates an image into a figure that stands out and a background, and in this image either region can be the figure. Closure concerns filling in gaps, so it does not explain the reversal.
A drawing shows a fence partly blocking the view of a house behind it. Which statement describes the depth cue and what it tells the viewer?
relative size, because the fence looks smaller than the house
retinal disparity, because the two eyes see different images
interposition, because the fence is judged to be in front of the house
aerial perspective, because the house looks hazy

Interposition (overlap) is a monocular cue in which the object that blocks another is judged to be closer. Relative size concerns the size of images, and retinal disparity needs two eyes, so it is not shown in a single drawing.
Fans in a crowded stadium wear the same team colours and are spread across several rows. Viewers see them as one block of supporters. Which Gestalt principle explains this?
Similarity groups elements that share a feature such as colour, so the spread-out fans are seen as one team. Proximity would require the fans to be grouped by how close they are to one another.
Which list contains only monocular depth cues?
retinal disparity, aerial perspective, motion parallax
Interposition, linear perspective and relative size can each be used with one eye. Each of the other lists contains a binocular cue, either retinal disparity or convergence.
Which of the following is NOT a Gestalt principle of perceptual organisation?
Relative size is a monocular depth cue that judges distance from the size of images. Proximity, similarity and closure are all Gestalt grouping principles, so the answer is the depth cue.
A 3D film is watched through glasses that send slightly different pictures to each eye, making the screen appear to have objects at different distances. Which depth cue is the film mainly using?

Retinal disparity is the difference between the images received by the two eyes, and the 3D effect exploits this difference. Motion parallax needs movement of the observer or the objects, and the other two options are monocular cues.
A photograph of a tiled hallway shows the tiles becoming smaller and more tightly packed towards the far end, while the side walls appear to meet at a point. Which two monocular depth cues are shown?

Tiles that shrink and crowd together show texture gradient, and walls that converge show linear perspective. The other options either contain binocular cues or name cues, such as aerial perspective, that the photograph does not show.
Which statement about retinal disparity is correct?
Closer objects produce a larger difference between the two retinal images
Distant objects produce a larger difference between the two retinal images
The difference between the two retinal images is the same at all distances
Disparity is a monocular cue that works when one eye is closed
Because the eyes are separated, a nearby object projects to more different positions on each retina than a distant one. Disparity is binocular, so it does not work when one eye is closed.
Which statement about Gestalt principles is correct?
They are monocular cues that judge distance
They describe how elements are grouped into organised wholes
They require both eyes to work together
They measure how far away an object is

Gestalt principles describe how the brain groups separate elements into organised wholes. Monocular cues and binocular disparity are depth cues, which form a different category and are not Gestalt principles.
Which statement best distinguishes convergence from retinal disparity?
Convergence depends on the shape of the lens, while disparity depends on haze in the air
Convergence is the difference between the two retinal images, while disparity is the inward turning of the eyes
Convergence is the inward turning of the eyes, while disparity is the difference between the two retinal images
Both are monocular cues that depend on the thickness of the lens

Convergence is the eye-movement signal for near objects, and disparity is the difference between the two retinal images; both are binocular. The other options swap these definitions, attribute them to lens shape or haze, or wrongly call them monocular.
Define convergence and state whether it is a monocular or binocular depth cue. (2 marks)
Convergence is the inward turning of the two eyes to focus on a near object, with the muscle effort used as a distance signal [1]; it is a binocular cue because it requires both eyes [1].
Name the process by which the lens of the eye changes shape to bring near and far objects into focus. (1 mark)
Explain why the two eyes receive slightly different images of the same object. (2 marks)
The eyes are set apart horizontally, so each eye views the object from a slightly different position [1]; the difference is larger for nearby objects, which the brain uses as a depth cue [1].
Describe texture gradient and explain how it helps a viewer judge the distance across a field of grass. (3 marks)

Texture gradient is the change in the size and density of surface detail as distance increases [1]; near blades of grass are large and widely spaced, while distant ones are small and tightly packed [1]; the smooth change in detail signals a surface that extends away from the viewer, so the far end is judged to be further away [1].
A student claims that a bird that looks smaller in a photograph must be further away than a bird that looks larger. Evaluate this claim, using at least two depth cues in your answer. (4 marks)

Partly valid: relative size suggests the smaller bird is further away if both birds are assumed to be the same size [1]; however, the birds may differ in actual size, so relative size alone is unreliable [1]; a second cue, such as interposition if one bird partly blocks the other, or aerial perspective, would support or refute the judgement [1]; the claim is therefore reasonable only when other cues confirm it [1].
A bus map colours all bus routes red and all train lines blue. Explain how the Gestalt principle of similarity helps a commuter read the map. (3 marks)

Similarity groups elements that share a visual feature such as colour [1]; all red lines are perceived as one type of service and all blue lines as another [1]; the commuter can therefore identify the train network quickly without reading every label [1].
Explain how the figure-ground principle helps a person pick out a friend in a crowd. (2 marks)

The friend's outline or clothing is organised as the figure that stands out against the crowd as background [1]; because the figure is perceived as a distinct object, the person can locate it quickly [1].
A person who can see with only one eye could still use which depth cues?
Retinal disparity, convergence and linear perspective
Retinal disparity only, because it uses a single retina
None at all, because every depth cue needs two eyes
Monocular cues (pictorial cues and accommodation) work with one eye. Retinal disparity and convergence are binocular cues.
vce-psych12-gustatory-perception: psych12a3-gp-1
Taste receptor cells are located in
taste buds, which sit within papillae on the tongue
the thalamus
the retina
the olfactory epithelium
Taste receptor cells are grouped in taste buds, most of which are found in papillae on the tongue. The olfactory epithelium holds smell receptors.
psych12a3-gp-2
Which of the following is a basic taste?
Creamy
Spicy
Metallic
Umami
The five basic tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Spicy heat is detected as pain/temperature, not as a basic taste.
psych12a3-gp-3
Nikos has a cold and finds that his favourite soup tastes bland. This is best explained by
the close interaction between gustatory and olfactory sensation in flavour perception
taste receptors being damaged by the virus
loss of the somatosensory cortex
an increased number of papillae
Much of what we call flavour depends on olfaction; a blocked nose reduces smell input, so food seems bland even though taste receptors still work.
psych12a3-gp-4
A person with a very high density of fungiform papillae finds black coffee and broccoli extremely bitter. This person is most likely a
anosmic
medium taster
non-taster
supertaster
Supertasters have a higher density of taste buds and papillae, and experience certain tastes, especially bitter, more intensely.
psych12a3-gp-5
The pathway of gustatory information in perception is best described as
receptor cells in taste buds, then sensory neurons, then the gustatory cortex
papillae, then the occipital lobe, then taste buds
olfactory bulb only, then the frontal lobe
tongue, then the auditory cortex
Chemicals dissolved in saliva stimulate receptor cells in taste buds, which transduce the stimulus into neural impulses sent along sensory neurons to the gustatory cortex (parietal/insula region).
psych12a3-gp-6
Describe how a sweet food is detected and perceived, starting at the tongue and finishing in the brain. (3 marks)

Chemicals from the food dissolve in saliva and contact taste receptor cells in taste buds within papillae on the tongue (1); the receptors transduce the chemical stimulus into neural impulses that travel along sensory neurons (1); the information reaches the gustatory cortex where it is interpreted as sweet taste (1).
psych12a3-gp-7
Explain why the sense of smell contributes to the perception of flavour. (2 marks)

Flavour is the combined perception of taste and smell (1); odour molecules from food travel to the olfactory receptors at the back of the nasal cavity while chewing/swallowing, and the brain integrates this with gustatory input (1).
psych12a3-gp-8

A researcher compares two groups of participants who differ in taste-bud density. Explain one way in which supertasters and non-tasters would be expected to differ in their perception of a bitter drink. (2 marks)
Supertasters have more taste buds/papillae (1); so they would rate the drink as much more intensely bitter (or find it unpleasant) than non-tasters, who would rate it as mild (1).
psych12a3-gp-9
Sour taste is detected when
sodium ions from table salt bind to receptors on the sides of the tongue
hydrogen ions (H⁺) from acidic substances enter taste receptor cells
sugar molecules bind to receptors at the back of the tongue
odour molecules travel up the nasal cavity to the olfactory bulb
Sour taste is triggered by hydrogen ions from acids entering taste receptor cells. The salt option mixes up sour with salty, which is triggered by sodium ions.
psych12a3-gp-10
Circumvallate papillae, which each contain many taste buds, are located
on the tip of the tongue, where they are the only papillae with taste buds
in the middle of the tongue, between the fungiform papillae
in a V-shaped row towards the back of the tongue
in the throat, beyond the soft palate
Circumvallate papillae form a V-shaped row at the back of the tongue. Fungiform papillae, which are mushroom-shaped, sit on the front and sides, so the tip is not the only place with taste buds.
psych12a3-gp-11
Filiform papillae are the most numerous papillae on the tongue, but they
contain no taste buds and are mainly involved in texture and grip
contain the most taste buds of any papilla type
are the main location of salt receptors
are the only papillae that detect bitter tastes

Filiform papillae are the most numerous type but have no taste buds, so they do not contribute to taste. Circumvallate papillae hold the most taste buds per papilla, which is why the option claiming filiform papillae hold the most is wrong.
psych12a3-gp-12
Taste receptor cells are short-lived and are replaced regularly. Each taste receptor cell lives for about
a few hours
one year
a lifetime, because receptor cells are never replaced
about 10 days
Taste receptor cells last around 10 days before being replaced from surrounding cells. Claims of a year or a lifetime overstate how long these cells last.
psych12a3-gp-13
After eating a very salty snack, a person finds the next salty food much less salty. This decline in sensitivity to a constant taste is called
sensory interaction
adaptation
conditioned taste aversion
supertasting

Adaptation is the gradual reduction in sensitivity to a continuing stimulus. Sensory interaction describes one sense influencing another, and conditioned taste aversion is a learned dislike of a food, so neither describes a fall in sensitivity.
psych12a3-gp-14
Keri ate an unfamiliar seafood dish and became ill with food poisoning several hours later. Now the thought of eating the same dish makes her feel nauseous. This is best explained by
supertasting, which makes the seafood taste intensely bitter
damage to the gustatory cortex caused by the food poisoning
conditioned taste aversion, a learned link between a food and illness
the vagus nerve being unable to carry taste signals

Conditioned taste aversion is a learned avoidance of a food that has been paired with illness, and it can form after a single pairing. Supertasting describes heightened sensitivity to bitterness, not a learned dislike.
psych12a3-gp-15
Newborn infants show an innate preference for which taste?
sweet
bitter
sour
salty
Newborns are born with a liking for sweet tastes and tend to reject bitter and sour ones, which suggests a biological basis. Bitter is rejected rather than preferred, so it cannot be the answer.
psych12a3-gp-16
Individual differences in how bitter a compound tastes are partly explained by
the density of olfactory receptors in the nasal cavity
exposure to salt in childhood
the number of papillae on the back of the tongue only
variation in a gene that codes for bitter taste receptors

Variation in genes such as TAS2R38 affects how strongly people perceive bitter compounds like PTC and PROP. Olfactory receptor density and childhood salt exposure do not explain this difference in bitterness.
psych12a3-gp-17
The 'tongue map', which divided the tongue into separate zones for sweet, sour, salty and bitter, is now regarded as
accurate, since the tip contains the only sweet receptors
a myth, since receptors for all basic tastes occur across the tongue, with only small differences in sensitivity
accurate, since each papilla type responds to one taste only
accurate for sweet and salty, but sour and bitter receptors are absent from the tongue

Receptors for every basic taste are found across the tongue, and the original tongue map exaggerated small differences in sensitivity. The options describing exclusive zones repeat the common misconception.
psych12a3-gp-18
As people age, their sense of taste typically
becomes more sensitive to all tastes
shifts so that bitter is detected before sweet
is unaffected, because taste receptors never regenerate
declines, partly because of fewer taste buds and slower replacement of receptor cells
Taste sensitivity generally declines with age, partly because the number of taste buds falls and receptor cell renewal slows. Taste receptors do regenerate, so the claim that they never do is false.
psych12a3-gp-19
Umami taste is most closely associated with which substance?
glutamate, as found in monosodium glutamate (MSG)
sucrose from table sugar
citric acid from lemons
caffeine from coffee

Umami is triggered mainly by glutamate and similar amino acids, which are found in MSG, aged cheese and tomatoes. Sucrose is linked to sweet, citric acid to sour, and caffeine is typically perceived as bitter.
psych12a3-gp-20
Many plant toxins taste bitter. Biologists suggest that sensitivity to bitterness evolved mainly as a
way to signal that fruit is ripe
protective response that helps detect potentially toxic substances
means of attracting animals to salt sources
method of storing energy in carbohydrates

Bitterness acts as a warning, so sensitivity to it helped people avoid many toxic plant compounds. Ripeness is signalled more by sweetness, and the other options describe functions unrelated to bitter taste.
psych12a3-gp-21
Which sensation is detected by the somatosensory system rather than by taste receptors?
sweetness of sugar
saltiness of crisps
sourness of lemon juice
temperature of a hot soup

Temperature is detected by thermoreceptors in the mouth and skin, which are part of the somatosensory system, and it adds to the overall flavour experience. Sweet, salty and sour are basic tastes detected by taste receptor cells.
psych12a3-gp-22
People often judge a drink coloured red as sweeter than the same drink coloured pale, even though both contain the same amount of sugar. This best illustrates
adaptation, where receptors become less sensitive over time
conditioned taste aversion, where a food is linked to illness
sensory interaction, where vision influences taste perception
supertasting, where taste buds are more densely packed
Sensory interaction occurs when one sense, here vision, changes how another sense is perceived. Adaptation, aversion and supertasting do not explain a change in perceived sweetness caused by colour.
psych12a3-gp-23
Which statement correctly distinguishes sensation from perception in taste?
Sensation is the detection of chemicals by receptors, while perception is the brain's interpretation of that information
Sensation occurs in the brain, while perception occurs on the tongue
Sensation and perception are two names for the same process
Perception occurs only after food is swallowed, while sensation occurs before

Sensation is the detection of a stimulus by receptors, and perception is the interpretation of that sensory input in the brain. The options that reverse the locations or treat the two terms as identical confuse the distinction.
psych12a3-gp-24
Approximately how many taste buds does an average adult have?
about 50
about 100 000
about 2000 to 8000
about 500 000
Estimates for adults are roughly 2000 to 8000 taste buds, spread across the tongue, palate and throat. The larger figures overstate the count, and 50 is far too few.
psych12a3-gp-25
Taste receptor cells are best described as
specialised epithelial cells that transduce chemical stimuli and synapse with sensory nerve fibres
neurons that carry signals directly to the thalamus
muscle cells that move the tongue to position food
glial cells that clear saliva from the taste buds

Taste receptor cells are specialised epithelial cells in taste buds that convert chemical stimuli into electrical signals and pass them to sensory nerve fibres. The options calling them neurons, muscle cells or glial cells confuse them with other cell types.
psych12a3-gp-26
Name one area of the mouth or throat, other than the tongue, that contains taste buds. (1 mark)
Soft palate, pharynx or epiglottis (1).
psych12a3-gp-27
Describe the location and appearance of fungiform papillae. (1 mark)
Mushroom-shaped papillae found mainly on the front and sides of the tongue (1).
psych12a3-gp-28
Describe the role of the thalamus in the gustatory pathway. (2 marks)
The thalamus receives taste information from the brainstem (1), and relays it onward to the primary gustatory cortex in the cerebral cortex (1).
psych12a3-gp-29
Explain why taste and smell are both described as chemical senses. (2 marks)
Both senses respond to chemical molecules from food or the environment (1); their receptors are activated when molecules bind to them, producing neural signals (1).
psych12a3-gp-30
Explain one possible survival advantage of being able to detect sourness. (2 marks)
Sourness signals acidity, which can indicate unripe or spoiled food (1); avoiding such food reduces the risk of ingesting harmful bacteria or toxins (1).
psych12a3-gp-31
Describe one difference between the location of taste receptors and the location of olfactory receptors. (2 marks)
Taste receptors are in taste buds on the tongue, soft palate, pharynx and epiglottis (1); olfactory receptors are in the olfactory epithelium at the roof of the nasal cavity (1).
psych12a3-gp-32

A food manufacturer reduces the salt in a snack food by half, and consumers say it tastes bland. Explain, with reference to taste receptor processes, why this occurs, and identify one other factor that could contribute. (3 marks)

Less sodium is available to stimulate the salt-sensitive receptor cells (1); fewer neural impulses are generated, so the signal reaching the gustatory cortex is weaker (1); flavour also depends on smell, texture or aroma, and reduced aroma or crunch can increase the perceived blandness (1).
psych12a3-gp-33
Outline the process of transduction in a taste receptor cell in three steps, from the binding of a chemical to the signal sent to a sensory neuron. (3 marks)

A chemical from food binds to or enters a receptor on the taste receptor cell (1); this changes the cell's electrical activity, producing a receptor potential (1); the cell releases a neurotransmitter onto a sensory neuron, which generates neural impulses sent to the brain (1).
vce-psych12-gu-c1
Food tastes bland when you have a blocked nose because:
Flavour depends heavily on smell (olfaction) as well as taste
Taste buds are located in the nose, so they are blocked
A cold destroys all of the taste receptors on the tongue
Saliva production stops, so taste molecules cannot dissolve
Taste receptors detect only basic tastes; aroma molecules reaching the nose create most of the flavour.
vce-psych12-distortions-of-perception-an: psych12a3-dpi-1
In the Müller-Lyer illusion, two lines of equal length appear unequal because of
movement of the lines
arrowheads or fins at their ends pointing inwards or outwards
differences in colour
different background brightness
The fins at the line ends create different depth/size cues, so the line with outward-pointing fins looks longer than the line with inward-pointing fins.
psych12a3-dpi-2
In the Ames room, a person standing in one corner looks much larger than a person standing in the other corner. This occurs because
the room is much larger than it appears
the two people differ greatly in height
the eyes have different focal lengths
the viewer assumes the room is rectangular when it is actually distorted
The room is trapezoidal, but viewed from one point it appears rectangular. The viewer wrongly uses size-distance cues, so the person in the further corner appears larger.
psych12a3-dpi-3
Two identical tigers are drawn on a photo of a railway track, one near the bottom of the image and one near the top where the rails appear to converge. The upper tiger looks larger. This is the
Ames room
Ponzo illusion
Müller-Lyer illusion
Rubin’s vase
The Ponzo illusion uses converging lines to create a linear perspective cue; the object that appears further away is perceived as larger.
psych12a3-dpi-4
A perceptual illusion differs from a hallucination because an illusion
occurs without any stimulus
is a misperception of a real stimulus
only occurs in people with a mental disorder
involves the sense of smell
In an illusion a real external stimulus is present but misinterpreted. Hallucinations involve perceptions without a stimulus.
psych12a3-dpi-5
Which is the most appropriate description of what a distortion of perception, such as the moon illusion, tells psychologists?
Sensory receptors are faulty in most people
Illusions only occur in vision
Perception is always an exact copy of the stimulus
Perception is a constructive process in which the brain applies assumptions and cues to interpret sensory input
Illusions show that perception depends on interpretation of sensory information, often using depth cues and learned assumptions, and can be misled.
psych12a3-dpi-6
Explain, with reference to depth cues, why the moon looks larger when it is near the horizon than when it is high in the sky. (3 marks)

The moon’s retinal image is the same size in both positions (1); near the horizon, objects such as trees and buildings provide depth cues (e.g. relative size/texture gradient) making the moon seem further away (1); the brain therefore perceives it as larger, whereas in the empty sky there are no cues, so it appears smaller (1).
psych12a3-dpi-7
Describe the Müller-Lyer illusion and explain one reason it occurs. (3 marks)

Two lines of equal length appear different in length (1); the line with outward-pointing fins (like an arrowhead pointing inwards) looks shorter than the line with inward-pointing fins (1); explanation: the fins are interpreted as depth cues, like the corners of a room, making one line appear further away and hence longer (1).
psych12a3-dpi-8
Outline what is meant by a visual perceptual distortion and give one example other than the Müller-Lyer illusion. (2 marks)
A perception in which the observer’s experience differs from the physical properties of the stimulus (1); example: Ponzo illusion, Ames room, moon illusion, Rubin’s vase (1).
psych12a3-dpi-9
Two parallel vertical lines drawn over a pattern of radiating lines appear to bow outwards. This is the Hering illusion, which shows that
a background pattern can distort the perceived straightness and orientation of nearby lines
the two lines are physically bent by the radiating lines, which pull on them
the eyes cannot focus on two lines that are placed close together
lines that are physically straight can only look straight when they are horizontal

The radiating lines alter the perceived orientation of the parallel lines, so the straight lines appear to bow. The distractors wrongly treat a perceptual distortion as a physical or focusing problem.
psych12a3-dpi-10
The Penrose triangle is a drawing that looks like a solid three-dimensional object but cannot exist as one. This is because
the drawing has been printed with an error in its angles
each corner looks plausible on its own, but the depth cues across the whole figure cannot be combined into one consistent object
the viewer’s eyes cannot converge on a flat drawing
the lines are too thin to be perceived as three-dimensional

Each part is read as a plausible 3D corner, but when the parts are joined the depth information contradicts itself. Printing errors and eye convergence are not the cause, since the figure is impossible in its design.
psych12a3-dpi-11
A wire-frame cube drawn without shading can be seen in two different three-dimensional orientations, and the two views alternate. This is an example of
a size-constancy illusion
a linear perspective depth cue
an ambiguous figure, which has more than one stable interpretation
a hallucination caused by fatigue

The drawing supports two equally consistent 3D readings, so perception alternates between them. Size constancy and linear perspective concern size and depth cues, and a hallucination involves no stimulus.
psych12a3-dpi-12
The same mid-grey square looks lighter when placed on a black background than when it is placed on a white background. This is best explained by
the grey square reflects more light when placed on black
a motion aftereffect caused by staring at the background
the Müller-Lyer effect, in which fins at the ends of lines change apparent length
simultaneous brightness contrast, in which the surrounding area changes the perceived lightness of a region

The square reflects the same amount of light in both cases, so the surrounding brightness is what changes its perceived lightness. Motion aftereffects and the Müller-Lyer illusion involve movement and line length, not brightness.
psych12a3-dpi-13
In the Zöllner illusion, long lines that are actually parallel look slanted or non-parallel because
short diagonal lines crossing the long lines distort the perceived angle of the long lines
the long lines are slightly curved on the printed page
parallel lines only look parallel when they are seen in peripheral vision
the long lines are printed with different thicknesses

The short oblique lines interact with the long lines and change how their angle is judged, so parallel lines appear non-parallel. The lines are physically parallel, so curvature and print thickness are not the cause.
psych12a3-dpi-14
A row of identical circles is shaded darker at the bottom, so they look like bulges. When the same circles are shaded darker at the top, they look like hollows. This effect is due to
linear perspective, in which parallel lines converge with distance
light and shadow, which the brain reads as showing the direction of light and the shape of a surface
interposition, in which one object partly hides another
aerial perspective, in which distant objects look hazy

The brain assumes light comes from above, so shading at the bottom signals a bulge and shading at the top signals a hollow. The other cues depend on converging lines, overlap and haze rather than shading.
psych12a3-dpi-15
A horizontal line and a vertical line are drawn with exactly the same length, yet the vertical line looks longer. This is the horizontal-vertical illusion, which is best explained by
the vertical line being physically thicker than the horizontal line
the horizontal line being partly hidden by a background pattern
a tendency to overestimate vertical length relative to horizontal length
the eyes scanning vertical lines more slowly, which makes them look stretched
Vertical extents tend to be judged as longer than equal horizontal ones, which produces the illusion. Line thickness and hiding do not explain why identical lines differ in apparent length.
psych12a3-dpi-16
A listener watches a video of a speaker’s lips making the sound ‘ga’ while hearing the sound ‘ba’, and often reports hearing ‘da’. This is the McGurk effect, which shows that
hearing is unaffected by what a person can see of the speaker
visual information from the lips can change the sound that is perceived, so speech perception combines the senses
the ears and eyes process speech in entirely separate, unconnected areas of the brain
people who lip-read are always more accurate than people who only listen
Speech perception integrates auditory and visual input, so the brain blends them into a third sound. The other options contradict this integration or make claims the effect does not show.
psych12a3-dpi-17
Two boxes have exactly the same mass, but one is much larger than the other. When lifted, the smaller box feels heavier. This is the size-weight illusion, which is best explained by
the smaller box being denser, so it has more mass
the larger box being lifted more slowly, which reduces its perceived weight
the brain expecting a larger object to be heavier, so the larger box feels lighter than expected
the muscles in the hand tiring more quickly when lifting the larger box

Prior expectation about how heavy objects should be shapes the weight judgment, so the mismatch makes the smaller box feel heavier. Density, lifting speed and fatigue do not explain why equal masses feel different.
psych12a3-dpi-18
In a completely dark room, a single small light that is actually stationary is viewed and appears to drift. The best explanation is
the light physically moves because of air currents in the room
the observer’s photoreceptors are fatigued by the bright light
the observer is hallucinating because of the darkness
the lack of reference points and small involuntary eye movements make a stationary light appear to move

Without fixed reference points the visual system cannot judge the light’s position, so small eye movements are read as movement of the light. The light does not move and no stimulus is missing, so this is not a hallucination.
psych12a3-dpi-19

Two lights placed a short distance apart are switched on one after the other in quick succession. The observer sees a single light moving from one position to the other. This is the phi phenomenon, which is an example of
apparent motion, in which a sequence of stationary stimuli is perceived as movement
a motion aftereffect, caused by prolonged watching of movement
real movement of light across the gap, caused by the lights’ brightness
a depth cue, in which nearer lights appear to move faster

The brain links the successive flashes into one moving object, even though nothing moves between them, and this principle underlies film and television. A motion aftereffect needs prior adaptation to movement, and the other options describe a physical or depth effect.
psych12a3-dpi-20
A sequence of tones is heard that seems to rise in pitch forever, yet the pattern repeats after a set interval. This auditory illusion is called
the McGurk effect
the Shepard tone, a paradox created by overlapping octaves with changing loudness
the phi phenomenon
the cocktail party effect, in which attention filters out background speech

The tones are built from stacked octaves whose loudness is shaped so the highest and lowest are quiet, which makes the rise seem endless. The McGurk effect involves vision and hearing, the phi phenomenon is visual motion, and the cocktail party effect concerns attention.
psych12a3-dpi-21

A diagonal line passes behind a rectangle and emerges on the other side looking offset, even though the two visible parts lie on one straight line. This is the Poggendorff illusion, which is best explained by
the line being physically broken into two pieces with a gap behind the rectangle
the eyes converging unequally on the two parts of the line
the rectangle’s vertical edges distorting the perceived angle of the diagonal, so the two parts look misaligned
the background being darker on one side of the rectangle than the other

The vertical edges change how the direction of the diagonal is judged where it meets them, so the two collinear parts look offset. The line is continuous, and eye convergence and background brightness are not the cause.
psych12a3-dpi-22
Describe the waterfall illusion and explain the neural process that causes it. (2 marks)

After prolonged viewing of downward motion, a stationary scene such as the rocks beside a waterfall appears to move upward [1]; motion-detecting neurons tuned to downward movement become fatigued, so neurons responding to upward movement dominate when the still scene is viewed [1].
psych12a3-dpi-23
Outline how the hollow-face illusion shows the role of top-down processing in perception. (4 marks)

A hollow mask viewed from the inside is perceived as a normal convex face [1]; the viewer’s stored knowledge that faces are convex is applied to the sensory input [1]; this prior expectation (top-down processing) overrides depth cues such as shading and perspective that indicate a concave surface [1]; the percept is therefore constructed from sensory data and experience, not a direct copy of the stimulus [1].
psych12a3-dpi-24
Describe the Kanizsa triangle and explain how the brain produces the triangle it perceives. (2 marks)

Three black circles with wedges removed are arranged so that a triangle with clear edges appears to lie over them, although no triangle outline is drawn [1]; the brain completes the missing contours from the arrangement of the shapes, which is a form of perceptual organisation (closure) [1].
psych12a3-dpi-25
Describe the Shepard table illusion and explain why the two tabletops look different in shape and size. (3 marks)

Two tabletops that are identical in shape and size are drawn in perspective and appear to differ [1]; the brain interprets the drawing as a three-dimensional scene and applies perspective and size-distance scaling to the tabletops [1]; the apparent depth makes one tabletop look longer and narrower than the other [1].
psych12a3-dpi-26
Describe the cross-cultural finding about the Müller-Lyer illusion and state what it suggests about perception. (2 marks)

People from environments without many right-angled, rectangular buildings (non-carpentered environments) were less susceptible to the Müller-Lyer illusion than people from carpentered urban environments [1]; this suggests that experience with the surroundings shapes the depth cues and assumptions used to perceive illusions [1].
psych12a3-dpi-27
State what is meant by figure-ground organisation, using Rubin’s vase as an example. (1 mark)

Figure-ground organisation is the perceptual separation of a scene into an object (the figure) and its background, which can reverse in images such as Rubin’s vase, where either the vase or two faces can be seen as the figure [1].
psych12a3-dpi-28
Describe the Ebbinghaus illusion and explain how the surrounding circles change the perceived size of the central circle. (3 marks)

Two identical central circles look different in size when one is surrounded by larger circles and the other by smaller circles [1]; the central circle surrounded by larger circles looks smaller, and the one surrounded by smaller circles looks larger [1]; this is size contrast, in which perceived size is judged relative to the size of nearby objects [1].
psych12a3-dpi-29
Explain how perceptual set can change what a person perceives in an ambiguous image. Use a situation in which two people expect different things from the same image. (4 marks)

Perceptual set is a readiness to perceive a stimulus in a particular way, based on expectations, experience or context [1]; the same ambiguous image is interpreted according to what each viewer expects, so each may see a different object [1]; for example, a viewer told the image shows an animal may see an animal, while a viewer told it shows a plant may see a plant [1]; the resulting perception is shaped by top-down processing rather than determined by the stimulus alone [1].
vce-psych12-di-c1
The Müller-Lyer lines still look different even after you measure them and know they are equal. This suggests that:
The lines really are different lengths, and the ruler used to measure them was inaccurate
Illusions affect only people with poor eyesight, whose retinas send blurred signals
The illusion comes from automatic processes, such as reading the arrowheads as depth cues, that knowledge cannot override
The illusion is caused by the retina alone, before any information reaches the brain
One explanation (the carpentered world hypothesis) links it to experience of corners in buildings, which also explains cultural differences.
vce-psych12-scientific-methodologies-and: A researcher investigates whether different amounts of sleep affect reaction time. The amount of sleep is the
The independent variable is the variable manipulated by the researcher; reaction time is the dependent variable that is measured.
Which of the following is a correctly worded experimental hypothesis?
Participants who sleep for 8 hours will have faster reaction times than participants who sleep for 4 hours
To investigate sleep and reaction time
A hypothesis is a testable, predictive statement that specifies the relationship between the IV and DV and the population. Options A and C are vague/question, and D is an aim.
A study measures the relationship between students’ hours of social media use and their self-reported sleep quality, without manipulating either variable. The method is a
Correlational studies examine the relationship between variables as they naturally occur, without manipulation. No IV is manipulated, so this is not an experiment.
A variable that was not intended to be studied, but which systematically varies with the independent variable and affects the dependent variable, is a
A confounding variable systematically varies with the IV, making it impossible to tell whether the IV or the confound produced the change in the DV.
A researcher groups participants into left-handed and right-handed people and compares their performance on a spatial task. Participants cannot be randomly allocated to groups. This is a
A classification study uses a naturally occurring characteristic (here, handedness) to categorise participants; the IV is not manipulated.

A researcher tests whether listening to classical music while studying improves recall of word lists. Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and one extraneous variable that should be controlled. (3 marks)

IV: whether participants listen to classical music (or the type of music/no music) while studying (1); DV: number of words recalled correctly (1); extraneous variable e.g. length of word list, time of day, prior knowledge/age, noise in room, study time (1).
Distinguish between a case study and a controlled experiment as scientific methodologies. (3 marks)

A case study is an in-depth investigation of a single individual, group or event (1); it typically collects detailed qualitative data without manipulating variables (1); a controlled experiment manipulates an IV and measures its effect on a DV while controlling other variables, so it can establish cause and effect (1).
Explain the difference between an aim and a hypothesis, using an example. (2 marks)

An aim states the purpose of the investigation (what is being investigated), e.g. to investigate the effect of caffeine on reaction time (1); a hypothesis is a testable prediction of the outcome, stating the relationship between the IV and DV, e.g. participants given caffeine will have faster reaction times than those given none (1).
In a placebo-controlled trial of a new headache tablet, the control group is given
the new tablet at a higher dose
a placebo that looks identical to the tablet
the tablet at a different time of day
a higher dose of the tablet given to younger participants

A control group receives a placebo so that any effect of simply taking a tablet can be separated from the effect of the active drug. Giving a different dose or timing is an experimental condition that tests the IV, not a baseline for comparison.
Random allocation of participants to experimental and control groups is used mainly to
make the sample representative of the wider population
let the researcher choose which participants receive the treatment
make the groups roughly equivalent at the start so differences can be attributed to the IV
increase the number of dependent variables measured

Random allocation spreads individual differences across groups by chance, so any differences after the manipulation are more likely due to the IV. Making a sample representative is the purpose of random sampling, which is a separate process.
Which statement correctly describes random sampling?
It assigns participants to experimental and control conditions
It removes all extraneous variables from a study
It ensures that a study demonstrates cause and effect
It selects participants so each member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen

Random sampling selects participants from the population in an unbiased way, which supports generalisation of the findings. Assigning participants to conditions is random allocation, a different process, and random sampling alone does not control variables or establish cause and effect.
A researcher watches and records children's play in a school playground without intervening or changing the setting. This method is

Naturalistic observation records behaviour in its normal setting without manipulating variables. A laboratory experiment would involve changing an IV in a controlled setting, which the researcher does not do here.
A researcher finds that a memory test gives almost identical scores when the same participants take it on two occasions one week apart. The test is said to be

Reliability refers to the consistency of a measure across repeated use under the same conditions, which is what the near-identical scores show. Validity concerns whether the test measures what it claims, which consistent scores alone do not establish.
A researcher designs a 'memory test' that in fact measures attention span rather than memory. The test therefore lacks

Validity is the extent to which a measure assesses what it is intended to measure, and this test measures something else. Reliability concerns consistency of results, which a test can have even while measuring the wrong thing.

A survey finds that people who drink more coffee report lower fitness levels, and a researcher concludes that coffee causes low fitness. Which statement best explains why this conclusion is not justified?
A third variable, such as a busy lifestyle, may be responsible for both
Correlational studies cannot include more than one variable
The survey should have been replaced by a case study of one participant
Fitness should have been defined as the independent variable

A correlation shows that two variables are related but not that one causes the other, because a third variable could influence both. Correlational studies always involve two or more variables, so the problem is the inference drawn rather than the number of variables measured.
Participants in a study guess its purpose and change their behaviour to match what they think the researcher wants. This is an example of

Demand characteristics are cues in a study that lead participants to change their behaviour to fit the expected outcome. Random error is unpredictable variation in measurements, not a participant response to the purpose of the study.
Which research method is most appropriate for establishing whether a new teaching program causes an improvement in exam results?

A controlled experiment manipulates the IV (the program) and controls other variables, which allows cause and effect to be inferred. A correlational study could show that program participation and results are related, but could not establish that the program caused the change.
A laboratory study uses artificial tasks that bear little resemblance to everyday activities. The study is therefore low in

Ecological validity is the extent to which findings apply to real-life settings and behaviour, and artificial tasks reduce it. Internal validity concerns whether the IV alone caused the change in the DV, not whether the tasks resemble real life.
In an experiment, the group that receives the level of the independent variable being tested is called the
The experimental group is exposed to the level of the IV being tested, while the control group does not receive it. The other options are not standard terms for the group that receives the IV.
A researcher keeps room temperature, lighting and task instructions the same for all participants. These are called

Controlled variables are held constant across all conditions so they cannot affect the DV. Confounding variables are uncontrolled variables that vary along with the IV, which is the problem these controls prevent.
Participants in a drug trial improve after taking an inert tablet because they believe it is an active drug. This improvement is known as the

The placebo effect is a real change in symptoms or behaviour caused by participants' expectations rather than an active treatment. Random error is unpredictable measurement variation, so it does not explain a consistent improvement produced by belief.
A study in which participants do not know whether they are receiving the treatment or a placebo is described as

In a single-blind study only the participants are unaware of their condition. In a double-blind study the researchers delivering the treatment are also unaware, so that option describes a stronger design than the one given.
Which sequence correctly orders the steps of the scientific method?

Scientists observe a phenomenon, form a testable hypothesis, test it by collecting data, and then conclude whether the hypothesis is supported. A hypothesis must come before testing, so the other sequences do not describe the process.
Why is replication of a study important?
it guarantees the original results were correct
it helps establish whether findings are reliable
it removes the need for a hypothesis
it replaces the need for operational definitions

Replication repeats a study to check whether its findings can be obtained again, which supports the reliability of the results. A single replication cannot guarantee that the original result was correct, and replication does not remove the need for a hypothesis or operational definitions.
In a study where every participant completes both the low-noise and high-noise conditions, the design is a

A repeated measures design tests the same participants in every condition, so each person serves as their own control. An independent groups design uses different participants in each condition, which is not the case in this study.
Define the term reliability as it applies to psychological measures. (1 mark)
The consistency of a measure, so that it produces similar results when the same test is repeated under the same conditions [1].
A researcher measures anxiety in students using a self-report questionnaire. Identify one threat to the validity of this measure and explain how it could be reduced. (3 marks)

Social desirability bias: students may answer in ways that make them look favourable rather than honestly [1]; this means the questionnaire measures self-presentation rather than true anxiety, reducing validity [1]; it could be reduced by ensuring anonymity, reassuring students that responses are confidential, or supporting results with another measure such as a physiological indicator [1].

A researcher wants to know whether a new maths app improves Year 9 test scores. Outline how the steps of the scientific method would be applied to this investigation, from observation to conclusion. (4 marks)

Observation of a problem, such as students' low maths scores, leading to a question about whether the app helps [1]; a testable hypothesis, e.g. students who use the app will score higher than students who do not [1]; a controlled experiment with app use as the IV and test score as the DV, using a control group and collecting data [1]; analysis of the results to decide whether the hypothesis is supported, followed by a conclusion that can be reported and replicated [1].

A researcher surveys only first-year university students about their sleep habits and wants to generalise the findings to all adolescents. Explain one reason this limits the generalisability of the findings. (2 marks)

The sample is not representative of the target population, because university students differ from adolescents in general in age, independence and lifestyle [1]; so the findings may not apply to adolescents more broadly [1].
In a study of word recall, noise from a nearby building is louder during some testing sessions than others. Explain how the researcher could control this situational extraneous variable. (2 marks)

Keep the noise level constant across all participants and sessions, e.g. by testing everyone in a sound-proofed room [1]; this stops noise varying systematically with the IV, so differences in recall can be attributed to the IV [1].
Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of using a repeated measures design rather than an independent groups design, and suggest how the disadvantage could be reduced. (3 marks)

Advantage: fewer participants are needed, and individual differences are controlled because each person serves as their own control [1]; disadvantage: order effects, such as practice or fatigue, may influence performance in the second condition [1]; reduce by counterbalancing the order in which participants complete the conditions [1].

A researcher tests a new reading program. Students in the program group are taught by their own teachers, who volunteered for the study. Control group students come from a different school and do not receive the program. Identify two confounding variables and explain how each could affect the results, then suggest one way to reduce them. (4 marks)

Teacher differences: volunteer teachers may be more motivated or skilled, so gains could reflect the teacher rather than the program [1]; school differences: the schools may differ in resources or student background, so outcome differences could reflect the school [1]; because these variables are not controlled, the effect of the program cannot be isolated [1]; reduce by randomly allocating students or classes from the same school to the program and control groups, which balances these variables across groups [1].
Explain the purpose of conducting a pilot study before a main experiment. (2 marks)

To test the procedures, materials and measures so that problems can be identified and fixed before the main study [1]; to check whether the manipulation of the IV works and the study is feasible, saving time and resources [1].

A researcher spends two years studying one adult who has recovered from a stroke, using interviews and brain scans. Identify the research method used and state one strength and one limitation of this method. (3 marks)

Method: case study [1]; strength: provides rich, detailed in-depth data about an individual, including rare cases [1]; limitation: findings cannot be generalised to other people, and cause and effect cannot be established because no variables are manipulated [1].
Explain what is meant by the term validity in psychological research. (1 mark)
The extent to which a measure or study measures what it is intended to measure [1].
A study finds that adolescents who use social media more report lower mood. Researchers cannot conclude that social media causes low mood because:
The sample was too large, so small differences in mood appear to be significant
Mood cannot be measured, so the results cannot support any conclusion at all
Correlations are always close to zero, so the link found must be due to chance
It is correlational: nothing was manipulated, and other variables or reverse causation could explain the link
Only a controlled experiment, where the IV is manipulated and other variables controlled, supports cause-and-effect conclusions.
vce-psych12-sampling-and-experimental-de: psych12a3-sed-1
A researcher obtains a list of every student in a school and uses a random number generator to choose 100 students. This is
random allocation
convenience sampling
random sampling
stratified sampling
In random sampling every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected. Stratified sampling would first divide the population into subgroups.
psych12a3-sed-2
A researcher divides the school population into year levels and then selects students from each year level in proportion to the number of students in that year level. This is
convenience sampling
random allocation
a within-subjects design
stratified sampling
Stratified sampling ensures key subgroups (strata) are represented in the same proportions as in the population.
psych12a3-sed-3
In an experiment, participants in a sample are assigned to the experimental or control condition by drawing numbers from a hat. This procedure is called
convenience sampling
random sampling
random allocation
stratified sampling
Random allocation gives each participant in the sample an equal chance of being placed in any condition, helping control participant variables.
psych12a3-sed-4
Which experimental design uses the same participants in every condition of the independent variable?
Between-subjects (independent groups)
Within-subjects (repeated measures)
Mixed design
Classification
In a within-subjects design all participants are exposed to every condition, controlling for individual participant differences but risking order effects.
psych12a3-sed-5
A disadvantage of a within-subjects design compared with a between-subjects design is
needing a larger sample
inability to compare conditions
participant variables differ between groups
order effects such as practice or fatigue
Because each participant experiences all conditions, performance may be affected by the order, e.g. practice or fatigue. Counterbalancing can reduce this.
psych12a3-sed-6
A researcher recruits participants by asking students passing the library to complete a study. Name this sampling method and describe one limitation. (2 marks)
Convenience sampling (1); the sample may not be representative of the population, limiting generalisability, or may be biased (1).
psych12a3-sed-7
Explain the difference between random sampling and random allocation. (3 marks)

Random sampling is the selection of participants from the population so that each member has an equal chance of being chosen (1); random allocation is the assignment of the sample’s participants to experimental or control groups by chance (1); sampling aims to produce a representative sample, whereas allocation aims to distribute participant characteristics evenly across groups to control participant variables (1).
psych12a3-sed-8

An experiment examines whether a new teaching method improves test scores. Describe how this could be conducted as a between-subjects design, and outline one strength of this design over a within-subjects design. (3 marks)
