Two separate groups are formed, one taught with the new method and one with the usual method, and their test scores are compared (1, with random allocation as an acceptable addition); each participant experiences only one condition (1); strength: no order effects/practice effects, since participants do not repeat the task (1).
psych12a3-sed-9
Why do researchers aim for a representative sample?
so that participants can be randomly allocated to conditions
so that findings can be generalised to the wider population
so that the dependent variable is measured without error
so that every participant experiences all conditions

A representative sample reflects the characteristics of the population, allowing findings to be generalised beyond the sample. Random allocation and within-subjects designs concern experimental control rather than generalisability.
psych12a3-sed-10
Half of the participants complete Task A before Task B, and the other half complete Task B before Task A, to reduce order effects. This technique is called
random sampling
random allocation
counterbalancing
operationalisation

Counterbalancing spreads the order of conditions across participants so that order effects are distributed evenly rather than removed. Random allocation assigns participants to groups, so it does not control the order in which one person completes tasks.
psych12a3-sed-11
Two classes are randomly allocated to either a new or a standard teaching method. Within each class, every student sits a test before and after the lesson. Which design does this study use?
within-subjects design
mixed design
matched-pairs design
correlational design

A mixed design includes a between-subjects factor (teaching method, with each class in one condition) and a within-subjects factor (testing before and after). A purely within-subjects design would have every student experience both teaching methods.
psych12a3-sed-12
What is the main purpose of including a placebo group in an experiment?
to control for participants' expectations of receiving a treatment
to make the sample representative of the population
to ensure the dependent variable is measured precisely
to allow participants to be randomly sampled

A placebo group receives an inactive treatment, so any effect of expecting treatment can be separated from the effect of the treatment itself. Representativeness depends on how the sample is selected, not on the groups' experimental conditions.
psych12a3-sed-13
In a double-blind design, which people are kept unaware of which participants are in the experimental or control group?
only the participants
only the researcher who analyses the data
only the person who designed the study
both the participants and the people who interact with them during testing
Double-blind procedures stop both participant and experimenter expectations from influencing results. In a single-blind design, only the participants are unaware of their group.
psych12a3-sed-14
Which statement best explains why a larger sample is generally preferred to a smaller sample drawn from the same population?
a larger sample removes the need for random allocation
a larger sample always increases the validity of the independent variable
a larger sample reduces sampling error, so it is more likely to reflect the population
a larger sample ensures each participant experiences every condition
Larger samples tend to give estimates closer to the true population values, reducing sampling error. The other options describe features of experimental design rather than of sample size.
psych12a3-sed-15
A researcher surveys 400 Year 12 students selected from schools across Victoria. In this study, the population is
all Year 12 students in Victoria
the 400 students who completed the survey
the schools that agreed to take part
the researchers who designed the survey

The population is the whole group the researcher wants to draw conclusions about, while the sample is the 400 students actually studied. The schools are a means of selecting participants, not the population.
psych12a3-sed-16
An advantage of a within-subjects design over a between-subjects design is that it
eliminates order effects altogether
requires fewer participants
requires a larger number of participants
removes the need to measure the dependent variable
Each participant contributes data to every condition, so fewer people are needed than in a between-subjects design. Within-subjects designs still face order effects, so they do not eliminate them.
psych12a3-sed-17
A survey about exercise habits is distributed only through a fitness app. The main concern about the sample is that
it is too large to analyse
it lacks a control group
it may over-represent people who already exercise regularly
the dependent variable is confounded

Only people who use the app are invited, so the sample is biased towards active individuals and may not represent the wider population. A missing control group is a concern for experiments rather than surveys.
psych12a3-sed-18
A population of 1 200 people has 800 females and 400 males. A stratified sample of 60 people is selected in proportion to sex. How many males are in the sample?
Males make up 400 ÷ 1 200 = 1/3 of the population, so 1/3 × 60 = 20 males. Splitting the sample equally (30) ignores the different proportions in each subgroup.
psych12a3-sed-19
Which of the following is a participant variable that random allocation is designed to spread evenly across conditions?
the temperature of the testing room
the prior knowledge or motivation of each participant
the wording of the instructions read aloud
the time of day the test is conducted

Participant variables are characteristics of individuals, such as prior knowledge or motivation, and random allocation tends to distribute them evenly across groups. Room temperature, instructions and time of testing are situational factors that should be standardised across conditions.
psych12a3-sed-20
Define the term sampling bias. (1 mark)
Systematic error in the way participants are selected, so that the sample is not representative of the population [1].
psych12a3-sed-21
Describe the difference between a within-subjects design and a between-subjects design. (2 marks)
In a within-subjects design the same participants experience every condition of the independent variable [1]; in a between-subjects design different participants are allocated to each condition [1].
psych12a3-sed-22
Explain why a researcher using a within-subjects design would use counterbalancing. (2 marks)
To control order effects such as practice or fatigue [1], by varying the order of conditions across participants so that order effects are spread evenly between conditions [1].
psych12a3-sed-23

A researcher investigates whether a 10-minute walk improves concentration. Outline how this could be run as a between-subjects design and as a within-subjects design, then identify one advantage of the within-subjects design and one disadvantage of the between-subjects design. (4 marks)

Between-subjects: participants are randomly allocated to a walking group or a sitting group, and each person completes the concentration task in one condition only [1]; within-subjects: the same participants complete the task after walking and after sitting [1]; advantage of within-subjects: fewer participants are needed because each person contributes data to both conditions [1]; disadvantage of between-subjects: individual differences may affect the groups unevenly, since each person completes only one condition [1].
vce-psych12-se-c1
What is the difference between random sampling and random allocation?
They are the same thing
Random sampling selects participants from a population; random allocation assigns them to conditions
Random allocation selects participants; random sampling assigns them to groups
Random sampling is only used in within-subjects designs
Random sampling helps representativeness (generalisation); random allocation spreads participant variables evenly between groups.
vce-psych12-data-analysis-and-conclusion: psych12a3-dac-1
Which of the following is quantitative data?
An interview transcript
A participant’s description of how nervous she felt
The number of errors made on a task
A researcher’s observation notes about mood
Quantitative data are numerical measurements. The others are qualitative data in the form of descriptions and words.
psych12a3-dac-2
The scores of seven participants on a memory test are 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. The median is
The median is the middle value of the ordered scores: with 7 scores, the 4th value is 6. The mean is 44/7 ≈ 6.3 and the mode is 5.
psych12a3-dac-3
A set of scores has one very high outlier. Which measure of central tendency is most affected by the outlier?
Range
Median
Mode
Mean
The mean uses every value in its calculation, so an outlier pulls it up or down. The median and mode are resistant to outliers.
psych12a3-dac-4

A researcher finds that the experimental group had a higher mean score than the control group, but concludes the result is not generalisable beyond the sample. Which feature of the study would most justify this conclusion?
The use of a convenience sample from one school
A well-defined operational definition of the DV
Use of a control group
Random allocation to groups
A small, non-random sample from a single setting is not representative, so conclusions can only be applied to the sample and not confidently to the wider population.
psych12a3-dac-5
A conclusion in a research report should
introduce new variables
ignore results that were unexpected
restate the hypothesis only
state whether the results support the hypothesis, relate to the aim, and acknowledge limitations
A good conclusion is based on the data, indicates whether the hypothesis was supported, considers the extent to which results can be generalised, and acknowledges limitations.
psych12a3-dac-6
Participants completed a reaction-time test. Times (in ms) were: 210, 220, 230, 240, 250, 250, 260. Calculate the mean and state the mode. (2 marks)
psych12a3-dac-7
Distinguish between qualitative and quantitative data and give one example of each in a psychology study. (3 marks)

Qualitative data are descriptive, non-numerical information about qualities or experiences (1); quantitative data are numerical measurements that can be statistically analysed (1); examples: interview responses or observation notes (qualitative); scores on a questionnaire, time taken or number correct (quantitative) (1 for both examples).
psych12a3-dac-8

A study found that the mean memory score for the sleep-deprived group was lower than for the control group. The researcher concluded that sleep deprivation causes poorer memory. Evaluate whether this conclusion is justified if the groups were not randomly allocated. (3 marks)

The conclusion may not be justified (1); without random allocation, participant variables (e.g. age, ability, motivation) may differ between groups and act as confounding variables (1); so the difference may not be due only to sleep deprivation and a causal conclusion cannot be confidently drawn (1).
psych12a3-dac-9
Which measure of central tendency can be used with nominal (categorical) data, such as the most popular colour chosen by a group?
Mean
Median
Range
Mode

The mode is the most frequently occurring category, so it can be found for categorical data. The mean and median need numerical values, and the range is a measure of spread rather than central tendency.
psych12a3-dac-10
Which of the following measures the spread of a set of scores rather than their central tendency?
Range
Mean
Median
Mode
The range is the difference between the highest and lowest scores, so it describes how spread out the scores are. The mean, median and mode all describe a typical or central value.
psych12a3-dac-11
Six participants scored 12, 15, 18, 20, 22 and 25 on a memory test. What is the median score?
With an even number of scores, the median is the average of the two middle values: (18 + 20) ÷ 2 = 19. Choosing 18 or 20 uses only one of the two middle scores.
psych12a3-dac-12
Four participants scored 6, 8, 10 and 12 on a task. What is the mean score?
The mean is the total divided by the number of scores: (6 + 8 + 10 + 12) ÷ 4 = 36 ÷ 4 = 9. The total of 36 has not been divided by the number of scores.
psych12a3-dac-13
A researcher records how many students in a class chose each of four lunch options. Which graph is most appropriate for displaying these data?
Scatterplot
Bar graph
Line graph
Histogram

The lunch options are categories, so each should be a separate bar, which a bar graph shows. A histogram is for continuous numerical data grouped into intervals, and a line graph implies a trend across an ordered variable.
psych12a3-dac-14
A researcher wants to show whether hours of practice and test score are related, with each participant shown as one point. Which graph should be used?
Pie chart
Line graph
Scatterplot
Bar graph

A scatterplot displays paired values of two numerical variables, one point per participant, so any relationship can be seen. A pie chart shows parts of a whole, and a bar graph compares categories rather than paired numerical scores.
psych12a3-dac-15
In a sample of 40 participants, 30 completed the task. What percentage of participants completed the task?
30 ÷ 40 = 0.75, so 75% completed the task. Using 30 directly gives the count rather than the percentage, and 25% is the percentage who did not complete it.
psych12a3-dac-16
The experimental group had a mean score of 14.5 and the control group a mean score of 11.2. What is the difference between the two means?
14.5 − 11.2 = 3.3. Adding the two means gives 25.7, and 0.33 results from a misplaced decimal point.
psych12a3-dac-17
Scores on a quiz were 2, 3, 3, 5, 5 and 8. Which statement about the mode is correct?
The mode is 3 only
The mode is 4.3
There is no mode
There are two modes, 3 and 5
The values 3 and 5 each occur twice and no other value occurs more than once, so the data have two modes. The value 4.3 is the mean (26 ÷ 6 ≈ 4.3), not the mode.
psych12a3-dac-18

A researcher predicted that the experimental group would score higher on a memory test than the control group. Both groups had a mean score of 15.0. Which statement is the most appropriate conclusion?
The hypothesis was supported because both groups completed the same memory test
The hypothesis was not supported, as the sample showed no difference between the group means
The hypothesis was partly supported, because equal means still indicate a small effect
The results prove that the independent variable has no effect on memory in the population

The predicted difference did not occur in this sample, so the hypothesis is not supported by these data. Equal means cannot show a small effect, and a single sample cannot prove anything about the whole population.
psych12a3-dac-19
A study found that people who spent more hours on social media each night had lower sleep quality scores. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
Social media use causes poorer sleep quality
Poorer sleep quality causes people to spend more time on social media
Social media use and sleep quality are unrelated in this study
Social media use is associated with lower sleep quality, but this design cannot establish that one causes the other

The study shows an association between the two variables, and without manipulating either one, causation cannot be concluded. Claiming that either variable causes the other goes beyond the data, and claiming they are unrelated contradicts the findings.
psych12a3-dac-20
Which graph is most appropriate for showing how the average reaction time of one group changed across five practice sessions?
Pie chart
Histogram of individual scores
Line graph
Table of individual scores

Sessions are ordered over time, and a line graph joins the averages to show the trend. A pie chart shows parts of a whole, a histogram shows the spread of individual scores, and a table does not display the trend visually.
psych12a3-dac-21
A group’s mean score on a test rose from 40 before training to 46 after training. By what percentage did the mean increase?
The increase is 46 − 40 = 6, and 6 ÷ 40 = 0.15, so the mean increased by 15%. Dividing by the new mean (6 ÷ 46 ≈ 13%) uses the wrong starting value.
psych12a3-dac-22
Five participants’ scores were 14, 9, 22, 17 and 11. What is the range of these scores?
The range is the highest score minus the lowest score: 22 − 9 = 13. Adding the highest and lowest scores gives 31, and 22 is the highest score on its own.
psych12a3-dac-23
Researchers read participants’ open-ended responses and identify recurring themes, such as ‘feeling rushed’ or ‘lack of sleep’. Which data-analysis approach is being used?
Calculating the median
Constructing a scatterplot
Thematic analysis of qualitative data
Calculating the range
Identifying and grouping recurring themes in non-numerical responses is thematic analysis, which is used for qualitative data. The other options are techniques for numerical data.
psych12a3-dac-24
A study with eight participants found a large difference between the means of two groups. Which statement is the most accurate?
The difference is certain to exist in the wider population
A result from eight participants is more reliable than one from 80 participants
Sample size has no effect on the results of a study
A small sample can produce unstable results that may not replicate, so the finding should be interpreted cautiously

Small samples are more affected by chance and individual differences, so a result may not appear in a larger or different sample. A result from a small sample is less reliable, not more, and sample size strongly affects results.
psych12a3-dac-25
Five reaction times (in seconds) were 0.42, 0.38, 0.45, 0.40 and 0.35. What is the mean reaction time?
The total is 2.00 s, and 2.00 ÷ 5 = 0.40 s. The total of 2.00 s has not been divided by the number of scores, and 0.45 s is the highest value rather than the mean.
psych12a3-dac-26
Define generalisability as it applies to the conclusion of a research report. (1 mark)
The extent to which the findings of a study, based on its sample, can be applied to the wider population or other settings [1].
psych12a3-dac-27

A researcher reports that 45 of 60 participants improved after training. Calculate the percentage of participants who improved, and state whether the number of participants who improved is quantitative or qualitative data. (2 marks)
45 ÷ 60 × 100 = 75% [1]; the number of participants who improved is numerical, so it is quantitative data [1].
psych12a3-dac-28
Scores on a concentration test for five participants were 4, 7, 9, 10 and 12. Calculate the median and the range. (2 marks)
Median = 9, the middle value of the ordered scores [1]; range = 12 − 4 = 8 [1].
psych12a3-dac-29
Explain why a researcher should state the limitations of a study when writing its conclusion. (3 marks)

Limitations, such as a small or non-random sample or reliance on self-report, affect how confidently the results can be interpreted [1]; stating them shows the extent to which the findings can be generalised [1]; this avoids overstating the findings or implying causation that the design cannot support [1].
psych12a3-dac-30

A researcher tested 15 first-year university students’ reaction times before and after they drank a caffeinated drink. Reaction times improved, and the student concluded that caffeine improves reaction time for all adults. Give two reasons this conclusion is not justified, and suggest a better wording for it. (3 marks)

The sample is small and specific (15 first-year university students), so the finding cannot be generalised to all adults [1]; with no control group, practice effects or other factors could explain the improvement, so caffeine cannot be confirmed as the cause [1]; a better conclusion would state that reaction times improved after caffeine in this sample of 15 students, and that further research is needed [1].
psych12a3-dac-31

A researcher compares an experimental group (mean 18.4, n = 20) and a control group (mean 15.1, n = 20) from a single school. Calculate the difference between the means, and write a suitable conclusion that acknowledges the limitations of the study. (4 marks)

Difference = 18.4 − 15.1 = 3.3 [1]; the experimental group had the higher mean score [1]; suggested conclusion: the intervention was associated with higher scores in this sample of 40 students [1]; the result may not generalise beyond this one school, a limitation that should be acknowledged [1].
psych12a3-dac-32
Explain the difference between a conclusion stating that results ‘support’ a hypothesis and one stating that results ‘prove’ it. (2 marks)
‘Support’ means the data are consistent with the hypothesis [1]; ‘prove’ overstates certainty, as a single study with a limited sample cannot establish a claim beyond doubt [1].
psych12a3-dac-33
Reaction times (in ms) for six participants were 310, 295, 330, 305, 320 and 300. Calculate the mean, the median and the range. (3 marks)
psych12a3-dac-34
A researcher leaves out three participants’ results because their scores were unusually high, and then concludes that the intervention ‘works for everyone’. Evaluate this conclusion. (4 marks)

Excluding participants because of their results, rather than a pre-stated criterion, biases the data and reduces validity [1]; the conclusion ignores the three excluded participants, so the findings do not reflect the whole group tested [1]; the claim that the intervention ‘works for everyone’ overgeneralises beyond the sample studied [1]; a justified conclusion would report the exclusions and limit its claims to the participants tested [1].
vce-psych12-da-c1
A study used 20 Year 11 volunteers from one Melbourne school. Its results can most validly be generalised to:
All adolescents worldwide, because adolescent brains develop in the same way
Only the population the sample came from, and only if the sample represents it
All Australians, because the school was in Australia's second-largest city
Anyone at all, because the results were found to be statistically significant
A small, convenience sample limits generalisation. Conclusions should match the scope of the sample.
vce-psych12-ethics-in-psychological-rese: psych12a3-eth-1
Informed consent in research means that participants
are not told the aim at any stage
are paid for taking part
are told about the nature of the study, procedures and risks and agree to take part voluntarily
can never withdraw
Informed consent requires that participants understand what the study involves, including risks, before agreeing to take part. Parental consent is needed for minors.
psych12a3-eth-2
A researcher keeps participants’ names separate from their data and ensures that only the research team can access the data. This protects
confidentiality
deception
voluntary participation
debriefing
Confidentiality means that personal information is not disclosed or made accessible to others without permission.
psych12a3-eth-3
A study involves deceiving participants about its true aim. The most appropriate ethical safeguard to follow the experiment is
paying the participants
a debriefing session
destroying the data
removing the control group
Deception may only be used when justified and no alternative exists; it must be followed by a debrief explaining the true purpose and addressing any distress.
psych12a3-eth-4
Which of the following best represents the principle of voluntary participation?
Participants are told they must complete the study to receive course credit
Participants choose to take part without pressure or coercion and may withdraw at any time without penalty
Participants are offered a gift for staying
Participants are told they cannot leave once they begin
Participation must be free from coercion, and participants have the right to withdraw at any time without penalty.
psych12a3-eth-5
The 3Rs applying to the use of animals in research are
respect, responsibility and review
random, representative and relevant
replacement, reduction and refinement
reliability, replication and reporting
Researchers should replace animals with alternatives where possible, reduce the number used, and refine procedures to minimise harm and distress.
psych12a3-eth-6
A researcher wants to study stress in Year 10 students (aged 15–16) using a questionnaire. Describe two ethical considerations the researcher must address. (3 marks)

Informed consent must be obtained from the students and from their parents/guardians as they are under 18 (1); confidentiality and privacy of responses must be maintained, e.g. de-identified data stored securely (1); other acceptable: right to withdraw, voluntary participation, minimising distress with support available (1 for explaining how each is addressed).
psych12a3-eth-7
Explain the purpose of a debriefing session and what it should include. (3 marks)

Debriefing occurs at the end of the study to ensure participants leave in the same state in which they entered (1); it explains the true aim and any deception used and answers questions (1); it checks for distress/offers support and gives participants the opportunity to withdraw their data (1).
psych12a3-eth-8
Explain why the use of deception in psychological research may be considered ethical in some circumstances. (2 marks)

Deception may be necessary because knowing the true aim could alter participants’ behaviour and invalidate the results (1); it is acceptable only if the potential benefits outweigh the risks, there is no suitable alternative, it causes no more than minimal harm, and participants are fully debriefed (1).
psych12a3-eth-9
A questionnaire is described as anonymous when
the researcher knows participants’ names but does not publish them
no one, including the researcher, can link any response to the person who gave it
participants are told the aim of the study before they begin
the data is stored on a password-protected computer
Anonymity means identity cannot be linked to responses at any point, even by the researcher. Keeping names but not publishing them is confidentiality, which is a different form of protection.
psych12a3-eth-10
A participant asks to leave a study halfway through. The researcher asks them to finish first, as the data would otherwise be wasted. Which ethical principle is breached?
confidentiality
the 3Rs
replication
the right to withdraw

Participants may withdraw at any time without penalty, and pressuring them to continue breaches this right. Confidentiality concerns protecting personal information, not whether a person may stop taking part.
psych12a3-eth-11
A researcher is testing a memory task that may cause mild frustration. Which action best reflects the principle of minimising harm?
stopping the task and offering support if a participant becomes very distressed
increasing the difficulty of the task so that the results are more dramatic
keeping the frustration hidden so that participants respond more naturally
continuing the task because the participant consented at the start

A researcher has a duty of care to stop a procedure and provide support when a participant shows significant distress, even if they consented earlier. Increasing difficulty or hiding harm increases risk, and hiding harm also undermines informed consent.
psych12a3-eth-12
A psychology student plans to collect data from adults about their sleep habits. Before data collection begins, the study should be approved by
the student’s own tutor only
the journal in which the results will be submitted
a Human Research Ethics Committee
the participants’ employers

Research involving humans should be independently reviewed by an ethics committee, such as a Human Research Ethics Committee, before data collection begins. A tutor’s approval is not independent review, and journal submission does not replace this process.
psych12a3-eth-13
Which of the following is an example of research misconduct?
reporting a result that was not statistically significant
sharing preliminary results at a conference before journal publication
using a pilot study to refine procedures before the main study
presenting another researcher’s ideas as your own without citing them
Plagiarism, which means presenting someone else’s work or ideas as your own without acknowledgement, is research misconduct. The other options are honest and normal parts of the research process.
psych12a3-eth-14
Which statement best describes the cost-benefit principle in research ethics?
research with high risk is acceptable as long as the findings are eventually published
risks can be ignored once participants have signed a consent form
benefits only count if they increase the researcher’s career prospects
a study should proceed only if its potential benefits outweigh the risks to participants

Researchers must minimise risks and ensure they are justified by the benefits to participants or society. A signed consent form does not remove the researcher’s duty to protect participants from harm.
psych12a3-eth-15
Which group would most need additional ethical safeguards in psychological research?
adults with cognitive impairments who may be unable to give fully informed consent
adult volunteers who respond to a newspaper advertisement
adults who have completed a university degree
participants who are paid for their time

People with a reduced capacity to understand or consent, such as some adults with cognitive impairments, need extra protection, for example a substitute decision-maker. Responding to an advertisement, holding a degree or being paid does not make someone vulnerable.
psych12a3-eth-16
What should a participant information statement include?
the researcher’s private bank account details
the predicted results of the study, so participants can judge its value
the purpose, procedures and risks of the study, and how to contact the researcher or ethics committee
a list of the names of other participants

A participant information statement must describe the study’s purpose, procedures, risks and benefits, and how to ask questions or raise concerns. Predicted results could bias participants’ responses, and sharing other participants’ names breaches confidentiality.
psych12a3-eth-17
A teacher invites students in their class to take part in a university researcher’s survey during class time, in front of their peers. What is the main ethical concern?
the study will have too many participants to analyse
students may feel pressured to take part because of the teacher’s authority, threatening voluntary participation
the students may already know the researcher, which biases the results
the study cannot be published in a school journal

Voluntary participation requires that students feel free to decline without pressure, and the presence of a teacher and peers can make refusal difficult. The other options are methodological or practical concerns rather than ethical ones about consent.
psych12a3-eth-18
A researcher changes the procedures of an approved study so that participants now complete a much longer task. What should the researcher do?
continue without telling anyone, because the original approval still applies
inform only the journal that will publish the results
destroy all data collected under the original procedures
seek ethics approval for the changes and inform participants so they can decide whether to continue

Ethics approval covers specific procedures, so substantial changes need review, and participants must be told about changes that might affect their decision to take part. Destroying existing data is not required and does not replace seeking approval.
psych12a3-eth-19
During an interview, a participant discloses that they are at risk of harming themselves. What is the most ethical response?
provide support and a referral to appropriate services, recognising that confidentiality has limits when a person is at risk
keep it confidential and continue the interview as normal
publish the disclosure in the findings to highlight the issue
withdraw the participant’s data and end the interview without comment

A researcher’s duty of care to a participant at risk takes priority over normal confidentiality, so support and referral are needed. Continuing as normal or publishing the disclosure ignores the participant’s welfare and privacy.
psych12a3-eth-20
A researcher publishes a direct quote from a participant, with enough workplace detail that colleagues could identify them, and does not ask for permission. Which ethical principle is breached?
validity
reliability
confidentiality and privacy
replication

Publishing identifiable details without permission breaches the participant’s privacy and the promise of confidentiality. Validity, reliability and replication describe the quality and repeatability of research rather than ethical principles that protect participants.
psych12a3-eth-21
What is the main ethical purpose of a pilot study?
to guarantee that the main study will produce significant results
to identify problems that could harm or distress participants before the main study begins
to avoid needing ethics approval for the main study
to replace the need for informed consent in the main study

A pilot study helps reveal risks and unclear procedures so they can be fixed before the main study exposes participants to them. It cannot guarantee results, remove ethics requirements or replace informed consent.
psych12a3-eth-22
A participant withdraws from a study after their data has been collected. What should the researcher do with that data?
keep it, because it has already been collected and paid for
publish it anonymously in an appendix, because the participant consented to the study
share it with other researchers as long as names have been removed
remove it from the dataset where practicable and exclude it from analysis

Respecting the right to withdraw means removing a participant’s data where practicable and excluding it from analysis. Removing names does not undo the participant’s decision, so keeping or sharing the data is not acceptable.
psych12a3-eth-23
A researcher finds that a new therapy harmed some participants, but leaves this out of the final report to protect the therapy’s reputation. Which ethical principle is breached?
honesty and integrity in reporting results
the 3Rs for the use of animals in research
random allocation of participants to groups
the right to privacy of participants

Researchers must report results accurately, including harmful effects, so others can make informed decisions and avoid harm. The 3Rs apply only to animal research, and random allocation is a design feature rather than an ethical principle.
psych12a3-eth-24
Explain the difference between anonymity and confidentiality in research. (2 marks)

Anonymity means that no one, including the researcher, can link a participant to their data [1]; confidentiality means the researcher knows who the participant is but does not disclose or publish identifying information [1].
psych12a3-eth-25
Explain why the wording of a participant information statement should avoid technical jargon. (2 marks)

Informed consent requires participants to understand what the study involves, so the statement must be clear [1]; jargon may cause misunderstanding, meaning participants could agree without fully understanding the risks and procedures [1].
psych12a3-eth-26
A researcher asks adults to complete a questionnaire about past experiences of family conflict. Describe three steps the researcher can take to minimise psychological harm to participants. (3 marks)

Tell participants that they can skip any question and withdraw at any time without penalty [1]; provide a debriefing at the end of the study that checks participants’ wellbeing [1]; give participants a list of support services, such as a counselling line [1].
psych12a3-eth-27
A researcher observes children playing in a school playground without telling them or their parents. Identify two ethical concerns and suggest one way to address each. (4 marks)

Concern: the children cannot give informed consent and were not told they were being observed [1]; concern: their privacy is invaded because their behaviour is recorded without permission [1]; address the first by seeking ethics approval and consent from parents or guardians and the school, with the children’s assent where possible [1]; address the second by recording behaviour without identifying individuals and storing data securely [1].
psych12a3-eth-28
Explain how offering a very large payment could compromise voluntary participation. (2 marks)

A large payment may pressure people, particularly those experiencing financial hardship, to take part even though they would otherwise decline [1]; their participation is then not free, and they may accept risks they would normally avoid [1].
psych12a3-eth-29
A researcher tests a new drug on mice. Describe one example of how the researcher could apply each of the 3Rs. (3 marks)

Replacement: use cell cultures or computer models where possible instead of live mice [1]; reduction: collect multiple measurements from each mouse where scientifically appropriate, so fewer mice are needed [1]; refinement: use humane anaesthetic and appropriate housing to reduce pain and distress [1].
psych12a3-eth-30
Describe three responsibilities of a Human Research Ethics Committee. (3 marks)

Reviewing research proposals to assess their risks, benefits and ethical acceptability [1]; approving a study, or requiring changes, before data collection begins [1]; monitoring approved research, including adverse events and any changes to procedures [1].
psych12a3-eth-31
A researcher plans a study with people who have been diagnosed with depression. Identify four ethical considerations for this study and briefly explain each. (4 marks)

Informed consent: participants must understand the study and their right to withdraw, and agree without pressure [1]; minimising harm: questions about mood may cause distress, so the researcher should monitor wellbeing and stop if needed [1]; confidentiality: sensitive health information must be stored securely and not identifiable in reports [1]; duty of care: participants at risk should be given information about support services and referral procedures [1].
psych12a3-eth-32
Explain why researchers must report their results honestly, even when the results do not support the hypothesis. (2 marks)

Other researchers, practitioners and the public rely on accurate reports to build knowledge and make decisions [1]; withholding unsupported results would distort the evidence base and waste participants’ contributions [1].
psych12a3-eth-33
State the term for a researcher’s obligation to protect participants from harm during a study. (1 mark)
Duty of care [1]
vce-psych12-et-c1
A study uses deception that is necessary for its validity. Which procedure is then essential?
Confidentiality, so that no one outside the study learns about the deception
Debriefing, so participants learn the true purpose and any harm is addressed
Paying participants more, to compensate them for being deceived
Using a larger sample, so the deception affects each person less
Deception is allowed only if it is justified and participants are fully debriefed afterwards.
vce-psych12-validity-reliability-and-err: psych12a3-vre-1
A study’s results are said to be valid if
the same results are obtained every time
the study measures what it claims to measure and the conclusions drawn are justified by the data
the sample is large
the participants were happy to take part
Validity concerns whether the investigation actually investigates what it claims to and whether the conclusions are supported. Option A describes reliability/repeatability.
psych12a3-vre-2
In a study of caffeine and reaction time, the experimenter knows which participants received caffeine and unintentionally encourages them more. This is an example of
a placebo effect
an investigator effect
random error
a within-subjects design
The investigator effect is the unintentional influence of the researcher’s expectations on participants’ behaviour or the measurement of results. It can be reduced by a double-blind procedure.
psych12a3-vre-3
Participants in a control group are given a sugar pill but believe it is an active drug and report feeling better. This is the
systematic error
investigator effect
placebo effect
order effect
The placebo effect is a change in participants’ responses due to their expectations rather than the IV. Placebos help control it.
psych12a3-vre-4
A stopwatch used in an experiment runs 0.5 seconds fast on every measurement. This is an example of
systematic error
an outlier
a placebo effect
random error
A systematic error is a consistent, predictable difference from the true value in the same direction, affecting accuracy. Random errors vary unpredictably and affect precision.
psych12a3-vre-5
A researcher repeats an experiment several times and obtains very similar results each time. This shows the investigation has
no confounding variables
high reliability (repeatability)
high external validity only
no errors
Repeatability — consistent results when an investigation is repeated under the same conditions — is an indicator of reliability. It does not guarantee validity or the absence of systematic error.
psych12a3-vre-6
Distinguish between internal validity and external validity. (2 marks)

Internal validity is the extent to which the results are due to the manipulation of the IV and not other factors such as confounding variables (1); external validity is the extent to which the results can be generalised to other people, settings and times (1).
psych12a3-vre-7
Explain the difference between random errors and systematic errors, and describe one way each could be reduced. (4 marks)

Random errors are unpredictable variations in measurement that vary in size and direction and affect precision (1); systematic errors are consistent biases in the same direction that affect accuracy (1); random errors reduced by taking repeated measurements and averaging, or using a larger sample (1); systematic errors reduced by calibrating equipment, standardising procedures, or using a control group/blinding (1).
psych12a3-vre-8
A researcher testing a new memory strategy tells participants the expected outcome. Identify a threat to the study’s validity and describe how a double-blind procedure would address it. (3 marks)

Threat: participant expectations/demand characteristics or placebo effect, or investigator effect (1); in a double-blind procedure neither participants nor the researcher(s) collecting data know who is in the experimental or control group (1); this reduces the influence of expectations on responses and measurement, improving validity (1).
psych12a3-vre-9
A questionnaire measuring anxiety is given to the same group of people twice, one week apart, and their scores are almost identical both times. This shows that the questionnaire has high
reliability
validity
a placebo effect
random allocation
Consistent scores when the same measure is repeated under the same conditions show reliability. They do not show that the questionnaire measures anxiety, so validity has not been established.
psych12a3-vre-10
Two observers independently watch the same video and count how often a child shares a toy. Their counts agree almost exactly. This shows high
internal validity
inter-rater reliability
external validity
a placebo effect

Inter-rater reliability is the agreement between different observers recording the same behaviour. Agreement does not prove that sharing a toy is the behaviour the researcher intended to measure, so it says nothing about validity.
psych12a3-vre-11
A test is designed to measure intelligence. It gives the same score each time a person sits it, but it actually measures how quickly people can read words. The test is
valid and reliable
valid but not reliable
reliable but not valid
neither valid nor reliable
The consistent scores show the test is reliable, but because it measures reading speed rather than intelligence it is not valid. Consistency alone does not guarantee that a measure is valid.
psych12a3-vre-12
Participants in a memory study work out what the researcher hopes to find and try harder to produce the expected result. This is an example of
demand characteristics
a double-blind procedure
random error
external validity

Demand characteristics are cues that lead participants to guess the aim of a study and change their behaviour. A double-blind procedure is a control designed to reduce this problem, not an example of it.
psych12a3-vre-13
A reaction-time test is repeated on one participant five times, giving 241, 258, 236, 262 and 249 ms with no consistent pattern. The variation is best described as
systematic error affecting accuracy
random error affecting precision
an outlier caused by the investigator
a placebo effect
Unpredictable variation in both directions is random error, which reduces precision. Systematic error would shift all the values the same way, so it would affect accuracy instead.
psych12a3-vre-14
Which change is most likely to increase the reliability of a 10-item quiz that measures knowledge of one unit?
Making the questions much easier so that most students score highly
Giving the quiz only once to a larger group of students
Adding more questions that assess the same unit content
Telling students that the quiz results will count towards their final grade

More items measuring the same content give a more stable estimate of knowledge, so scores are more consistent. Making the quiz easier or increasing the sample size does not make the measure itself more consistent.
psych12a3-vre-15

A researcher tests the effect of background music on maths performance using students working on computers in a quiet laboratory. The researcher then claims the results apply to students studying at home. The main concern is
internal validity
inter-rater reliability
random error
external validity
External validity concerns whether results can be generalised to other settings, people and times. A quiet laboratory may differ greatly from everyday study conditions, so the claim is questionable.
psych12a3-vre-16
A set of kitchen scales always reads 2 g heavier than the true mass of any object placed on it. Which statement is correct?
The scales have a systematic error, so their measurements are inaccurate
The scales have random error, so their measurements are imprecise
The scales are valid because their readings are perfectly consistent
Taking repeated measurements and averaging them will remove the 2 g offset
A constant offset in one direction is systematic error, which affects accuracy. Consistent readings show precision rather than accuracy, and averaging repeated readings cannot remove a constant bias.
psych12a3-vre-17
Which of the following best describes an outlier in a set of data?
A score that lies in the same direction as most other scores
A score that lies far from the rest of the data set
The mean of all the scores in the data set
A score recorded with an incorrectly calibrated instrument
An outlier is an unusually extreme score that differs markedly from the rest of the data. A faulty instrument may cause an outlier, but that describes a possible cause rather than the definition.
psych12a3-vre-18

All participants complete Task A and then Task B. Their performance on Task B is better, but the researcher cannot tell whether this is due to the tasks or to practice gained on Task A. This problem is called
a placebo effect
random error
an order effect
a demand characteristic
An order effect occurs when the sequence of conditions changes performance, such as through practice or fatigue. Counterbalancing the order of the tasks across participants helps control it.
psych12a3-vre-19
A trial compares a new teaching program with a standard one. Which procedure best reduces investigator effect when students rate the programs?
Telling students in advance that the new program is expected to work
Having the teacher who delivers each program also collect the ratings
Asking students to rate the programs only after they know which program they received
Using an independent assessor who does not know which group each student is in to collect the ratings

An assessor who is unaware of group membership cannot unintentionally influence the ratings, so the researcher's expectations are removed from data collection. The other options would increase researcher or participant expectations.
psych12a3-vre-20

Two groups of students use different study methods to prepare for a test. The group using the new method had higher prior marks, and students were not randomly allocated to groups. Which is the main threat to internal validity?
The group differences may reflect prior ability rather than the study method
The sample was too small to represent all students
The test was marked by only one teacher
The results were not published in a peer-reviewed journal

Pre-existing differences in ability act as a confounding variable that could produce the result without the study method having any effect. The other options concern generalisation, marking or publication rather than whether the independent variable caused the change.
psych12a3-vre-21
Which statement about reliability and validity is correct?
Validity is necessary for reliability, but a valid measure need not be consistent
Reliability and validity are the same concept described in different terms
A valid measure must also be reliable, but a reliable measure may still be invalid
A measure can be valid whenever the sample is large, even when its results vary widely

A measure that accurately measures its construct must give consistent results, but consistency alone does not show that it measures the right thing. The other statements reverse the relationship or confuse the two terms.
psych12a3-vre-22
A researcher wants to check the accuracy of a new heart rate monitor. Which action would best assess its accuracy?
Measure one participant's heart rate ten times and calculate the range
Compare the monitor's readings with those from a criterion (gold-standard) device on the same participants
Ask participants to rate how accurate they think the monitor is
Increase the sample to 500 participants to reduce error

Accuracy is checked by comparing measurements with a known or criterion standard. Repeating measures on one person assesses consistency (reliability), while participant opinion or sample size cannot establish accuracy.
psych12a3-vre-23
A survey asks people how often they exercise. Many respondents report exercising more than they actually do because they want to appear healthy. This is an example of
random error
an investigator effect
social desirability bias
a confounding variable
Social desirability bias is the tendency to answer in ways that make the respondent look favourable to others. It reduces the validity of self-reported data.
psych12a3-vre-24
Before a main experiment, a researcher runs a small trial to check whether the instructions are clear and the timing of tasks works properly. What is the main purpose of this trial?
To replace the need for a control group
To increase external validity by testing a large sample
To prove the hypothesis is correct
To identify and fix problems in the procedure before the full study

A pilot study tests the procedure, materials and timing so that problems can be corrected before the main study, which improves its reliability and validity. It does not prove a hypothesis or replace controls.
psych12a3-vre-25
Which action would most reduce the effect of a confounding variable in an experiment?
Standardising procedures so that all participants experience the same conditions apart from the independent variable
Increasing the number of trials each participant completes
Making the instructions deliberately vague
Telling participants the aim of the study before they begin

Holding extraneous variables constant means they cannot vary with the independent variable, so they cannot offer an alternative explanation. Increasing trials mainly reduces random error, while vague instructions and disclosing the aim add error and bias.
psych12a3-vre-26
A researcher observes children's play through a one-way mirror, so the children do not know they are being watched. Which threat to validity is this procedure most likely to reduce?
The investigator effect caused by researcher expectations
Participants changing their behaviour because they know they are being observed
Disagreement between observers recording the same behaviour
Random error in the timing of events

Knowing they are being watched can make children act differently, so the observations may not reflect natural behaviour, and a one-way mirror reduces this. The other options describe researcher influence, observer agreement or timing error, which this procedure does not address directly.
psych12a3-vre-27
Explain what is meant by the reliability of a psychological test. (2 marks)
Reliability is the extent to which a test gives consistent results [1]; a reliable test produces similar scores when the same participants are tested again under the same conditions [1].
psych12a3-vre-28
Define a confounding variable. (1 mark)
A variable other than the independent variable that changes systematically with it and may affect the dependent variable, so it provides an alternative explanation for the results [1].
psych12a3-vre-29
Identify the type of validity that is threatened when results from a study of adults cannot be applied to children. (1 mark)
External validity (generalisability) [1].
psych12a3-vre-30
Explain how a pilot study can improve the reliability of a main experiment. (3 marks)

A pilot study tests the procedures, instructions and equipment with a small group before the main study [1]; problems such as unclear instructions or inconsistent timing are identified and corrected [1]; this leads to standardised procedures that produce more consistent results across all participants [1].
psych12a3-vre-31
Explain how standardising instructions and procedures improves the reliability of an experiment. (2 marks)

Standardised procedures mean all participants experience the same conditions, reducing variation caused by differences in instructions or handling [1]; this produces more consistent results that can be repeated [1].
psych12a3-vre-32

A digital thermometer is used to measure a water bath whose true temperature is 37.0 °C. Four readings are 37.8 °C, 37.6 °C, 37.7 °C and 37.5 °C. Calculate the mean reading, state the mean error, and identify the type of error present and what it affects. (4 marks)

Mean reading = 150.6 ÷ 4 = 37.65 °C [1]; mean error = 37.65 − 37.0 = +0.65 °C, so the thermometer reads too high [1]; this consistent offset in one direction is systematic error, which affects accuracy [1]; the small spread of readings (37.5–37.8 °C) shows low random error, so the thermometer is precise [1].
psych12a3-vre-33
A researcher uses a questionnaire to measure stress, but several questions are worded in a confusing way. Explain how this could affect the questionnaire's reliability and validity. (3 marks)

Confusing wording means participants may interpret questions differently, producing inconsistent answers [1]; this lowers the reliability of the questionnaire [1]; responses may reflect confusion about the wording rather than stress, which lowers validity [1].
psych12a3-vre-34
State the difference between the accuracy and the precision of a measurement. (2 marks)
Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value [1]; precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other, showing consistency [1].
vce-psych12-vr-c1
A set of scales always reads 2 kg too high. Its measurements are:
Accurate but not reliable, because of a random error
Affected only by random error, which averaging will remove
Reliable (consistent) but not accurate, because of a systematic error
Both accurate and valid, because the error is always the same
Consistency means reliability; the constant offset is a systematic error that repetition cannot remove.
vce-psych12-challenge: Compare Piaget's pre-operational and concrete operational stages, using conservation as an example.

Pre-operational (about 2–7): thinking is egocentric and focused on appearance, so a child thinks a tall thin glass holds more juice. Concrete operational (about 7–11): children can conserve, understanding that quantity stays the same, and can think logically about concrete situations.
Give an age range, a key feature and an example for each stage.
Which ethical guideline was most clearly undermined in Milgram's original obedience study?
Debriefing, because participants were never told anything
Voluntary participation, because participants were forced to attend
Withdrawal rights, because the experimenter used prods to make participants continue
Participants were told 'you have no other choice, you must go on', which pressured them not to withdraw. They were also deceived.
A 72-year-old reflects on her life and feels it had meaning and purpose. In Erikson's theory she has resolved the crisis of:
The final stage involves looking back on life with acceptance (integrity) or regret (despair).
A student who believes cheating is wrong cheats on a test. Explain how cognitive dissonance might change the student's attitude.

The conflict between the belief and the behaviour causes discomfort. Because the behaviour cannot be undone, the student may change the belief (for example, 'everyone cheats; it isn't a big deal') to reduce the dissonance.
Name the conflicting cognitions and the way the dissonance is reduced.
A person who believes a new diet works notices only the days they lose weight and forgets the days they gain. This shows:
Confirmation bias is seeking or remembering information that supports an existing belief.
You see a circle with a small gap as a complete circle. This is the Gestalt principle of:
Closure is the tendency to fill gaps to perceive whole objects.
Harlow's studies with infant rhesus monkeys showed that:
Contact comfort was more important than food in forming attachment
Food was the main basis of attachment
Monkeys formed no attachment to surrogate mothers
Wire surrogates were preferred for comfort
Infants clung to the soft cloth surrogate, especially when frightened, even when the wire surrogate provided milk.
Use the biopsychosocial approach to explain why an adolescent might take part in risky driving.

Biological: the prefrontal cortex is still developing, while reward systems are highly active. Psychological: optimism bias ('it won't happen to me') and sensation-seeking. Social: peer pressure and wanting approval from friends in the car.
Give at least one specific factor from each domain and explain how it contributes.
Which neuroimaging technique would give the most detailed image of a small brain tumour's structure?
MRI produces high-resolution structural images. PET and fMRI show function; EEG records electrical activity.
A researcher is unsure whether the order of conditions affected results in a within-subjects study. The best fix for future studies is:
Counterbalancing spreads practice and fatigue effects evenly across conditions.

X.title: A skateboarding accident and the adolescent brain
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: Jordan, aged 16, fell from his skateboard without a helmet and injured the front of his brain (his frontal lobe).

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Describe two functions of the frontal lobe that could be affected by Jordan's injury.
pieces.answer: Any two: planning, decision-making and problem-solving; controlling emotions and personality; voluntary movement (primary motor cortex); producing speech (Broca's area, usually in the left hemisphere).

steps.working: First function, for example: higher-order thinking such as planning, problem-solving and decision-making.
Second function, for example: initiating voluntary movement (primary motor cortex) or producing speech (Broca's area).

pieces.mistake: Naming functions of other lobes, such as vision (occipital) or hearing (temporal).

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Explain why Jordan's injury is classified as an acquired brain injury.
pieces.answer: It is brain damage that happened after birth, caused here by an external force (a blow to the head), rather than being present from birth or genetic.

steps.working: An acquired brain injury is damage to the brain that occurs after birth; Jordan's was caused by a blow to the head.

pieces.mistake: Saying it is acquired because it is permanent. 'Acquired' refers to when and how it happened, not how long it lasts.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Explain how neuroplasticity could help Jordan recover some of his abilities.
pieces.answer: Undamaged neurons can grow new branches and form new connections (sprouting) and take over functions of damaged areas (rerouting). Adolescent brains are especially plastic, which helps recovery.

steps.working: Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to change its structure in response to experience or injury.
Undamaged neurons form new connections (sprouting and rerouting) so other areas can take over some functions of the damaged area.

pieces.mistake: Saying damaged neurons regrow. Recovery mostly comes from healthy neurons forming new connections.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Jordan's friends often take risks on their skateboards. Explain why risk-taking is common in adolescence, referring to brain development.
pieces.answer: The prefrontal cortex, which controls planning, judgement and impulse control, is not fully developed until the mid-20s. The amygdala, involved in emotional responses, matures earlier, so emotions and rewards can outweigh rational judgement, leading to impulsive risk-taking.

steps.working: The prefrontal cortex, which supports judgement and impulse control, is still developing in adolescence.
The amygdala matures earlier, so emotional and reward-driven responses are more influential than rational control, which encourages risk-taking.

pieces.mistake: Saying the adolescent brain is simply smaller or 'less developed' overall. The point is the timing: emotional areas mature before the prefrontal cortex.

pieces.text: A researcher compares the reaction times of 20 adolescents who have recently had a concussion with those of 20 adolescents who have not, using a computer task.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Identify the type of investigation and justify your answer.
pieces.answer: A correlational study, because the researcher does not manipulate whether participants have had a concussion; they compare groups that already exist.

steps.working: Correlational study: the variable (having had a concussion) is not manipulated by the researcher; existing groups are compared.

pieces.mistake: Calling it a controlled experiment. In an experiment the researcher allocates participants to conditions, which is impossible (and unethical) for concussion.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Identify one ethical guideline the researcher must follow, and explain how it applies to this study.
pieces.answer: For example, informed consent: the participants are under 18, so a parent or guardian must give informed consent after the procedure and risks are explained. (Confidentiality or withdrawal rights are also acceptable with a suitable explanation.)

steps.working: Names a relevant ethical guideline, such as informed consent, confidentiality or withdrawal rights.
Applies it to this study, for example: because participants are under 18, a parent or guardian must give informed consent.

pieces.mistake: Naming a guideline without linking it to the study. Say what the researcher must actually do here.

X.title: First day at a new school
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: Sam is starting at a new school. In the first class, Sam sees another student, Alex, arrive ten minutes late.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Sam decides that Alex is lazy. State whether this is a dispositional or a situational attribution, and name the error Sam may be making.
pieces.answer: A dispositional attribution. Sam may be making the fundamental attribution error: overestimating personal factors and underestimating situational ones (for example, Alex's bus may have been late).

steps.working: Dispositional (internal) attribution: Sam explains the behaviour by Alex's personality.
This may be the fundamental attribution error, overestimating personal causes and underestimating the situation, such as a late bus.

pieces.mistake: Calling it situational. Laziness is a personal trait, so this is a dispositional attribution.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Explain how a stereotype could affect Sam's first impressions of other students.
pieces.answer: A stereotype is a generalised belief about the characteristics of members of a group. Sam may assume a student has certain traits just because of a group they belong to, instead of judging them as an individual.

steps.working: A stereotype is a generalised belief that all members of a group share the same characteristics.
Sam may assume a new student has those characteristics because of their group (for example, assuming a sporty student is not studious), rather than getting to know them.

pieces.mistake: Treating a stereotype as the same as prejudice. A stereotype is a belief; prejudice is a (usually negative) attitude.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: At lunch, everyone in Sam's new friendship group wears their jumper tied around their waist, and Sam starts doing the same. Identify the type of social influence, and one factor in this situation that increases it.
pieces.answer: Conformity. One factor: unanimity, because every member of the group behaves the same way. (Normative influence, the wish to be accepted by the group, is also acceptable.)

steps.working: Conformity: changing behaviour to match a group.
A factor that increases it here, such as unanimity (all members do the same thing) or normative influence (Sam wants to fit in).

pieces.mistake: Calling it obedience. Obedience follows an instruction from an authority figure; nobody told Sam to do this.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Sam reads a canteen sign with a smudged letter: 'Pl_ase return your trays'. Explain how top-down processing helps Sam read it.
pieces.answer: Top-down processing uses past experience, knowledge and context to interpret sensory information. Sam knows the word 'please' and the context of a canteen sign, so fills in the missing letter and reads 'Please'.

steps.working: Top-down processing interprets information using prior knowledge, past experience and expectations.
Sam's knowledge of English words and the context of the sign lets Sam fill the gap and read 'Please return your trays'.

pieces.mistake: Describing bottom-up processing. Bottom-up processing starts from the raw sensory features, which here are incomplete.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: After hearing a friend's vivid story about getting lost in the school's buildings, Sam thinks it is very likely that Sam will get lost too. Name the heuristic Sam is using, and explain one risk of using it.
pieces.answer: The availability heuristic: judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. A vivid, recent story is easy to recall, so Sam may overestimate the chance of getting lost and make a poor decision.

steps.working: Availability heuristic: judging the likelihood of an event by how easily examples come to mind.
Risk: memorable or recent examples make an event seem more likely than it is, so Sam's judgement may be inaccurate.

pieces.mistake: Naming the anchoring heuristic. Anchoring relies too much on the first piece of information given, not on how easily examples come to mind.

X.title: Attachment, thinking and identity
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: In Harlow's experiments, infant rhesus monkeys were raised with two artificial 'mothers': one made of wire that held a feeding bottle, and one covered in soft cloth that gave no food.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Describe the main finding of Harlow's experiments and what it suggests about attachment.
pieces.answer: The infants spent most of their time clinging to the cloth mother, going to the wire mother only to feed, and ran to the cloth mother when frightened. Contact comfort, not food, is central to attachment.

steps.working: Finding: the infants preferred the cloth mother, especially when frightened, and visited the wire mother only to feed.
Conclusion: comfort and security from contact matter more for attachment than feeding.

pieces.mistake: Saying the monkeys preferred whichever mother fed them. Feeding was not the basis of attachment.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Identify one ethical concern with Harlow's experiments.
pieces.answer: The infant monkeys suffered lasting psychological harm from being separated from their real mothers.

steps.working: The animals experienced significant psychological distress and long-term harm, raising concerns about animal welfare.

pieces.mistake: Mentioning informed consent. Animals cannot consent; the concern is harm to the animals.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: A 4-year-old says a tall, thin glass holds more juice than a short, wide glass, even after watching the same amount poured into each. Identify Piaget's stage and the concept the child lacks.
pieces.answer: The preoperational stage; the child lacks conservation.

steps.working: Stage: preoperational (about 2 to 7 years).
The child lacks conservation: understanding that quantity stays the same when its appearance changes.

pieces.mistake: Naming object permanence, which develops in the sensorimotor stage.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Describe Erikson's psychosocial stage for adolescence.
pieces.answer: Identity versus role confusion: adolescents explore roles, values and beliefs to form a stable sense of self; failure can leave them unsure of who they are.

steps.working: Stage: identity versus role confusion (about 12 to 18 years).
Adolescents explore roles and values; success gives a clear identity, while failure leads to confusion about who they are and where they belong.

pieces.mistake: Naming intimacy versus isolation, which is Erikson's stage for young adulthood.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Use the biopsychosocial approach to explain a child's shyness.
pieces.answer: Biological: an inherited temperament. Psychological: learned beliefs or low self-esteem. Social: few chances to mix with peers or family modelling. These factors interact.

steps.working: Names at least two levels, for example a biological factor (inherited temperament) and a psychological one (low confidence).
Includes a social factor (such as family or peer experiences) and explains that the factors interact.

pieces.mistake: Choosing only nature or only nurture. The approach combines biological, psychological and social factors.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Name one approach to deciding whether a behaviour is typical or atypical.
pieces.answer: For example: statistical rarity, social norms, cultural perspective, personal distress or maladaptive behaviour.

steps.working: One approach, such as statistical rarity or social norms, with a brief description.

pieces.mistake: Saying atypical simply means abnormal or wrong. Psychology uses specific criteria.

X.title: Seeing and tasting
X.source: Original question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: Visual perception begins when light enters the eye.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Describe the processes of reception, transduction and transmission in the visual system.
pieces.answer: Reception: light is focused onto the retina. Transduction: photoreceptors (rods and cones) convert light into neural impulses. Transmission: impulses travel along the optic nerve to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe.

steps.working: Reception: the eye detects light, which is focused onto the retina.
Transduction: rods and cones convert light energy into electrochemical neural impulses.
Transmission: the impulses travel along the optic nerve to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.

pieces.mistake: Sending visual information to the temporal lobe. The primary visual cortex is in the occipital lobe.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: In the Müller-Lyer illusion, two equal lines look different in length. Give one explanation.
pieces.answer: We interpret the fins as depth cues: the line with outward fins looks like a far corner, so the brain assumes it is further away and perceives it as longer (misapplied size constancy).

steps.working: The fins act like perspective cues, making one line look like a near corner and the other like a far corner.
Applying size constancy, the brain judges the 'further' line to be longer, so the lines look unequal.

pieces.mistake: Saying the eyes are faulty. Illusions come from how the brain interprets sensory information.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Explain retinal disparity as a depth cue.
pieces.answer: Each eye receives a slightly different image; the brain compares them, and the greater the difference, the closer the object is judged to be.

steps.working: Because the eyes are a few centimetres apart, each retina receives a slightly different image.
The brain combines the images; a greater difference means the object is closer.

pieces.mistake: Calling it a monocular cue. It needs both eyes, so it is binocular.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Define the Gestalt principle of closure.
pieces.answer: The tendency to perceive incomplete figures as complete by mentally filling in the gaps.

steps.working: We perceive incomplete shapes as complete, filling in missing parts.

pieces.mistake: Confusing closure with proximity (grouping objects that are close together).

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Explain why food tastes bland when you have a blocked nose.
pieces.answer: Flavour combines taste with smell. When olfaction is blocked, the brain receives much less information, so flavour seems weak even though taste receptors still work.

steps.working: Flavour depends on combining gustatory (taste) and olfactory (smell) information.
A blocked nose reduces olfactory input, so the perceived flavour is weaker.

pieces.mistake: Saying the taste buds stop working. Taste receptors still work; the loss of smell reduces flavour.

X.title: Challenge: a risky decision at sixteen
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: Jess, 16, is at a party where her friends are jumping from a roof into a pool. She feels anxious but jumps anyway. Later she says, 'I knew it was dangerous, but everyone else was doing it and I didn't think I would get hurt.' Jess's older brother had a similar accident last year.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Explain how the development of Jess's brain could have contributed to her decision.
pieces.answer: Her amygdala and reward systems are well developed, so emotion and the desire for social reward are strong, but her prefrontal cortex, which supports judgement and impulse control, is not fully mature.

steps.working: The emotional and reward regions develop earlier and drive the impulse.
The prefrontal cortex, responsible for planning and judgement, is still developing.

pieces.mistake: Saying the teenage brain is simply 'not finished' without naming regions and roles.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Identify one biological, one psychological and one social factor in this scenario.
pieces.answer: Biological: immature prefrontal cortex (or adrenaline). Psychological: optimism bias, 'I didn't think I would get hurt'. Social: peer influence, 'everyone else was doing it'.

steps.working: A correct biological factor.
A correct psychological factor.
A correct social factor.

pieces.mistake: Placing peer pressure under psychological factors.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Explain Jess's behaviour in terms of normative influence.
pieces.answer: Normative influence is conforming to gain acceptance or avoid rejection. Jess jumps, despite her anxiety, to fit in with her friends.

steps.working: Defines normative influence: conforming to be liked or accepted.
Links it to Jess jumping despite her doubts.

pieces.mistake: Confusing it with informational influence, which is conforming because others seem to know more.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Jess knew her brother had been hurt, but still thought she wouldn't be. Name and explain this bias.
pieces.answer: Optimism bias: believing we are less likely than others to experience negative events.

steps.working: Names optimism bias.
Explains it using the scenario.

pieces.mistake: Calling it the availability heuristic. Her brother's accident should have made the risk feel more likely, not less.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Explain why adolescence is described as a period of significant neuroplasticity.
pieces.answer: Synaptic pruning removes unused connections and myelination increases, so experiences strongly shape which neural pathways are strengthened.

steps.working: Refers to pruning or myelination and experience shaping the brain.

pieces.mistake: Saying new neurons are mainly formed in adolescence.

X.title: Challenge: does context change what we see?
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of a Units 1 & 2 end-of-semester exam

pieces.text: Forty Year 11 students were randomly allocated to two groups. Group 1 saw an ambiguous figure that could be read as 'B' or '13', placed in the sequence A ? C. Group 2 saw the same figure in the sequence 12 ? 14. Each participant wrote what they saw.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Identify the independent and dependent variables.
pieces.answer: IV: the context of the figure (letters or numbers). DV: what the participant reported seeing (B or 13).

steps.working: Correct IV.
Correct DV.

pieces.mistake: Naming the ambiguous figure itself as the IV. It is the same in both conditions.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Calculate the percentage of each group that reported the response matching its context, and explain the results.
pieces.answer: Group 1: 85% reported B; Group 2: 80% reported 13. Context created a perceptual set, so participants used top-down processing to interpret the same sensory input differently.

steps.working: Identifies top-down processing or perceptual set.
Explains that identical sensations were interpreted according to context.

pieces.mistake: Explaining the results with bottom-up processing. The visual features were identical.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Name the experimental design and state one limitation of it here.
pieces.answer: Between-subjects (independent groups). Participant differences (for example, reading habits or maths interest) may differ between groups, although random allocation reduces this.

steps.working: Between-subjects design.
A valid limitation.

pieces.mistake: Calling it within-subjects.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Distinguish between sensation and perception in this task.
pieces.answer: Sensation: light from the figure is received and transduced by photoreceptors and transmitted to the brain (the same for both groups). Perception: the brain organises and interprets it as B or 13.

steps.working: Sensation described as receiving and transducing the stimulus.
Perception described as interpreting it, which differed by context.

pieces.mistake: Saying the groups had different sensations.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Give one reason the conclusion may not generalise to all people.
pieces.answer: The sample was 40 Year 11 students, likely from one school, so it may not represent other ages or cultures.

steps.working: Refers to sample size or representativeness.

pieces.mistake: Saying the results were wrong.
